findings.title: privacy.html never mentions the game, and game.html never links to privacy — yet the game stores player-typed nicknames and free-text notes
findings.evidence:
privacy.html:41 frames the whole page as "what happens to your voice". privacy.html:44 states: "No account, no name, no email, no tracking pixels." privacy.html:53 lists third parties as Google (Gemini), Vercel, Supabase only. Nothing on the page mentions the game.

But game.html:85 is `<input type="text" id="nickname" placeholder="nickname for the board" maxlength="20">`, and api/scores.js:104-107 takes that string and api/scores.js:130-137 INSERTs it into Supabase `scores` (schema: supabase/schema.sql, `nickname text not null`, no TTL). api/scores.js:61 then serves it back to everyone via GET /api/scores. api/clip-report.js:81 stores `note: clean(b.note, 240)` — free text a player types into game.html:153 `<input id="flagNote" placeholder="anything else? (optional)">`.

game.html's footer (line 161) reads "clips stream from their public archives · credits shown after each round" — there is no privacy link anywhere on the page. index.html links privacy twice (line 156, line 171); game.html links it zero times.
findings.userImpact: A player types their real first name (or Instagram handle) into the nickname box because it says "nickname for the board", and it is published on a public leaderboard and stored indefinitely in Supabase. The page collecting it offers no link to any privacy policy, and the policy that does exist affirmatively says "no account, no name" and describes only the voice-analysis flow. Someone who later wants that name removed has no route: the only deletion instruction on privacy.html:50 is for donated audio clips.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a privacy link to game.html's footer next to the existing text, and add a short section to privacy.html covering the leaderboard (nickname is public and stored, no way to tie it to you, how to ask for removal) and clip reports (the optional note is stored). One paragraph each.

findings.title: YouTube embeds ship on most game decks but privacy.html says "no tracking pixels" and never lists YouTube
findings.evidence:
js/media.js:35 injects `s.src = 'https://www.youtube.com/iframe_api'` and js/media.js:45 constructs `new window.YT.Player(...)`, which mounts an iframe on `www.youtube.com` (not `youtube-nocookie.com`). Counting js/clips.js: 44 of 155 clips are `kind: 'yt'` — English deck 13 of 22, Hindi–Urdu 9 of 13, French 6 of 13, Chinese 5 of 12, German 3 of 3, Spanish 4 of 14, Portuguese 4 of 12. Only Arabic (40/40) and World Languages (26/26) are fully local mp3.

privacy.html:44 claims "no tracking pixels"; privacy.html:53 lists third parties as Google (Gemini), Vercel, Supabase. YouTube is absent. So are three other origins the pages contact on every load: fonts.googleapis.com / fonts.gstatic.com (index.html:22, game.html:22), unpkg.com (index.html:23/173, game.html:23/168), and basemaps.cartocdn.com (js/theme.js:11).
findings.userImpact: A player picks the English deck, hits play, and a `www.youtube.com` iframe loads — setting YouTube/Google cookies and attributing a view to their signed-in Google account. They were told on the linked privacy page that there are no tracking pixels and that only Gemini, Vercel and Supabase are involved. No consent prompt exists. For a public launch with EU/UK traffic this is the claim most likely to be wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Two things: switch the player host to `youtube-nocookie.com` (YT.Player accepts `host: 'https://www.youtube-nocookie.com'` in its options), and extend privacy.html:53 to name YouTube, Google Fonts, unpkg and CARTO as origins that receive the user's IP when a page loads.

findings.title: Leaflet is loaded from unpkg.com with no fallback and no guard — if it doesn't load, both pages render fully but every control is dead
findings.evidence:
index.html:173 and game.html:168 load `https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.js` as a plain classic script with no SRI, no fallback, no `onerror`.

js/app.js:79 calls `map = L.map('map', {...})` unguarded, from `initMap()` which is invoked at top level on js/app.js:1307, immediately before `bindUI()` on line 1308. js/game.js:43 does the same, invoked at js/game.js:788, immediately before `renderModeCards()` on line 789.

If `L` is undefined, `L.map(...)` throws a ReferenceError, which aborts the remainder of the classic script — verified: `node -e "L.map('x'); console.log('AFTER-RAN')"` throws and never prints. So `bindUI()` and `renderModeCards()` never run.

sw.js:40 makes this permanent for installed users: `if (url.origin !== self.location.origin) return;` — cross-origin requests are deliberately never cached, while all of index.html, game.html, style.css and every local js file ARE cached (sw.js:9-23).
findings.userImpact: Two real paths. (1) A visitor on a school/corporate network or in a region where unpkg.com is blocked or slow: index.html paints the full card, headline and mic button from local cached CSS, and tapping the mic does nothing — no error, no message. game.html paints "Hear it. Pin where it's from." over a completely empty deck grid. (2) The installed PWA opened offline (which is the entire reason sw.js exists): the shell loads from cache, Leaflet cannot, and the app is inert in exactly the same way. Either way it looks like the app is broken rather than the network.
findings.suggestedFix: Self-host leaflet.js/leaflet.css under /js and /css and add them to sw.js's SHELL — that fixes both the blocked-CDN and the offline case at once, and removes a third-party origin from the privacy surface. If keeping the CDN, at minimum wrap initMap() in a try/catch that shows a real "couldn't load the map, check your connection" message instead of dying silently.

findings.title: hometongue.me/game and /privacy 404 to a bare plain-text Vercel error page; there is no custom 404
findings.evidence:
Verified live:
  GET https://www.hometongue.me/game     -> 404
  GET https://www.hometongue.me/privacy  -> 404
  GET https://www.hometongue.me/Game.html -> 404 (paths are case-sensitive)
Body of the 404, in full: `The page could not be found\n\nNOT_FOUND\n\nyul1::5r9fv-1786703603459-972abea72da5`, served as `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`, 79 bytes.

vercel.json contains only a `functions` block — no `cleanUrls`, no `rewrites`. There is no 404.html at the repo root.

(The apex/www story is fine: hometongue.me 308s to www.hometongue.me preserving both path and query, http 308s to https, HSTS is set. og:url on index.html:12 and game.html:12 correctly point at the www host.)
findings.userImpact: The launch is on TikTok, where URLs get spoken aloud and typed by hand. Someone hears or reads "hometongue.me slash game" and lands on a page of monospace error text with a Vercel request ID and no link back to the site — it reads as the whole site being down, not as a typo. Same for anyone typing /privacy after seeing "privacy" in the footer.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `"cleanUrls": true` to vercel.json (makes /game and /privacy work and 308s the .html forms to the clean ones), and add a 404.html at the repo root with the site's header and a link home — Vercel serves it automatically for static deployments.

findings.title: "Nope" corrections are silently thrown away for 64 of the 79 countries in the picker, and the user is told they were logged
findings.evidence:
js/app.js:1247-1250 (`fillCountryPicker`) fills `#fbActual` from every key in `COUNTRIES`. js/places.js:9 defines 79 of them: eg, sd, sy, lb, jo, ps, iq, sa, kw, ae, ye, ly, tn, dz, ma, **es, mx, ar, uy, cl, co, ve, pe, bo, ec, py, cu, do, pr, gt, cr, fr, ca, be, ch, sn, ci, cd, cm, ht, br, pt, ao, mz, cv, gw, st, tl, ru, ua, by, kz, kg, uz, ge, am, md, lv, ee, il, in, pk, cn, tw, hk, sg, my, us, gb, ie, au, nz, za, ng, gh, ke, na, jm, tt**.

api/feedback.js:9: `const VALID_CODES = new Set(['eg','sd','sy','lb','jo','ps','iq','sa','kw','ae','ye','ly','tn','dz','ma','msa','weak','dialect','unclear','']);` — 15 real country codes, all Arab.

api/feedback.js:122: `actual_code: VALID_CODES.has(b.actual_code) ? b.actual_code : null`. For 'fr', 'us', 'in', 'br', 'cn' etc. this is `false`, so the correction is stored as `null`.

Compounding it: api/feedback.js:134-137 puts `guess_city` and `actual_city` inside `if (consent)`, so a user who corrects but doesn't donate stores neither. The surviving row is `{correct: false, region, confidence, source, platform}` — "someone said we were wrong", with no record of where they were actually from.

Meanwhile js/app.js:1190-1193 fires the toast "Logged. This is exactly how it learns." before the response comes back, unconditionally.
findings.userImpact: A French, American, Indian or Brazilian user — i.e. almost everyone the TikTok launch reaches, since the product now advertises "any language" (index.html:9, index.html:45) — gets a wrong guess, presses "nope", picks their country from the dropdown, presses send, and reads "Logged. This is exactly how it learns." The country they picked is discarded at the API boundary. The correction data this feature exists to collect is only actually collected for Arab countries.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the hardcoded VALID_CODES set with a check against the same country list the client uses (or a plain `/^[a-z]{2}$/` test plus the four special values). Also move `actual_city`/`guess_city` out of the `if (consent)` block or accept that non-donors contribute nothing but a boolean.

findings.title: game.html's meta description promises "Nine decks" — only eight are playable
findings.evidence: game.html:9: `` — this is the text Google shows under the result and what some link-preview tools fall back to. js/game.js:6 sets `MIN_DECK = 10`, and js/game.js:129 `playableModes()` filters `MODES` to decks with at least that many clips. Counting js/clips.js: arabic 40, accents 22, languages 26, spanish 14, french 13, hindi-urdu 13, chinese 12, portuguese 12 — and **italian 0, german 3**. So `renderModeCards()` (js/game.js:626) renders exactly 8 tiles, and the live counter at js/game.js:647-650 correctly writes "eight decks" over the static markup. game.html:45 also still hardcodes `nine decks` as the pre-JS value.
findings.userImpact: Someone finds the game in search or sees a shared link, is told "Nine decks", opens it and counts eight. Small, but it is the one number in the preview and it is wrong — and the code already went to the trouble of computing the real count for the on-page copy (see the comment at js/game.js:644 explaining why the static "nine" was a bug).
findings.suggestedFix: Change the meta description to "Eight decks" (or drop the number: "Real recordings from around the world"), and change the static fallback at game.html:45 to match.

findings.title: privacy.html has no description or share tags and uses a different favicon from the rest of the site
findings.evidence:
privacy.html:7 sets the icon to an inline data-URI SVG of three concentric circles with a red dot — a completely different mark from the map pin at index.html:7 and game.html:7 (`/assets/logo-mark.svg`).

privacy.html's head (lines 3-16) has no `<meta name="description">`, no `og:*` tags and no `twitter:card`, unlike index.html:9-15 and game.html:9-15.
findings.userImpact: Two small things. A user who opens the privacy link from the footer sees the browser tab icon change to an unrelated mark, which reads as having left the site. And pasting the privacy URL anywhere that renders previews (a TikTok bio tool, a Discord mod channel, an app-store style listing that asks for a privacy URL) produces a bare card with a machine-generated snippet instead of a title and description.
findings.suggestedFix: Point privacy.html:7 at `/assets/logo-mark.svg` like the other two pages, and add a description plus the four og tags copied from index.html with the title/url/description swapped.

findings.title: Offline, the privacy link silently serves the home page instead of the policy
findings.evidence:
sw.js:9-23 lists the precached SHELL: '/', '/game.html', the css, six js files, the manifest, icon-192 and the logo. `/privacy.html` is not in it.

sw.js:57-60 is the offline path: on a failed fetch it tries `caches.match(e.request)`, and on a miss returns `caches.match('/')` for anything with `mode === 'navigate'`. A first-time offline visit to /privacy.html misses the cache and therefore renders index.html's bytes at the /privacy.html URL.
findings.userImpact: An installed-PWA user with no signal taps "privacy" in the footer and lands back on the recording screen with /privacy.html still in the address bar. It looks like the link is broken or the policy was removed, rather than like they are offline.
findings.suggestedFix: Add '/privacy.html' to the SHELL array in sw.js and bump VERSION (sw.js:8).

findings.title: No robots.txt, and the internal PRD, eval data and tooling are served from the public domain
findings.evidence:
Verified live against www.hometongue.me:
  /robots.txt          -> 404
  /sitemap.xml         -> 404
  /PRD.md              -> 200, 36,542 bytes, text/markdown
  /docs/PRD.md         -> 200, 6,298 bytes
  /data/candidates.json -> 200, 14,123 bytes
  /tools/eval.mjs      -> 200
  /dev-server.js       -> 200
  /supabase/schema.sql -> 200
No `X-Robots-Tag` header on any of them, and no robots.txt to disallow them.

I checked for credentials in everything that is served — `grep -rnoE "(AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{10,}|eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{30,}|sbp_[a-z0-9]{20,}|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,})" data/ tools/ docs/ PRD.md` returns nothing, no Supabase project URL appears in any served file, and supabase/schema.sql shows RLS enabled with no policies on all four tables. So this is not a credential leak. The repo is also already public on GitHub (github.com/moha-arab/hometongue, `"private": false`), so the content is not newly exposed.
findings.userImpact: The exposure itself is not new, but serving it from the brand domain means Google can index `hometongue.me/PRD.md` under the product's own name. PRD.md:24 states the app's first-priority reason to exist is "Resume... A recruiter goes from link → talked → map flew to their hometown in under 90 seconds", and the file carries the roadmap, accuracy caveats and rejected experiments. A curious viewer poking at the site during a launch surge can read all of it in one click. Confidence is 'likely' rather than certain because whether Google actually indexes text/markdown responses is not something I can verify from here.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a robots.txt disallowing /data/, /tools/, /docs/, *.md and /supabase/, or add a .vercelignore so those directories are never uploaded to the deployment at all (they are only needed locally). A three-URL sitemap.xml is cheap to add at the same time.

findings.title: Starting a game downloads 9.3 MB of audio before round 1 — the "skip big files" guard never fires
findings.evidence:
function warmDeck() {
  for (const clip of deck) {
    if ((clip.size || 0) > 0 && clip.size <= 3_000_000) {
      fetch(clip.url, { mode: 'no-cors' }).catch(() => {});

The comment above it says "big spoken-article files stream fine on demand, so skip them" — but the largest clip on disk is 1,920,989 bytes (1.83 MB), so `size <= 3_000_000` is true for EVERY file clip. Nothing is ever skipped. `warmDeck()` is called unconditionally from `startGame()` (js/game.js:180) and again from `$('#againSame').onclick` (js/game.js:797).

Measured live at http://localhost:8123/game.html — tapped "World Languages", then read performance.getEntriesByType('resource'):
  6 clip requests, 9,269 KB total
  lang-hindi.mp3 1876 KB, lang-hungarian.mp3 1876 KB, lang-hausa.mp3 1876 KB,
  lang-italian.mp3 1764 KB, lang-french.mp3 1876 KB  (all initiatorType "fetch")

Expected bytes per game start, computed from js/clips.js:
  languages   7.60 MB   chinese 4.62 MB   portuguese 4.86 MB
  spanish     4.64 MB   french  4.00 MB   accents    2.71 MB
Against 0.76 MB of audio the player can actually hear (5 rounds x 20 s @ 64 kbps) — a 10x overshoot.

For contrast, the entire HTML/CSS/JS shell of game.html is 68 KB brotli from production. The page is lean; this one function is 136x the weight of everything else combined.
findings.userImpact: A TikTok viewer opens the game on mobile data and taps a deck. Five full-length 1.9 MB files start downloading in parallel, and the round-1 clip the player is waiting on has to share the pipe with four files they may never even reach. On a weak 4G connection (~1.5 Mbps) that is roughly 50 seconds of contention before audio settles, during which tapping play shows "Clip is loading, one sec…" (js/game.js:301). Bandwidth cost is the other half: at 9.3 MB per game start, Vercel's 100 GB Hobby allowance is gone in ~11,000 game starts, and a video that lands does that in an afternoon — at which point the project is throttled and the site is down. On Pro it is ~113,000 starts against the 1 TB included, then $0.15/GB.
findings.suggestedFix: Two independent fixes, either one helps, both together are correct. (a) Only warm the clip for the round about to be played, and warm round N+1 during the reveal screen instead of all five at once. (b) Fetch only the bytes the window needs — `fetch(clip.url, {headers: {Range: `bytes=${startByte}-${endByte}`}})` computed from the CBR bitrate and clip.start — rather than the whole file. Note the `size <= 3_000_000` threshold is dead code either way; if a size guard is kept it needs to be below 1.9 MB to mean anything.

findings.title: 90% of the shipped audio is unreachable by design — clips are 240 s long to play a fixed 20 s window
findings.evidence:
CLIP_WINDOW_S = 20 (js/game.js:8). 65 of the 111 file-backed clips in js/clips.js carry an explicit curated `start`, so `ensureOffset()` (js/game.js:270-280) pins them to exactly one 20-second window — the same 20 seconds for every player, every game, forever.

Those 65 files ship 98.8 MB to deliver 9.9 MB of ever-playable audio. Exactly 10.0x.

ffprobe on the shipped assets:
  clips/languages/lang-swahili.mp3 -> duration=240.000000, bit_rate=64032, 22050 Hz mono, 1,920,989 bytes
  46 of the 138 files on disk are exactly 240.000000 s.

For the 46 clips WITHOUT a curated start, ensureOffset picks `Math.min(15 + Math.random() * dur * 0.4, dur - 30)`. For a 240 s file that caps the offset at 111 s, so the window can never extend past 131 s — the final 109 s (45%) of every one of those files is unreachable by any player on any roll.

A 20 s window at the same 64 kbps mono encoding is 160 KB. The files shipped to deliver it are 1,876 KB.
findings.userImpact: This is what makes the prefetch above cost 9.3 MB instead of 800 KB, and it makes every clip slow even if the prefetch is fixed: a player who taps a deck on a phone waits on a 1.9 MB download to hear 20 seconds. It also inflates the deployment: 111 MB of the 140 MB in clips/ is referenced, but only ~11 MB of that is audio anyone can ever hear.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-encode the 65 curated clips down to just their window plus a small margin (say start-2 s to start+24 s) — 98.8 MB becomes ~13 MB with zero change to what any player hears. For the 46 random-offset clips, either trim to the reachable 0-131 s region or drop the random offset and curate them too. Both are offline batch jobs in tools/; clips.js `size` and `start` fields need regenerating alongside.

findings.title: Leaflet is loaded from unpkg.com with no fallback, and it is the first thing both pages call — a CDN blip leaves dead pages
findings.evidence:
<script src="https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.js"></script>  — no defer, no integrity hash, no local fallback.

`initMap()` is the FIRST top-level statement executed in both entry scripts:
  js/app.js:1307   initMap();  then bindUI();
  js/game.js:788   initMap();  then renderModeCards(); then every $('#…').onclick = … binding
and initMap's second line is `map = L.map('map', {…})` (js/app.js:79, js/game.js:43). If unpkg does not deliver, `L` is undefined, the ReferenceError propagates out of initMap uncaught, and the rest of the top-level script never runs.

Concretely that means: on index.html `bindUI()` never runs, so the mic button is inert — the page looks completely normal and does nothing. On game.html `renderModeCards()` never runs, so the deck picker is an empty card and none of the eight buttons exist.

The service worker cannot cover this: sw.js:39 is `if (url.origin !== self.location.origin) return;`, so leaflet is never cached, on any visit.

Separately, unpkg is on the first-paint critical path with no connection warmup. Measured in-page on index.html, `renderBlockingStatus === 'blocking'` for exactly three resources: the Google Fonts CSS, https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.css, and /css/style.css. index.html:20-21 preconnects fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com but there is no preconnect for unpkg.com, so that render-blocking stylesheet pays a cold DNS + TCP + TLS handshake before any pixel is painted.
findings.userImpact: Anyone arriving from TikTok while unpkg is having a bad minute gets a page that renders its text and branding perfectly and then does absolutely nothing — the mic does not respond, the deck list is blank. There is no error, no retry, nothing to suggest reloading. Separately, on every normal load, first paint on mobile waits an extra handshake to a third-party host that was never preconnected.
findings.suggestedFix: Vendor leaflet.js and leaflet.css into the repo (they are 42 KB and 3.5 KB brotli) and serve them same-origin — that removes the outage risk, removes the un-preconnected origin from the critical path, and lets sw.js cache them like the rest of the shell. If keeping the CDN, at minimum add `<link rel="preconnect" href="https://unpkg.com" crossorigin>` and wrap the `initMap()` calls so a missing `L` still lets bindUI/renderModeCards run.

findings.title: Service worker is network-first with no timeout, so a stalled connection blocks the cached copy instead of falling back to it
findings.evidence:
e.respondWith(
    fetch(e.request)
      .then((res) => { … })
      .catch(() => caches.match(e.request).then((hit) => { … })),
  );

There is no AbortController, no Promise.race against a timer, no stale-while-revalidate. The cached fallback is reachable only through `.catch()`, i.e. only once the network request actually rejects. A hanging TCP connection — signal present but no data moving, which is the common mobile failure, not a clean offline — does not reject until the browser's own timeout expires.

The shell this blocks is fully cached: all 13 SHELL entries (sw.js:9-23) return 200 locally, so the offline copy is sitting there ready the whole time.

On the question of whether the SW can pin an old build: it cannot. Network-first means fresh always wins online, and sw.js:53-54 re-`put`s every healthy response into the current cache, so entries self-refresh. That part is sound.
findings.userImpact: A returning player — someone who already opened the site once, so the SW is installed — walks into a subway, an elevator, or a dead-zone with full bars and no throughput, and taps their home-screen icon. They get a white screen for as long as the browser takes to give up, typically tens of seconds, even though a complete working copy of the app is already on their device. The offline fallback that was built for exactly this moment never gets a chance to run.
findings.suggestedFix: Race the network against a short timer and let the cache win when the network is merely slow: `Promise.race([fetch(e.request), new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(rej, 3000))]).catch(() => caches.match(...))`. Keep network-first semantics — this only changes how long a stalled request is allowed to hold the page hostage.

findings.title: vercel.json sets no cache headers, so immutable clip files revalidate on every single use
findings.userImpact: A player who finishes a game and taps "play again" in the same deck hits warmDeck for five more clips. Any clip they already downloaded still costs a conditional GET before the browser will reuse it — five extra round trips before audio is available, which on a 300 ms mobile RTT is a noticeable stall on top of an already slow start. The bytes are saved by the 304; the latency is not.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a headers block for the immutable assets: `{"source": "/clips/(.*)", "headers": [{"key": "Cache-Control", "value": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"}]}`. Do NOT do this for /js/ — js/clips.js is regenerated under the same filename, so it needs the revalidating default unless filenames get content hashes.

findings.title: No .vercelignore: 28 MB of unreferenced audio plus internal working files are deployed and publicly fetchable
findings.evidence:
There is no .vercelignore, and deployment is git-connected (origin https://github.com/moha-arab/hometongue.git, no .vercel dir), so everything git-tracks ships.

Orphan audio — cross-referenced every URL in js/clips.js against clips/ on disk:
  clips.js references 111 urls; 138 mp3s are tracked in git.
  27 files, 28.0 MB, are shipped and referenced by nothing.
  Largest: wild-sarnia-milton-ontario-canada.mp3, wild-texas-hill-country-stonewall-usa.mp3, wild-boston-massachusetts-usa.mp3, wild-the-bronx-new-york-city-usa.mp3, wild-toronto-canada.mp3 (1,876 KB each).
  Nothing is missing in the other direction — 0 referenced clips absent from disk.

Internal files, verified live on production with curl:
  200  36542  https://www.hometongue.me/PRD.md
  200  27285  https://www.hometongue.me/data/eval-notes.md
  200 122667  https://www.hometongue.me/data/clips-backup-pre-localfix.js
  200   3147  https://www.hometongue.me/supabase/schema.sql
  200   2989  https://www.hometongue.me/dev-server.js
(/README.md and /package.json correctly 404 — Vercel excludes those itself.)

I checked supabase/schema.sql before rating this: it is properly locked down (`alter table feedback enable row level security` with no policies, service-role only, private storage bucket), so the schema leak does not open a data path. .env is gitignored and untracked, so it does not ship — production is clean there. The harm here is disclosure of the product plan and internal model-eval notes, not a security hole.
findings.userImpact: Nobody stumbles into this on a normal path — nothing links to these URLs. But a curious visitor who guesses /PRD.md gets the full 36 KB product and business plan, and /data/eval-notes.md gets 27 KB of internal model comparison notes. On a TikTok launch, someone will poke. The 28 MB of orphan audio costs nothing at runtime but bloats every deployment and the repo.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a .vercelignore with PRD.md, docs/, data/, tools/, supabase/, dev-server.js, test-audio/. Separately, either delete the 27 orphan mp3s or wire them into js/clips.js — right now they are paid for and unused.

findings.title: /api/analyze caps how MANY requests a day, not how BIG one is — a stranger can inflate the day's Gemini bill by 100x+
findings.evidence: Type mode has no length cap at all: `const typed = (body.text || '').trim();` (line 372) then `if (typed.length >= 8)` (383) and the raw string is embedded straight into the prompt (386-390). Nothing slices it. The only ceiling is the body reader at 8MB (line 34) / Vercel's 4.5MB platform limit — so ~4MB of text, roughly 1M input tokens, per request. Audio has the same shape of hole: `if (bytes.length > 6 * 1024 * 1024)` (line 378) is a byte cap, not a duration cap — 6MB of Opus at 24kbps is ~33 minutes of audio (~60k tokens) versus the ~25s clip the UI actually produces (~800 tokens). The wallet guard is `DAILY_CAP = Number(process.env.DAILY_ANALYSES || 20000)` (line 285) and `countAnalysis()` (320) inserts ONE row per request regardless of size, so the cap counts invocations. The comment at line 282-284 states the intent: 'a deliberate, known maximum bill instead of an open tab.' The bill is not known, because cost per invocation is unbounded. Verified the endpoint accepts a scripted request at all: `curl -X POST http://localhost:8123/api/analyze -H 'Origin: http://localhost:8123' -d '{}'` returns 422 no_speech (403 without the header), so the only gate is a header a script sets for free.
findings.userImpact: A hostile viewer who sees the TikTok pastes a loop that POSTs 2MB of junk text to /api/analyze. Each request is ~500k input tokens instead of the ~30 a real typed sentence costs. The rate limiter allows 30/hr per IP per serverless instance, so one machine from one IP runs ~30 x 500k = 15M tokens an hour, all night, and Vercel spreading concurrent requests across instances multiplies that. The daily cap still stops it at 20,000 invocations, but 20,000 fat invocations is billions of tokens rather than the ~30M the owner budgeted for. The owner wakes up to a Gemini bill orders of magnitude past what he decided a bad day was allowed to cost, and once the cap trips every real user gets 'HomeTongue has hit its listening limit for today.'
findings.suggestedFix: Cap the text: `const typed = (body.text || '').trim().slice(0, 2000);` — no honest type-mode input is longer. For audio, drop the byte ceiling to what the client actually produces (the UI records ~20-60s; 1.5MB is generous) and/or decode the container to check duration before sending. Better still, make the daily cap count cost rather than calls: store the payload size per row and cap on the sum, so 20,000 really is a known bill.

findings.title: The leaderboard is fully forgeable: tokens are minted free to anyone, are replayable, and the only score check is arithmetic
findings.evidence: Three gates, all satisfiable by a stranger with curl. (1) Free token mint: `if (q.get('start')) return res.end(JSON.stringify({ ok: true, token: mintToken() }));` sits in the GET branch ABOVE any origin check or rate limit — verified: `curl 'http://localhost:8123/api/scores?start=1'` with no Origin header returns a token, three times in a row, instantly. (2) Origin gate is a header: `sameOrigin(req)` (lines 29-33) only compares `req.headers.origin` to the host. (3) The token is never consumed — `tokenAge` (api/feedback.js:39-48) verifies an HMAC over a timestamp and returns the age; there is no nonce, no single-use marker, so ONE token works for every submission inside the 75s-2h window (scores.js:118). Score validation is `sum === points` with per-round caps (lines 122-124) — a perfect run is just five 5000s. Proved non-destructively (deliberate sum mismatch so no row was written): `curl -X POST /api/scores -H 'Origin: http://localhost:8123' -d '{"nickname":"probe","game_type":"arabic","points":24999,"token":"<minted 93s earlier>","rounds":[5x{pts:5000,km:0}]}'` returned `{"ok":false,"error":"invalid_score"}`, while the same request with a junk token returned `invalid_token`. Every gate except the addition was passed.
findings.userImpact: Someone watching the TikTok mints a token, sleeps 75 seconds, then posts 25,000/25,000 forty times an hour under forty different nicknames. The GET board returns best-per-nickname sorted points.desc (lines 68-76), so the top ten is permanently theirs — and the BANNED list (line 16) is a 13-word substring blocklist, so any slur not literally in it lands on the front of the leaderboard. There is no admin UI to delete rows; the owner has to open the Supabase console. Real players who actually earn 18,000 never appear on the board again, which kills the exact loop the launch depends on.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the token single-use and bind it to the game: mint it with a random nonce inside the signed payload, store spent nonces (a Supabase table or the same `usage` table), and reject a replay. Also validate the round IDs against the real deck server-side — `rounds[].id` is currently only `String(r.id).slice(0, 40)` (line 135), never checked against window.CLIPS — and reject a run whose five clip IDs are not five distinct real clips from that deck. Move the ?start=1 mint below sameOrigin() and the rate limiter so it is not a free faucet.

findings.title: The clip-upload consent gate does not do what the code says: any stranger can push arbitrary 2.5MB blobs into the Supabase storage bucket without ever calling /api/analyze
findings.evidence: The comment on line 139 states the guarantee: 'Clip additionally requires a fresh token minted by a real /api/analyze call'. The check is `tokenValid(b.token)` (line 142), which is HMAC-over-timestamp plus age < 30min (lines 50-59). There is zero domain separation — `mintToken()` and `tokenSecret()` (lines 26-35) are shared verbatim with /api/scores, and `api/scores.js:57` hands out an identical token to anyone who GETs `?start=1` with no origin check and no rate limit. So the analyze call is not required at all. Nothing validates that the bytes are audio either: the code trusts the client-declared `b.mime` against the AUDIO_MIME map (line 10) and only checks length, `bytes.length >= 1000 && <= MAX_CLIP_BYTES` (line 144), before POSTing the raw buffer to `${url}/storage/v1/object/clips/${path}` (line 146).
findings.userImpact: A stranger scripts: GET /api/scores?start=1 for a free token, then POST /api/feedback with `Origin` forged, `consent:true`, `mime:'audio/mpeg'`, and 2.5MB of any bytes at all. Twelve per hour per IP per instance (line 23), and serverless instances each keep their own counter. That is arbitrary unauthenticated writes into the owner's private Supabase bucket: storage quota burned, and whatever content they choose to upload is now sitting in the pile the owner intends to publish as a research dataset. It also poisons the donation set with non-audio junk that has to be sifted out by hand.
findings.suggestedFix: Give the token a purpose field inside the signed payload ('analyze' vs 'game') and have tokenValid() require purpose==='analyze', so a game token cannot buy an upload. Sniff the first bytes against the declared container (webm/EBML 0x1A45DFA3, mp4 'ftyp', ID3/mp3 frame sync, OggS, RIFF) and drop anything that does not match. Consider a daily storage cap mirroring DAILY_ANALYSES.

findings.title: GET /api/scores has no origin check, no rate limit and no cache headers — unlimited Supabase reads and Vercel invocations from anyone
findings.evidence: The whole GET branch (lines 53-82) sits above `if (!sameOrigin(req))` (88) and above `rateLimited(ip)` (95), both of which only run on the POST path. Every hit fires `fetch("${url}/rest/v1/scores?select=nickname,points,ts&game_type=eq.${gameType}&order=points.desc,ts.asc&limit=100")` (line 61) — a fresh 100-row Supabase query, uncached (no Cache-Control header is ever set; line 48 sets only Content-Type). Verified: three consecutive `curl 'http://localhost:8123/api/scores?start=1'` with no Origin header all succeeded. The client hits this on every board view and every tab switch (js/game.js:589, js/game.js:761).
findings.userImpact: One person with a laptop runs `while true; do curl https://hometongue.me/api/scores; done`. Each iteration costs one Vercel function invocation and one Supabase query with a 100-row payload. Nothing throttles it. Supabase's egress/compute allowance and Vercel's invocation allowance both drain against an attacker who never loads the site, and when either quota trips the leaderboard (and on Vercel, the whole /api surface, including /api/analyze) goes down for real users mid-launch. Even without malice, a viral spike hits Supabase once per board view instead of serving a cached copy.
findings.suggestedFix: Move the rate limiter above the method split so GET is covered too, and set `res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 's-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=120')` on the leaderboard response — a board that is 30 seconds stale is indistinguishable from live and collapses the Supabase load to two queries a minute per deck no matter how much traffic arrives.

findings.title: Leaflet loads from unpkg and the service worker refuses to cache it, so an offline or CDN-blocked visit paints a complete page whose every button is dead
findings.evidence: `initMap()` is a bare top-level statement at js/game.js:788 and js/app.js:1307, and its first line is `map = L.map('map', {...})` (game.js:43, app.js:79). `L` comes only from `<script src="https://unpkg.com/leaflet@1.9.4/dist/leaflet.js">` (index.html:173, game.html:168) — there is no guard, no typeof check, no try/catch anywhere. If that script has not run, initMap() throws a ReferenceError out of a top-level statement, which aborts the rest of the script: in game.js that is the entire wiring block right below it ($('#playBtn').onclick, #lockBtn, #nextBtn, #submitScore, #boardsBtn, lines 789-806), and in app.js it is `bindUI()` on line 1308, which binds the mic button. Meanwhile sw.js caches the full shell — '/', '/game.html', '/css/style.css', all the js (lines 9-23) — but bails on anything cross-origin: `if (url.origin !== self.location.origin) return;` (sw.js:40). Leaflet's JS and CSS are therefore never cached, on a site that registers a service worker on all three pages and ships a manifest so it can be installed to a home screen.
findings.userImpact: A phone user installs the PWA (the manifest and SW invite exactly that), then opens it on the subway or with no signal. The shell loads instantly from cache — logo, headline, styled buttons, the whole page — and then nothing works. Tapping the mic does nothing, tapping a deck does nothing, no error, no message. Same outcome any time unpkg.com is slow, rate-limiting, or blocked by a corporate/school/ISP filter while the same-origin shell comes back from the SW cache immediately. There is no SRI hash on the script either, so unpkg is also an unverified third party executing on the page.
findings.suggestedFix: Self-host leaflet.js and leaflet.css (they are 42KB and 15KB), add them to the sw.js SHELL list, and bump VERSION. That fixes offline, CDN blocking, and the supply-chain exposure in one move. If the CDN has to stay, at minimum add integrity/crossorigin attributes and wrap the init calls: `if (typeof L === 'undefined') { showMaplessError(); } else { initMap(); } bindUI();` so the buttons still bind.

findings.title: YouTube embeds load on 6 of 10 decks and set third-party cookies, but privacy.html does not list YouTube as a third party
findings.evidence: js/media.js:35 injects `s.src = 'https://www.youtube.com/iframe_api'` and line 45 constructs `new window.YT.Player(mountId, {...})` with no `host` option, so it defaults to www.youtube.com rather than www.youtube-nocookie.com. js/clips.js contains 44 clips with `"kind": "yt"`, distributed: accents 13/22, hindi-urdu 9/13, french 6/13, chinese 5/12, spanish 4/14, portuguese 4/12. privacy.html:53 ('Third parties we use') names only Google/Gemini, Vercel and Supabase, and privacy.html:44 opens with 'No account, no name, no email, no tracking pixels.'
findings.userImpact: A player picks the English deck — the deck the TikTok will most likely feature — and 13 of its 22 clips silently load a YouTube iframe that drops YouTube/Google advertising and analytics cookies on their device. The privacy page they were pointed at from the footer tells them there are no tracking pixels and lists three third parties, none of which is YouTube. For an EU/UK visitor that is undisclosed third-party tracking without consent; for anyone it is a factually wrong privacy page on a site whose entire pitch is 'here is exactly what happens to your voice'.
findings.suggestedFix: Two lines. Pass `host: 'https://www.youtube-nocookie.com'` in the YT.Player config (media.js:45), which is YouTube's own privacy-enhanced mode and drops the tracking cookies. And add YouTube to the third-parties paragraph in privacy.html: 'Some game clips stream from YouTube; when one plays, YouTube sees the request.'

findings.title: /api/analyze returns raw Node.js internal error strings to the client, and the UI shows them in a toast
findings.evidence: The catch block returns `error: err.code || 'server_error'` and `detail: String(err.message || err).slice(0, 300)` (lines 450-458) for anything unexpected. js/app.js:593 falls back to that string when the error code is not in its ERRORS map: `err.userMessage = ERRORS[data && data.error] || (data && data.detail) || ''`, and it is toasted at app.js:529/618. Reproduced against localhost:8123: POST `{"audio":123}` with a forged Origin returns HTTP 500 `{"error":"ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE","detail":"The first argument must be of type string or an instance of Buffer, ArrayBuffer, or Array or an Array-like Object. Received type number (123)"}`, and POST `{` returns `{"error":"server_error","detail":"Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2)"}`. Line 68 similarly returns 'GEMINI_API_KEY not set' as a client-visible detail.
findings.userImpact: Nobody using the app normally can reach this — blobToBase64 always yields a string — so no real user sees a Node stack message. What it costs is reconnaissance: a stranger poking the endpoint learns the runtime, the exact failing call, and the names of the environment variables the server expects, which is a free map for the person deciding how hard to push the other holes above. The `detail` for `upstream_failed` also echoes up to 200 bytes of Google's raw error body (line 145).
findings.suggestedFix: Keep the code, drop the free-text detail on the 500 path: return the specific `detail` only for the codes the UI actually renders (audio_too_large, audio_too_short, no_speech, out_of_credit, at_capacity) and send a fixed string for everything else, with `console.error(err)` for the real message.

findings.title: Every feedback row records confidence 0 — the field name does not match the view model
findings.evidence: `normalizeServer` builds the view model with `conf: Math.max(0, Math.min(100, r.confidence | 0))` (js/app.js:640) — the key is `conf`. `window._lastResult` is set to that object (app.js:790). Both feedback payloads then read a key that does not exist on it: `confidence: last.confidence || 0` at app.js:1182 (saveFeedback) and again at app.js:1282 (the donate button). The server dutifully stores it: `confidence: Number.isFinite(+b.confidence) ? ... : null` (api/feedback.js:120).
findings.userImpact: No user sees anything wrong. The owner does: privacy.html:44 promises the anonymous scorecard includes 'the confidence score', and the feedback table's confidence column is uniformly 0 for every row ever collected. Any post-launch analysis of 'was the model overconfident when it was wrong?' — the single most useful question the flywheel exists to answer — is silently unanswerable, and the zeros look like real data rather than a missing field.
findings.suggestedFix: `confidence: last.conf || 0` in both places (app.js:1182 and app.js:1282). Worth checking whether existing rows are all zero before treating any of that column as signal.

findings.title: The per-IP rate limiter wipes every counter once it holds 5000 entries, so it stops limiting during exactly the traffic it exists for
findings.evidence: `if (buckets.size > 5000) buckets.clear();` — the whole Map, not an eviction of the oldest entry. Identical code in api/scores.js:25, api/feedback.js:22, api/clip-report.js:36. Combined with the fact that the Map is per-serverless-instance in-memory (acknowledged at api/analyze.js:260), the effective ceiling is 30/hr multiplied by however many instances Vercel is running, and reset to zero for everyone the moment any one instance sees its 5001st distinct client.
findings.userImpact: Under the traffic a TikTok actually produces — thousands of distinct IPs per instance per hour — the limiter clears repeatedly, so an abuser sitting in that traffic gets their counter reset for free alongside everyone else's and never hits 30. The speed bump is flattest precisely when the wallet is most exposed. This is not a user-facing break; it matters because the daily cap is then the only thing standing between a script and the Gemini budget, and per finding 1 that cap does not bound cost.
findings.suggestedFix: Evict rather than clear: delete entries whose `reset` is already in the past, and only if that frees nothing, drop the oldest ~20%. Or accept the in-memory limiter as decorative and put the real limit in Supabase alongside the daily cap.

findings.title: Repo internals are committed and will be served as static files on the public domain
findings.evidence: vercel.json declares only a maxDuration for api/analyze.js — no build step, no outputDirectory, no framework — so Vercel serves the repo root as static assets, which is how index.html reaches '/'. `git ls-files` shows these are all committed and will therefore ship: PRD.md (36KB), docs/PRD.md, docs/architecture-research-2026-08-09.md, supabase/schema.sql, dev-server.js, all 30 files in tools/, and 40 files in data/ (eval runs, leak audits, quarantine lists, clip provenance). Confirmed served by path on the dev server: GET /PRD.md -> 200, 36542 bytes; GET /data/quarantine.json -> 200, 3798 bytes. Separately and dev-only: dev-server.js:37-40 resolves any path under ROOT, so `curl http://localhost:8123/.env` returns 200 with all 564 bytes of the real key file — that file is gitignored and never deployed, so this is a local-machine exposure, not a production one. No secrets are in any tracked file; I grepped for AIza/sk-ant/gsk_/eyJhbGci/supabase.co across everything and only found `process.env.X` references.
findings.userImpact: Nothing breaks and no key leaks. What is exposed is the internal record: the full PRD, the schema (table and column names for feedback/scores/clip_reports/usage), the eval and leak-audit data, and the tooling. For someone probing the app, supabase/schema.sql at a guessable URL hands them the exact table names to aim the other findings at, and the PRD narrates which guards exist and why. Worth a deliberate decision rather than an accident on launch day.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a .vercelignore with PRD.md, docs/, data/, tools/, supabase/, dev-server.js — it keeps them in git and off the domain. For local dev, add an early `if (/^\/\.|node_modules/.test(url.pathname)) { res.writeHead(404); return res.end('not found'); }` in dev-server.js so dotfiles are never served.

findings.title: Every rate limiter trusts a client-writable header name; worth confirming Vercel actually overwrites x-real-ip
findings.evidence: `const ip = (req.headers['x-real-ip'] || (req.headers['x-forwarded-for'] || '').split(',')[0]).trim() || 'unknown';` — identical in api/scores.js:94, api/feedback.js:100, api/clip-report.js:60. The comment above each asserts 'x-real-ip is platform-set', and the earlier fix correctly stopped trusting the leftmost x-forwarded-for entry for exactly this reason. The code has no way to verify that assertion, and I could not verify Vercel's behaviour from this environment. On the local dev server the header is trusted outright: `curl -X POST /api/analyze -H 'Origin: http://localhost:8123' -H 'x-real-ip: 203.0.113.99'` was accepted, which confirms only that nothing in the app validates it — dev-server.js has no proxy in front, so this is not evidence about production.
findings.userImpact: If Vercel's edge does strip or overwrite an inbound x-real-ip, this is fine and there is no issue. If it passes a client-supplied value through, then every limiter in the app — 30/hr on analyze, 40/hr on scores, 12/hr on feedback's clip upload, 20/hr on clip-report — is bypassed by a single extra header with a random value per request, and the abuse paths in findings 1, 2 and 3 all lose their last speed bump. I am flagging this as unverified rather than asserting a bug, because it is the single load-bearing assumption under all four endpoints and it is currently unchecked.
findings.suggestedFix: Verify once against the deployed function: `curl -s https://hometongue.me/api/scores?start=1 -H 'x-real-ip: 1.2.3.4'` is not a test, so instead log `req.headers['x-real-ip']` from a deployed request sent with a bogus value and see whether the bogus value arrives. If it does, drop x-real-ip and derive the IP from the RIGHTMOST x-forwarded-for entry, or use Vercel's own request.ip / x-vercel-forwarded-for.

findings.title: Internal curation notes ship as the player-facing clip note, cut off mid-word
findings.evidence:
`$('#revealHint').textContent = clip.hint || ''` (js/game.js:509) prints the `hint` field verbatim into the reveal sheet. 14 hints across the shipping decks are internal sourcing notes, and 12 of them are hard-truncated at exactly 190 characters, mid-word. Verified rendered on the running site (element is 526x42px, display:block, sheet visible) and confirmed identical on production (curl of https://www.hometongue.me/js/clips.js). Actual strings a player sees:

- Mexico: "NOT the already-used Mexican medical-article reading · this is a different reader/topic. Short (1:36) but clean. Country-level tag only, no specific city, pinned at Mexico City with wide rad"
- Guatire, Venezuela: "...Used the transcoded MP3 (original FLAC was slightly over the 40M"
- Minas, Uruguay: "Checked full text on Wikisource: ... Archival 1946 radio recording, PD un"
- Spain: "...Only regional-category documentation (no specific city), pinned at Madrid with wide radiu"
- Argentina: "Ideal case: topic is a Brazilian town, completely unconnected to Argentina. Country-level accent tag only, pinned at Buenos Aires with wide radius."
- Peru: "...so the pin is placed at the capital, Lima, with a wide accept radius. Duration 2:38, verified via direct file-page fetch."
- Delhi–Meerut Region: "9m42s, verified direct file. ... treat the pin location as the broad Delhi–Meerut belt, not"
- Hong Kong: "...Any 20s window works; the first few seconds just name the article subject (an American scientist), not the speaker's locati"
- Hong Kong (2nd): "Dense science-article reading, no intro chit-chat. Any segment works. Same voice as the Carver clip above."
- Shanghai: "...the essay's subject (Yueyang, Hunan) is a different province from the speaker's"
- Northeast Scotland: "He switches between his home dialect and English; the clip needs the English stretch."
- Thomastown, Ireland: "...telling stories about the holy well behind his house (14:46 total, pick any segment)"

Exposure, computed from the deal logic (js/game.js:207-224 dedupes by label, draws 5): Spanish has 11 distinct labels of which at most 5 are clean, so a clean Spanish game has probability ~0.1% — effectively every Spanish game shows at least one. Chinese 89%, English 82%, Hindi–Urdu 78%.
findings.userImpact: A stranger arrives from TikTok, plays the Spanish deck, gets the answer, and reads a note that says "NOT the already-used Mexican medical-article reading" and stops mid-word at "with wide rad". It reads as an unfinished build with the developer's private scratchpad left in. It also tells players the pins are placed at capital cities with a "wide accept radius", which undercuts the game they are being scored on.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the 14 flagged `hint` values in js/clips.js as one player-facing sentence each, in the voice of the clean ones ("Two grandparents genuinely reminiscing, not reading a script..."). Then add a guard so this cannot recur: a load-time check that no hint exceeds ~160 chars or ends without terminal punctuation, and drop the sourcing metadata into a separate non-rendered field.

findings.title: The "so what is it really?" country picker mixes demonyms with country names and omits most of the world, so many users cannot send a correction at all
findings.evidence: The picker is filled from `COUNTRIES[c].en` (js/app.js:1140-1142). The 15 Arabic entries store adjectives — `eg: { en: 'Egyptian' }`, `lb: { en: 'Lebanese' }`, `sa: { en: 'Saudi' }` — while all 64 others store country names. Read live from the running page, the alphabetical list runs: "DR Congo, Ecuador, Egyptian, Emirati, Estonia, France, Georgia, Ghana". There are 79 entries total and no Japan, Germany, Italy, Turkey, Korea, Greece, Poland, Netherlands, Sweden, Iran, Indonesia, Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Ethiopia or Somalia. js/app.js:1248: `if (!sel.value) { toast('Pick the country first.'); return; }` — there is no free-text or "other" escape, and the city box alone cannot be submitted.
findings.userImpact: Someone from Tokyo talks in Japanese, gets a Tokyo verdict, taps "nope" to correct a wrong guess, opens the dropdown and there is no Japan. Every attempt to send returns "Pick the country first." They are stuck. Everyone else sees a list where "Egyptian" sits between "Ecuador" and "Emirati", which reads as a half-finished data file on a product whose whole pitch is "any language".
findings.suggestedFix: Add a plain `name` field to js/places.js for the 15 Arabic codes (Egypt, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia…) and use it in the picker, keeping `en` for wherever the demonym is actually wanted. Backfill the missing countries, or replace the `<select>` with a type-ahead over a full ISO country list plus an "somewhere else" free-text option, and let #fbSend accept a city-only correction.

findings.title: Mic-failure copy tells everyone to click a Chrome address-bar icon that does not exist on phones
findings.evidence:
js/app.js:480: `toast('Your mic barely picked anything up 🎤, check Chrome\'s mic icon (address bar) is using the right microphone, then try again.')`
js/app.js:552, ERRORS.no_speech: `"I couldn't hear any real speech in that. If the bars weren't moving while you talked, your browser is probably using the wrong microphone (click the mic icon in the address bar)."`
Both fire on the two mic-failure paths (micPeak < 0.02 at js/app.js:474, and a server `no_speech` reply). Neither iOS Safari nor Android Chrome shows a per-site mic icon you can click in the address bar, and iOS users are not in Chrome.
findings.userImpact: The launch audience arrives from TikTok on a phone. A user with a muted mic or the wrong input device records for twenty seconds, gets told to check "Chrome's mic icon (address bar)", finds no such thing on their iPhone, and leaves. The one message whose entire job is to get them un-stuck names a browser they aren't using and a control that isn't there. The sentence is also ungrammatical — a mic icon doesn't "use" a microphone.
findings.suggestedFix: Split by platform using the existing `detectPlatform()` (js/app.js:1146), or write one device-neutral line: "I barely heard anything. Check your phone isn't muted and nothing is covering the mic, then try again — or type instead." Same for ERRORS.no_speech. While in there: js/app.js:403 says "Type instead 👇" but the toast sits at `bottom: 72px` (css/style.css:643) with the type box above it, so the arrow points at nothing.

findings.title: Corrections are silently discarded server-side, and the privacy page states they are kept
findings.evidence:
privacy.html:44 promises the scorecard holds "the country code we guessed, the broad region, the confidence score, whether you said we were right, the country you corrected us to". Three of those never land:
1. `guess_code` is not in the payload at all (js/app.js:1176-1187 sends `guess_city`), so api/feedback.js:118 stores null every time.
2. `confidence: last.confidence || 0` (js/app.js:1182, and again at 1282) reads a field the view model never sets — normalizeServer writes `conf` (js/app.js:640). Every row stores 0.
3. api/feedback.js:9 `VALID_CODES` accepts only 15 Arabic codes plus msa/weak/dialect/unclear. js/places.js offers 79. So 64 of 79 selectable countries fail the check at api/feedback.js:122 and store null — and without consent `actual_city` is nulled too (api/feedback.js:126-128, correctly per the privacy contract).
findings.userImpact: A user from Spain is guessed wrong, taps "nope", picks Spain, taps send, and sees "Logged. This is exactly how it learns." Nothing about what the right answer was is stored — the row is `correct: false` with every identifying field null. The correction flywheel collects nothing outside Arabic, and the privacy page describes a record the code does not write.
findings.suggestedFix: Fix `last.confidence` -> `last.conf` in both payloads; either send `guess_code` or drop it from privacy.html:44; and widen VALID_CODES to the full key set of COUNTRIES in js/places.js (or validate against a shared list so the two cannot drift again).

findings.title: The only stated route to delete a donated voice clip is a public GitHub issue
findings.evidence: "Since there are no accounts, tell us roughly when you donated (date, time, and the guess the app made) and we'll find and delete it: open an issue here". The repo is real and public with issues enabled (verified via the GitHub API: private:false, has_issues:true). There is no email address anywhere in index.html, game.html, privacy.html, or the footer.
findings.userImpact: Someone donates a recording of their own voice, then changes their mind. To get it deleted they must create a GitHub account and post — publicly, under a handle — the date, time, and the guess the app made about where they grew up. Most of a TikTok audience will not do this, and the ones who do have to publish the request. A privacy page whose deletion route requires publishing a request reads badly to anyone who reads it carefully.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a mailto: contact as the primary route and keep the GitHub issue as a secondary option.

findings.title: "Nine decks" is claimed in two places; eight ship
findings.evidence: game.html:9 ``; game.html:45 `nine decks`; manifest.webmanifest description "...the listening game across nine decks". Italian has 0 clips and German has 3, both below `MIN_DECK = 10` (js/game.js:6), so `playableModes()` filters them out. Read from the running page: `deckCount` resolves to "eight decks" and eight tiles render. Production serves the same wrong meta description (verified by curl).
findings.userImpact: Someone shares the game link on TikTok, iMessage or Twitter and the preview card says "Nine decks" while the page shows eight. The static "nine decks" in the eyebrow also flashes before JS corrects it.
findings.suggestedFix: Change both meta description and manifest to "eight decks" (or drop the number: "Real recordings from around the world"), and set the game.html:45 fallback to "eight decks" so the flash isn't wrong either.

findings.title: Privacy page describes donation as ticking a box; it is a button that uploads on press
findings.evidence: privacy.html:46 heading: "If you tick the \"donate this clip\" box". The UI is a button (index.html:156 `<button class="donate-btn" id="donateBtn">donate this clip</button>`) whose handler uploads the audio immediately on click (js/app.js:1257-1298), which the code comment at js/app.js:1253 explicitly notes replaced the old checkbox design.
findings.userImpact: A cautious reader checks the privacy page before recording, goes looking for a checkbox they can leave unticked, and instead finds a button that has already uploaded their voice the instant they pressed it. The described consent mechanic and the real one are different — the real one is less reversible than the page implies.
findings.suggestedFix: Retitle to "If you press \"donate this clip\"" and add that pressing it uploads the recording straight away.

findings.title: Privacy page says there is no transcription step, but the model returns a transcript, the card shows it, and donation stores it
findings.evidence: privacy.html:44: "There is no transcription step and no separate speech-to-text service — the model listens to the audio directly." The response schema asks for one: api/prompt.js:86 `transcript: { type: 'string', description: 'what they said, in its own script, written EXACTLY as pronounced...' }`. It is displayed under the heading "what we heard" (index.html:146, js/app.js:695), stored in localStorage (js/app.js:1168) and written to the server on donation (api/feedback.js:137).
findings.userImpact: A user reads "there is no transcription step", records, and then sees their own words typed back at them verbatim under "what we heard". The half of the sentence that is true ("no separate speech-to-text service") is buried behind a half that is plainly contradicted on screen, which makes the whole page look like it is being careless with the truth.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "There is no separate speech-to-text service — the model listens to the audio directly. It does write down what it heard, and that is shown to you on the card, but it is discarded with the recording unless you donate the clip."

findings.title: The refusal card explains itself with a "second listen" that no longer happens
findings.evidence: js/app.js:664: "Everything I could point to was either something you told me or something I could not hear again on a second listen." There is no second listen. api/analyze.js:419 documents "THE SECOND JUDGE WAS REMOVED HERE on 2026-08-12", and the only gate that now sets `content_led = 'fed'` is `heardSomething()` (api/analyze.js:445), which is a regex over the evidence strings (api/verdict.js:15-21) — a single pass, no re-listen.
findings.userImpact: The one card that has to justify refusing someone an answer gives them a reason that is half fiction. It is invisible to the user, but it is exactly the kind of unmeasured claim the rest of the codebase goes out of its way to avoid.
findings.suggestedFix: "Everything I could point to was something you told me rather than something I heard in your voice. That is not a reading, so I would rather give you nothing than make it up. Try once more, about twenty seconds, without saying your name or where you are from."

findings.title: Thirty seconds is asked for in two user-facing strings; the app is built around twenty
findings.evidence: index.html:9 `<meta name="description" content="Talk for thirty seconds in any language...">`; js/app.js:664 redo copy: "Try once more, ideally about thirty seconds". The product's floor is `MIN_RECORD_S = 20` (js/app.js:62); the button unlocks at 20 (js/app.js:323) and the meter says "that's enough to read you" at 20 (js/app.js:334). js/app.js:54-62 states explicitly that nothing above 20s is claimed in either direction.
findings.userImpact: A user finds the site through search or a shared link reading "Talk for thirty seconds", then the app tells them twenty is enough. Small, but it is the app contradicting its own headline promise on the first screen, and it contradicts the measured position the code is careful to hold.
findings.suggestedFix: Say twenty in both, matching the meter.

findings.title: "Lock a guess or skip ahead" offers a skip control that does not exist
findings.evidence: js/game.js:313: `toast('The audio is stuck this round. Lock a guess or skip ahead.')` — fired after two failed clip swaps. The dock (game.html:105-124) contains only back-5s, play, forward-5s and "lock it in", and `#lockBtn` stays disabled until a pin is dropped (js/game.js:258, enabled at js/game.js:66). There is no way to skip a round.
findings.userImpact: A player on a bad connection gets a round with dead audio, is told to "skip ahead", hunts the screen for a skip button, and finds none. The only way forward is to guess blind on the map, which is exactly what they were trying to avoid.
findings.suggestedFix: "The audio is stuck this round. Drop a pin anywhere and lock it in to move on." Or add a real skip that scores the round zero.

findings.title: The posted-score rank does not match the position shown on the leaderboard right beneath it
findings.evidence: js/game.js:575 toasts `Posted! You're #${d.rank} on ${deckName}.` The server computes rank as a raw count of every row with more points (api/scores.js:143-147), while the board it renders immediately afterwards (loadBoard, js/game.js:576) is deduped to one best row per nickname (api/scores.js:71-76).
findings.userImpact: A player who has played the deck three times, or plays a deck where others have, is told "You're #14" and then sees themselves at #6 on the board that appears in the same moment. Two different numbers for the same fact on one screen.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the rank against the same deduped best-per-nickname set the board uses, so the toast and the list agree.

findings.title: Game footer says clips stream from their public archives; 111 of 152 stream from hometongue.me
findings.evidence: game.html:161: "clips stream from their public archives · credits shown after each round". Counting `url` values in js/clips.js across the eight shipping decks: 111 clips are local paths on the site's own origin (`/clips/ar/*.mp3`, `/clips/languages/*.mp3`, …), and only 41 are YouTube embeds. The clips' own metadata says so — `source.note` on the local ones reads "trimmed and re-encoded for the game".
findings.userImpact: Anyone who reads the footer as a statement about where the audio comes from — including a rights holder checking how their CC-licensed recording is being used — gets a description that is wrong for three quarters of the library. The recordings are re-encoded copies hosted by HomeTongue, not hotlinks.
findings.suggestedFix: "clips are used under their original licences · full credits after every round" — true for both the hosted copies and the YouTube streams.

findings.title: "a long look usually means a close call" is a reassurance the repo's own data does not support
findings.evidence: js/app.js:353, last of the SCAN_NOTES shown after ~20s of waiting: 'still going, a long look usually means a close call'. The only paired latency data in the repo is data/length-latency.json (94 calls with both `ms` and `km`). Spearman correlation between call latency and error is -0.09 pooled, and the sign flips between arms (+0.12, +0.15, -0.19, -0.14). The code's own comment at js/app.js:345 attributes the wait to model inference, not deliberation.
findings.userImpact: No visible breakage — but it is an invented explanation presented as fact to a user who is already waiting, on a page whose entire design principle (js/app.js:29-62, api/prompt.js:14-19) is to claim only what was measured.
findings.suggestedFix: 'still going, this one is taking a while' — honest, and does the same job of proving the page is alive.

findings.title: Voice and terminology drift across the two pages: I / we / it, deck / mode, test set / training
findings.evidence: On one card: index.html:46 "I'll find where you grew up", index.html:60 "Don't tell it where you're from", index.html:146 "what we heard", index.html:153 "did I get it?". index.html:156 says donated clips become "the test set that sharpens future versions" while privacy.html:47 says they are used for "training a model" — different things. game.html:45 and the leaderboard say "decks" while js/game.js:797 labels the button "switch mode" and js/game.js:174 toasts "This mode is still being stocked". index.html:102 button says "guess my dialect" where every other CTA is about place. js/game.js:411 mid-sentence capitalisation: "listening time up. Trust your ear, drop the pin". js/clips.js uses "Streamed from YouTube — the creator gets the view." 38 times and the same sentence with a middot 3 times. index.html:171 claims "it listens to your accent, not your words" while type mode (index.html:62) judges words only and api/prompt.js:55 explicitly instructs the model to use "any regional vocabulary you hear".
findings.userImpact: Nothing breaks, but a reader moving from the hero line to the result card is addressed by three different narrators, and the footer contradicts a button four lines above it. Across a page this short it reads as copy assembled in passes rather than written.
findings.suggestedFix: Pick one narrator — the first-person "I" already carries the personality — and sweep index.html, privacy.html and the toasts for it. Settle on "deck" everywhere, on "training data" in both places, and either soften the footer to "it listens to how you say things, not just what you say" or drop that clause.

findings.title: flyHome() is unguarded against a 0-size map, and a throw there destroys a finished "no answer" verdict
findings.evidence:
flyToGuess (js/app.js:161-173) is heavily hardened against a 0x0 Leaflet container — it checks map.getSize() before flying and renderResult wraps it in try/catch at line 789. flyHome (js/app.js:177-181) does neither: it calls map.flyToBounds(HOME_BOUNDS) directly after ensureMapReady(), which cannot help if the container genuinely has no size. renderResult's FED branch calls it bare at line 666, inside onRecordingReady's try, so the throw lands in the catch at line 528 -> fallbackOrFail('Something went wrong on our end.') -> state='idle', show('idleCard').

Verified live against the running dev server with the tab in the hidden/0-size state: flyHome() -> "THREW: Invalid LatLng object: (NaN, NaN)"; renderResult({content_led:'fed',...}) -> "THREW: Invalid LatLng object: (NaN, NaN)" with redoCard already painted and visible before the throw. The same call at #againBtn (line 1238) and #redoBtn (line 1240) throws too — on #redoBtn it throws before startListening(), so "record again" silently does nothing.
findings.userImpact: Someone whose take produced a content-led verdict gets the redo card painted with the honest explanation, then it is instantly replaced by the idle card and a generic "Something went wrong on our end. Try again, or use type mode." They lose 20+ seconds of talking and a burned analysis, and are told the app broke rather than why it declined. Trigger is narrow (map container never laid out — page opened into a background tab), but it is exactly the case the author already measured and fixed once for flyToGuess.
findings.suggestedFix: Give flyHome the same guard as flyToGuess: `if (map.getSize().x > 0 && map.getSize().y > 0) { try { map.flyToBounds(...) } catch {} }`. Also wrap the FED branch's flyHome() call in try/catch, and move flyHome() after startListening() in the #redoBtn handler.

findings.title: Donate button says "donated ✓ thank you" when the server stored no clip at all
findings.evidence:
Client: `if (!r.ok || !j || !j.ok) throw new Error('upload failed');` then unconditionally shows 'donated ✓ thank you'. It never inspects `j.stored`.

Server (api/feedback.js:176): `return res.end(JSON.stringify({ ok: true, stored: row.clip_path ? 'clip+labels' : 'labels' }))`. clip_path stays null — with ok:true — whenever any of these hold: tokenValid(b.token) is false (feedback.js:142, TOKEN_MAX_AGE_MS = 30 min, line 12); baseMime is not in AUDIO_MIME; bytes are outside 1000..2.5MB (line 144); or the Supabase storage POST fails (line 151-155, which only console.errors).

The app's own saveFeedback already knows the distinction — js/app.js:1202 checks `d.stored === 'clip+labels'`. The donate handler does not.
findings.userImpact: A user reads their result, shows a friend, comes back 31 minutes later and presses "donate this clip". The fb_token minted at analyze time has expired, the server drops the audio, returns ok:true, and the button turns green with "donated ✓ thank you". They believe they contributed their voice; nothing was stored. The same false confirmation covers every storage-side failure (bucket misconfigured, RLS, quota), so a broken Supabase bucket would look like 100% successful donations on launch night while collecting zero clips.
findings.suggestedFix: Only paint success on `j.stored === 'clip+labels'`; otherwise restore the button and toast something true ("that clip expired — do a fresh take and donate right after"). Optionally re-mint a token or extend TOKEN_MAX_AGE_MS.

findings.title: "Nope" corrections silently discard the country for 64 of the 79 countries the picker offers
findings.evidence:
api/feedback.js:9 — `const VALID_CODES = new Set(['eg','sd','sy','lb','jo','ps','iq','sa','kw','ae','ye','ly','tn','dz','ma','msa','weak','dialect','unclear',''])` — 15 ISO codes, all Arabic-speaking, left over from the Arabic-only era. Line 122: `actual_code: VALID_CODES.has(b.actual_code) ? b.actual_code : null`.

The picker is built from the full country table: js/app.js:1140 `Object.keys(COUNTRIES)`. Ran it: 79 countries offered, 15 accepted, 64 stored as null — including us, gb, fr, ca, in, br, es, mx, ar, de, pt.

For a non-donating user, actual_city is also null (feedback.js:135-137 is inside `if (consent)`, and consent = !!window._donated, js/app.js:1156). So the row for a British user who corrects the app is {correct:false, actual_code:null, actual_city:null} — the correction carries no location at all. Related, same block: `region: clean(b.region, 20)` (line 119) truncates at 20 chars, so "the Arabian Peninsula" is stored as "the Arabian Peninsul".
findings.userImpact: A user in Manchester gets placed in Dublin, taps "nope", picks "United Kingdom" from the dropdown, presses send, and is told "Logged. This is exactly how it learns." The server throws the country away. Since HomeTongue is now global and about to be pushed on TikTok, the overwhelming majority of corrections — the single most valuable signal the launch will generate — land as unusable rows.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace VALID_CODES with a validity test (`/^[a-z]{2}$/` plus the four special tokens), or import the same COUNTRIES key set the picker is built from so the two can never drift. Raise the region cap to 60.

findings.title: A recording cut short by a phone call is analyzed anyway, bypassing the 20-second floor the whole app is built on
findings.evidence:
stopListening (js/app.js:464-494) enforces three gates before spending a call: elapsed >= MIN_RECORD_S (20s), micPeak >= 0.02, voicedS >= 1.5s.

onRecordingReady's spontaneous-stop branch (js/app.js:512-516) enforces none of them — it just sets state='analyzing', shows the analyzing card, and falls through to the post. The only gate on that path is `blob.size < 2000` (line 520). At the opus bitrates Chrome's MediaRecorder actually uses (24-128 kbps), 2000 bytes is roughly 0.1-0.7 seconds of audio, so any interruption after ~1 second sails straight through to Gemini.

The comment at line 508-511 assumes "a take interrupted at 20 seconds is still a take", but nothing checks that it was 20 seconds — `startedAt` is right there and is never consulted on this path.
findings.userImpact: Someone starts recording on their phone, a call or Siri or another app grabs the mic four seconds in. Instead of "that got cut off, try again", they wait ~12 seconds and get a confidently-worded verdict, a pin, a radius and a shareable card built from four seconds of audio. The app's own paired measurement (js/app.js:29-56) says 12 seconds already yields a 166 km median with 5 of 18 answers over 1000 km wrong; 4 seconds is far worse, and it is presented identically to a real reading. It also burns an analysis against the daily cap.
findings.suggestedFix: In the `state === 'listening'` branch, compute `(Date.now() - startedAt)/1000` and route anything under MIN_RECORD_S through the same toast-and-return the manual stop uses, instead of posting it.

findings.title: A suspended AudioContext is indistinguishable from a dead microphone, and the guard throws away the take
findings.evidence:
startMeter (js/app.js:235-267) sets `micPeak = 0` at line 245 immediately before entering the rAF loop, and the whole body is wrapped in `try { ... } catch { /* no meter, no problem */ }`. The design intent is visible in startListening line 400 (`micPeak = -1`) and the guard at line 474 (`if (micPeak >= 0 && micPeak < 0.02)`): -1 means "meter unavailable, skip the check".

But unavailability is only detected by an exception. An AudioContext that constructs fine and then sits in 'suspended' state throws nothing — getByteFrequencyData just returns zeros forever, micPeak stays at exactly 0, and the guard fires. Line 238 attempts `audioCtx.resume().catch(() => {})`, which is fire-and-forget and whose failure is swallowed; the context state is never re-checked at stop time. Note that on a first visit the resume() happens after `await getUserMedia`, i.e. after the permission prompt, by which point transient user activation has long expired.

I could not test this on a real iOS device, so I cannot say whether Safari actually leaves the context suspended here — hence the confidence flag. The code-level gap (a silently non-running meter is treated as a confirmed-dead mic) is certain either way.
findings.userImpact: If it fires, a first-time visitor on iPhone Safari talks for 20-60 seconds, presses "done, guess now", and the entire take is discarded with "Your mic barely picked anything up 🎤, check Chrome's mic icon (address bar), then try again." There is no Chrome and no address-bar mic icon on their phone, so there is no recovery action and the app is unusable for them. This is the single highest-consequence unknown in the recording path for a TikTok launch, where most traffic will be first-visit iOS in-app browsers.
findings.suggestedFix: Cheap and safe regardless: at the top of stopListening, treat a non-running meter as no meter — `if (!audioCtx || audioCtx.state !== 'running') micPeak = -1;` before the guard. Then test one real take end-to-end on an iPhone before launch.

findings.title: Raw JavaScript exception text is shown to users — 'server_error' has no entry in the error map
findings.evidence:
api/analyze.js:449 falls back to `const code = err.code || 'server_error'` and always ships `detail: String(err.message || err).slice(0, 300)` (line 457). The client's ERRORS map (js/app.js:551-563) has no 'server_error' key, so postAnalyze line 593 falls through to `(data && data.detail)` and toasts the raw message verbatim.

Demonstrated against the running server:
  $ curl -X POST http://localhost:8123/api/analyze -H 'Origin: http://localhost:8123' --data '{"text":"not json'
  {"ok":false,"error":"server_error","detail":"Unterminated string in JSON at position 17 (line 1 column 18)"}

The toast would read: "Unterminated string in JSON at position 17 (line 1 column 18) Try again, or use type mode." A reachable-from-the-real-client version is `sane(raw)` (analyze.js:411) dereferencing a null model response, which yields "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'lat')". 'method_not_allowed' is also uncovered; conversely 'swamped' (line 555) is in the map but the server never emits it.
findings.userImpact: On the one path where something genuinely unexpected breaks, a stranger sees an internal stack-trace-flavoured string in the toast instead of plain English. It reads as an unfinished app at exactly the moment they were going to judge it.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `server_error: 'Something went wrong on our end. Try again in a moment.'` to ERRORS, and stop preferring raw `detail` for unknown codes — only surface `detail` for codes you know are human-readable.

findings.title: recorder.start() sits outside the try/catch that guards the MediaRecorder constructor
findings.userImpact: On an affected device the user sees a normal-looking recording — bars moving, countdown ticking, the button enabling at 20s — talks for the full take, presses "done, guess now", and gets "I didn't catch any audio. Try again, or use type mode." Repeating produces the same result every time with no clue that the browser is the problem.
findings.suggestedFix: Move `recorder.start(500)` inside the same try block as the constructor.

findings.title: Every feedback and donation row records confidence 0 — the field name does not exist on the view model
findings.evidence:
normalizeServer stores the server's confidence under the key `conf` (js/app.js:640: `conf: Math.max(0, Math.min(100, r.confidence | 0))`). Grepping app.js, `conf` is never read anywhere. Both consumers read a key that was never set:
  js/app.js:1182  confidence: last.confidence || 0,   // saveFeedback
  js/app.js:1282  confidence: last.confidence || 0,   // donate
