last.confidence is undefined -> 0. Server side, api/feedback.js:120 `Number.isFinite(+b.confidence)` is true for 0, so it stores 0 rather than null — indistinguishable from a genuine zero-confidence verdict.

This is the same bug class the comment at js/app.js:1172-1175 describes fixing for guess_city/region; confidence was missed.
findings.userImpact: Invisible to users, but it silently corrupts the dataset the launch exists to collect: every row in the feedback table will report the model was 0% confident, so "is it wrong more often when it is unsure?" is unanswerable for all launch traffic.
findings.suggestedFix: Either rename the view-model field to `confidence`, or read `last.conf` at both call sites.

findings.title: "Logged ✓" is shown before the POST is sent, and every failure is swallowed
findings.evidence: js/app.js:1190-1204: the toast (`'Logged ✓ every answer makes it sharper.'` / `'Logged. This is exactly how it learns.'`) fires at line 1193, then the fetch starts at line 1195 and ends in `.catch(() => {})`. Nothing in that chain can ever contradict the toast. api/feedback.js rate-limits at 12 requests/hour/IP (line 23) and returns not_configured (line 109) or 500 on insert failure (line 173) — none of which the user ever learns about. Note the donate button shares that same 12/hour budget, so a user doing six takes with a donate plus a rating on each exhausts it.
findings.userImpact: A user on a flaky phone connection, or the 13th feedback action of the hour, taps "nailed it", reads "Logged ✓ every answer makes it sharper", and nothing was recorded. If Supabase is down on launch night, 100% of users see the confirmation and 0% of ratings land.
findings.suggestedFix: Move the toast into the .then() when the response is ok, and toast something honest on failure (or queue for retry).

findings.title: Two dead-end error messages tell mobile users to click a Chrome address-bar icon that does not exist on their phone
findings.evidence:
js/app.js:480 — "Your mic barely picked anything up 🎤, check Chrome's mic icon (address bar) is using the right microphone, then try again."
js/app.js:552 (ERRORS.no_speech) — "...your browser is probably using the wrong microphone (click the mic icon in the address bar)."

detectPlatform() already exists at js/app.js:1146-1149 and is used for the feedback payload, so the platform is known but not used for this copy. Neither iOS Safari nor Chrome on Android exposes a per-site mic picker in the address bar; on iOS it is Settings > Safari > Microphone, and on Android it is the padlock/tune icon > Permissions.
findings.userImpact: Both messages are dead ends — the recording is already discarded and the only instruction given points at UI the user cannot find. On a launch whose traffic is overwhelmingly phone-first, the two failure paths that most need a recovery action give a desktop-Chrome one.
findings.suggestedFix: Branch on detectPlatform(): iOS -> "Settings > Safari > Microphone", Android -> "tap the icon left of the address bar > Permissions", desktop -> the current wording. Or drop the browser-specific instruction and say "check which microphone your phone is using — AirPods in the case are a common cause."

findings.title: AbortSignal.timeout gates the whole app on Safari 16+ / iOS 16+, and older iOS fails with a generic error on every take
findings.evidence: js/app.js:576 `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(75_000)` is evaluated inside postAnalyze's try. On a browser without AbortSignal.timeout (Safari < 16, i.e. iOS 15 and below) it throws TypeError synchronously; the catch at line 578 does not match TimeoutError/AbortError, so it rethrows -> onRecordingReady's catch -> fallbackOrFail('Something went wrong on our end.'). Same call at js/app.js:1286 (donate) and js/game.js:680. Grepped the rest of the client JS — no other API in app.js requires anything newer than Safari 14, so this one line is what excludes those devices.
findings.userImpact: On an iPhone still on iOS 15 (older 6s/7/8 hardware, a small but real slice of a viral consumer audience), every single recording ends in "Something went wrong on our end. Try again, or use type mode." The app is completely non-functional with an error that blames the server.
findings.suggestedFix: Two lines at the top of app.js: if AbortSignal.timeout is missing, define it from `new AbortController()` + setTimeout with `controller.abort(new DOMException('','TimeoutError'))`.

findings.title: The "no answer" card describes a second listen that was removed from the pipeline two days ago
findings.evidence:
js/app.js:664 (shown on the redo card): "Everything I could point to was either something you told me or something I could not hear again on a second listen."

That second listen no longer happens. api/analyze.js:419-442 documents removing the evidence verifier on 2026-08-12; the only remaining check is heardSomething() (api/verdict.js:18-21), a regex over the evidence strings. js/app.js:781-782 carries the matching stale comment ("the server checks every acoustic claim before it answers"), which is also no longer true.

Separately, heardSomething returns false for an empty evidence array (`[].some(...)` is false), so a verdict that simply cited nothing at all lands on this card and the user is told they were told-not-heard — when in fact nothing was pointed to either way.
findings.userImpact: The one screen whose entire purpose is being honest about why no answer is being given describes a verification step that does not run. If anyone screenshots this card and asks how it works, the copy is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the redo text to describe what actually happened: everything the model offered as evidence was something the speaker said rather than something in their voice. Update the stale comment at line 781.

findings.title: sane() will return a verdict with an empty place, which blanks the headline and then misdiagnoses itself
findings.evidence:
api/prompt.js:101 — `required: ['has_speech', 'note']`. `place` is optional in the response schema. api/analyze.js:182-190: sane() returns a full result whenever lat/lng are finite and in range, with `place: String(r.place || '').slice(0, 120)` — an empty string is accepted.

Downstream, three client paths then misbehave on the same result object:
  js/app.js:708  place.textContent = v.place    -> blank headline under "sounds like you grew up around", with "somewhere in <region>" and "±400 km" still rendered beneath it
  js/app.js:1159 if (!last.place) -> toasts "This result is gone from the page's memory because the tab was suspended" when the user rates a result that is right there on screen
  js/app.js:1089 if (!v || !v.place) -> "Nothing to share yet. Do a take first." on a card that is visibly showing a verdict

I could not make Gemini actually omit `place` in testing, so I cannot say how often this happens — with a responseSchema it fills optional strings nearly always. Flagging it because the fix is one line and the failure lands on the single most visible element on the page.
findings.userImpact: If the model ever omits the field, the user gets a result card with no city in it, and both buttons on that card ("nailed it" and "share your card") respond with messages that are flatly untrue about what is on their screen.
findings.suggestedFix: In sane(), treat a missing place the same way a missing coordinate is treated: `if (!String(r.place || '').trim()) return null;` — the caller already turns null into a clean 422 no_speech.

findings.title: If getUserMedia never settles, the mic button is permanently dead with no feedback at all
findings.evidence:
js/app.js:396-413: startListening sets `state = 'starting'` and then awaits getUserMedia with no timeout. The double-tap guard at line 396 returns early for state 'starting', so every subsequent tap of #micBtn is silently discarded. Nothing on the idle card changes while the await is pending — no pressed state, no spinner, no text. There is no path out of 'starting' other than the promise settling.

Every known browser rejects on an explicit deny/dismiss, so this needs the promise to hang — reported on Android Chrome when the app is backgrounded while the permission prompt is open — which is why I have flagged it unsure rather than certain.
findings.userImpact: A first-time visitor taps the mic, the permission sheet appears, they switch away to check something, come back and the sheet is gone. The button now does nothing, forever, with no message. Their only recovery is knowing to reload the page, and most people will just close the tab.
findings.suggestedFix: Race getUserMedia against a ~15s timer; on timeout, reset state to 'idle' and toast "the microphone prompt didn't come back — tap to try again". Also give the mic button a visible pending state so the wait reads as the app working rather than the button being broken.

findings.title: Keyboard users cannot place a pin, so "Guess the Voice" is unplayable without a mouse or touchscreen
findings.evidence: map.on('click', onMapClick) is the ONLY registration; onMapClick (js/game.js:62-71) is the only code that creates guessMarker and runs $('#lockBtn').disabled = false. game.html:123 ships the button as <button class="stop-btn dock-lock" id="lockBtn" disabled>, so while disabled it is not even in the tab order. Verified in the running app at localhost:8123: L.Map.Keyboard.prototype.keyCodes === {left:[37],right:[39],down:[40],up:[38],zoomIn:[187,107,61,171],zoomOut:[189,109,54,173]} and _onKeyDown's source contains no 'click' — Leaflet only pans, zooms and closes popups. Focusing #map (which Leaflet gives tabindex="0") and firing Enter then Space produced document.querySelectorAll('.pin-wrap').length === 0 and lockBtn.disabled === true, with #pinHint still reading "listen, then tap the map to drop your pin".
findings.userImpact: Someone playing with a keyboard only — a switch user, a screen reader user, anyone with a tremor or an RSI who does not use a pointer — picks a deck, hears the 20-second clip, and then has no way to answer. Tab reaches the map, the ± buttons, the play button and the scrubber, and stops. "lock it in" never becomes reachable because nothing can enable it. All 5 rounds, all 10 decks, both from the deck picker and from a shared link. The game cannot be completed or scored at all.
findings.suggestedFix: Give the map a keyboard path to the same onMapClick logic. Minimal version: on the focused #map container, handle Enter/Space by calling onMapClick({latlng: map.getCenter()}), and once guessMarker exists let Shift+arrows nudge it (Leaflet's own arrows already pan the view underneath). A visible "drop pin at map centre" button in the dock next to "lock it in" would also work and is discoverable for everyone.

findings.title: Zero live regions on either page — every error, the verdict, and the game reveal are silent to a screen reader
findings.evidence:
index.html:169 is
and game.html:159 is identical — no role, no aria-live. Verified live on both pages: document.querySelectorAll('[aria-live],[role=status],[role=alert],[role=log],output') returns []. toast() (js/app.js:210-216, js/game.js:151-157) only sets textContent and flips .hidden, then hides again after 3.2s / 3.0s. Everything else that changes without a click is also unannounced: show('resultCard') in js/app.js:669 just toggles [hidden] on six sections and moves no focus; #timer (app.js:289), #qLabel (app.js:332-334), #scoreSoFar (game.js:492), #listens going to "listening time up. Trust your ear, drop the pin" (game.js:411), and #revealLabel — the answer — (game.js:506).
findings.userImpact: A blind user taps record, talks for 25 seconds, and the app drops back to the idle card because micPeak was low. The only explanation ever given is the toast "Your mic barely picked anything up 🎤, check Chrome's mic icon…" (app.js:480), which is never spoken and is gone in 3.2 seconds. They press record again and loop forever with no idea what is wrong. Same for "Mic blocked" (app.js:410), "That was 14 seconds…" (app.js:465), "HomeTongue has hit its listening limit for today" (app.js:561) and, in the game, "Tap ▶ once more to start the sound" (game.js:301) and "Posted! You're #4 on Arabic" (game.js:575). The verdict itself also arrives in silence.
findings.suggestedFix: Give #toast role="status" aria-live="polite" on both pages (use role="alert" for the blocking failures), and keep it in the DOM rather than [hidden] — swap a class instead, since aria-live on a display:none node does not announce. Separately, move focus to the newly revealed card's heading (tabindex="-1" + .focus()) at the end of show() in app.js and setView() in game.js, which fixes announcement and the lost tab position in one move.

findings.title: --grey-2 text is 2.45:1 — barely over half the required contrast, and it is used for the small type on every screen
findings.evidence: --grey-2: #A2A498. Computed against --sheet #FCFBF8: 2.45:1. Against --paper #F3F1EC: 2.24:1. WCAG 1.4.3 AA needs 4.5:1 for text under 18.66px bold / 24px regular; every use here is 9–11px. Confirmed painting live (getComputedStyle color === 'rgb(162, 164, 152)'): .card-eyebrow span at 10px ("accent geolocation", "listening game"), #resultKicker at 10.5px ("sounds like you grew up around" — the line directly above the answer), #srcBadge/.verdict-lang at 10px, .type-desc at 11px (style.css:484 — the description under all ten deck tiles), .source-key (style.css:568), .lang-label (style.css:715), .back-link (style.css:857), .board li::before rank numbers (style.css:606), textarea::placeholder (style.css:244). .leaflet-control-attribution (style.css:640) is --grey-2 at 9px over map tiles: 2.28:1 over land, 2.12:1 over water.
findings.userImpact: This is a phone-first product being promoted on TikTok, so most first visits are outdoors on a handset at partial brightness. In that setting the deck descriptions on the game's front screen, the kicker over the verdict, and the leaderboard rank numbers read as blank space. The OSM/CARTO attribution at 2.28:1 is also a licence obligation that is effectively unreadable.
findings.suggestedFix: Darken --grey-2 to about #6E7066 (4.6:1 on --sheet) or #6A6C62 (4.9:1). The hue and warmth are preserved; only the value moves. If the eyebrow labels are meant to stay quiet, do it with size and letter-spacing rather than lightness.

findings.title: The "share your card" button is 3.13:1 — the lowest-contrast control on the result card
findings.evidence: .share-btn { background: var(--sheet); color: var(--amber); border: 1.5px solid var(--amber); font-size: 14.5px; font-weight: 600 }. --amber is #B8862F (css/style.css:30). #B8862F on #FCFBF8 = 3.13:1. 14.5px/600 is not WCAG large text (that needs >=18.66px bold), so the bar is 4.5:1. The hover state at style.css:305 (.share-btn:hover { background: var(--amber); color: #fff }) is 3.24:1 — also failing, in the opposite direction. Verified live: getComputedStyle(#shareBtn).color === 'rgb(184, 134, 47)' at fontSize 14.5px, fontWeight 600. #redoCard .card-eyebrow b (style.css:415) is the same amber at 10px.
findings.userImpact: Sharing is the growth loop for a TikTok launch and this is the button that drives it, yet it is the hardest thing on the result card to see. A user with mild low vision or a sun-washed phone screen sees an empty outlined rectangle where the call to action should be, and taps "go again" (solid green, 6.23:1) instead.
findings.suggestedFix: Darken --amber for text use to roughly #8A6421 (4.6:1 on --sheet) while keeping #B8862F for the fills and map marks where it is only a graphic and needs 3:1. Or invert the button to filled amber with #1B1C19 text (7.6:1), which keeps the amber identity and gains contrast.

findings.title: prefers-reduced-motion does not stop the infinite animations — it makes them strobe between two states at frame rate
findings.evidence: The reduce block is only: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; } } — it omits animation-iteration-count: 1 !important. Three animations are infinite: .mic-btn::after { animation: ring 2.6s ease-out infinite } (style.css:224), .pulse { animation: pulse 2s ease-out infinite } (style.css:441), .scan span { animation: blink 1.1s ease-in-out infinite } (style.css:347). Verified in the running browser by injecting exactly those two declarations and sampling the live Animation at frame-length intervals: `ring` returns progress 0 (opacity 0.45, matrix scale 0.94) at t=0 and t=83.5ms but progress 1 (opacity ~0, scale 1.22) at t=16.7/33.4/50.1/66.8/100.2ms. `pulse` behaves identically (opacity 0.8 scale 0.4 vs opacity ~0 scale 1.5). `blink` is harmless only by luck — both its endpoints are opacity 0.2.
findings.userImpact: A user who has switched on Reduce Motion (vestibular disorder, migraine, motion sickness) opens hometongue.me and the halo around the big record button — the first thing on the page — flickers between two sizes and two opacities at the display refresh rate instead of stopping. Same for the ring around the answer pin once the map flies to their result. The setting they turned on to protect themselves produces something worse than the original 2.6s ease.
findings.suggestedFix: Add animation-iteration-count: 1 !important; (and scroll-behavior: auto !important;) to the same block at css/style.css:182. That is the canonical form of this reset and it makes all three animations settle on their first frame.

findings.title: A focusable YouTube iframe lives inside aria-hidden="true", 10,000px off-screen
findings.evidence:
game.html:166 is
; css/style.css:644 sets .yt-mount { position: fixed; left: -10000px; top: 0; width: 320px; height: 180px; opacity: 0; pointer-events: none; }; js/media.js:45 calls new window.YT.Player(mountId, ...), which replaces #ytMount with an
findings.userImpact: A keyboard user tabbing through the dock during a round lands on an invisible element 10,000px off-screen. The focus ring vanishes from view with no scroll and no visual cue, and their next Tab presses go into YouTube's own document. It also violates aria-hidden's contract: the element is hidden from assistive tech but still reachable by the keyboard, which is the exact combination screen reader users cannot recover from.
findings.suggestedFix: Put inert on the wrapper: <div class="yt-mount" inert>. inert removes the subtree from the tab order and the accessibility tree without touching layout or playback, and it makes the aria-hidden attribute unnecessary.

findings.title: The country correction dropdown has no accessible name at all; four other fields are labelled only by placeholder
findings.evidence: index.html:158 is <select id="fbActual"></select> — no <label for>, no aria-label, no aria-labelledby, and <select> has no placeholder to fall back on, so its accessible name is empty. Verified live across every control on both pages (hasLabelEl:false, ariaLabel:'', labelledby:'' for all): #fbActual (index.html:158), #fbCity placeholder="which city? (optional)" (index.html:159), #typeBox placeholder="write the way you actually talk…" (index.html:101), #nickname placeholder="nickname for the board" (game.html:85), #flagNote placeholder="anything else? (optional)" (game.html:153). Not one form control on either page has a programmatic label.
findings.userImpact: A screen reader user presses "nope" to correct a wrong guess and lands on a combobox announced with no name — at best the selected option text "so what is it really?", at worst just "combobox". Nothing says it wants a country. And because the other four are labelled only by placeholder, the label disappears the instant the first character is typed: someone with a working-memory or attention impairment types half a nickname, loses the field's purpose, and has nothing on screen to recover it.
findings.suggestedFix: Add aria-label to each: aria-label="which country are you actually from" on #fbActual, "which city" on #fbCity, "type the way you talk" on #typeBox, "nickname for the leaderboard" on #nickname, "anything else about this clip" on #flagNote. Better for #typeBox and #nickname: turn the existing visible copy (index.html:100's .prompt-label, game.html's context) into a real <label for> so the name is visible as well as programmatic.

findings.title: --grey body copy sits just under 4.5:1, and the footer over the map is at 3.96:1
findings.evidence: --grey: #74766D. On --sheet #FCFBF8 = 4.46:1 (bar is 4.50) — a hair under, but it covers most secondary copy: .prompt-label 13.5px, .length-tip 13px ("Your home language reads sharpest…"), #qLabel 11px, .modes a 12px nav links, .comp-cue 12px. Three uses are further off because the backdrop is not --sheet: .chip small on --accent-soft = 3.86:1 (style.css:374); .heard-head and .verdict-radius span on --paper = 4.08:1 (style.css:379, 749); and .foot (style.css:630-635) is --grey at 10px on color-mix(in srgb, var(--paper) 85%, transparent) over live map tiles = 4.16:1 over roads, 4.12:1 over land, 3.99:1 over parks, 3.96:1 over water. All computed from the token hex values, not estimated.
findings.userImpact: Each miss is small on its own, but together they cover nearly all of the app's explanatory copy — including the one instruction that changes the answer ("Don't tell it where you're from, let it guess") and the persistent privacy footer, which sits at 3.96:1 wherever the map happens to be showing ocean.
findings.suggestedFix: Move --grey to about #6B6D64 (5.0:1 on --sheet, 4.6:1 on --paper), which clears every one of these including the footer over water. For .chip small on --accent-soft, either use the darker grey or drop the tinted chip background.

findings.title: Four of the ten leaderboard deck tabs fail contrast when selected
findings.evidence: .board-tab.active { color: var(--row); background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--row) 13%, transparent); font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600 } over --sheet. Computed per deck hue: Spanish #A8722C on its own #f1e9dd tint = 3.41:1; Hindi-Urdu #2F7A63 on #e1eae5 = 4.19:1; Arabic #A8563F on #f1e6e0 = 4.21:1; Italian #7A6A1E on #ebe8dc = 4.38:1. All under 4.5:1 at 12px. The other six (English 5.43, French 5.40, Chinese 5.05, Portuguese 4.70, German 6.42, World Languages 5.80) pass.
findings.userImpact: The selected tab is the only thing telling you which deck's top ten you are looking at — there is no heading and no aria-selected either — and on four decks it is the least legible label in the row. Someone checking the Spanish board cannot easily confirm they are on it.
findings.suggestedFix: Darken the four failing hues (--hue-spanish, --hue-hindi-urdu, --hue-arabic, --hue-italian, css/style.css:34-42) by roughly 8-12% lightness, or raise the active tab's tint to a stronger fill with near-black text. Separately, give #boardTabs role="tablist" and the buttons role="tab" + aria-selected so the selection is not colour-only (WCAG 1.4.1).

findings.title: The play button's accessible name stays "Play clip" while the clip is playing
findings.evidence: game.html:109: <button class="dock-play" id="playBtn" aria-label="Play clip" title="play / pause (space)">. js/game.js:326-328 updatePlayIcon() only does $('#playIcon').innerHTML = playing ? ICON_PAUSE : ICON_PLAY — it never touches aria-label or aria-pressed. Verified live: after starting playback, playBtn.getAttribute('aria-label') is still "Play clip".
findings.userImpact: A screen reader user cannot tell whether the 20-second clip is currently playing. They press the button, the icon changes to a pause glyph they cannot see, and the button still announces "Play clip" — so the natural reading is that the press did nothing, and they press again and stop the audio they wanted.
findings.suggestedFix: In updatePlayIcon(), also set $('#playBtn').setAttribute('aria-label', playing ? 'Pause clip' : 'Play clip').

findings.title: Arabic, Spanish and German text carries no lang attribute, so screen readers pronounce it with an English voice
findings.evidence: js/app.js:1128-1132 defines SAMPLES with label: 'مصري', 'شامي', 'Español', 'Deutsch'; js/app.js:1225 renders them with b.textContent = s.label and sets no lang. js/app.js:629-631 sets $('#heardText').dir = rtl ? 'rtl' : 'ltr' for the transcript but never sets lang, so a full Arabic transcript in #heardText inherits <html lang="en">. Verified live: every .sample-btn and #heardText returns lang === null. Same for #resultRegion, which carries place names in their own scripts.
findings.userImpact: A blind Arabic speaker on the type-mode screen hears the two Arabic sample buttons rendered as English phonemes — unintelligible noise where the label "مصري" should be. The "what we heard" transcript of their own speech gets the same treatment, which is the one place on the card where being read back correctly matters most.
findings.suggestedFix: Add lang to each sample button when building it (b.lang = s.lang, with 'ar'/'es'/'de'/'en' added to the SAMPLES entries), and set $('#heardText').lang alongside the existing dir assignment in normalizeServer using the language the server already returns in r.language.

findings.title: Space is intercepted for every dock button during a round, so the ±5s buttons do the wrong thing
findings.evidence: document.addEventListener('keydown', e => { if ($('#dock').hidden || /^(INPUT|TEXTAREA)$/.test(document.activeElement.tagName)) return; if (e.code === 'Space') { e.preventDefault(); if (playing) media.pause(); else playClip(); } ... }) — the preventDefault fires for the whole round regardless of which control has focus, and the guard only exempts INPUT and TEXTAREA, not BUTTON. Verified live: with #playBtn focused, a Space keydown comes back with defaultPrevented === true.
findings.userImpact: A keyboard user tabs to "Back 5 seconds" or "Forward 5 seconds" and presses Space — the standard way to activate a button — and instead of seeking, the clip starts or stops. Chromium suppresses a button's synthesized click when the Space keydown default is prevented, so the button's own action does not run either. Enter still works, so this is recoverable, but Space is what most keyboard users reach for first.
findings.suggestedFix: Widen the early return to skip the shortcut whenever the focused element is itself a control: add || document.activeElement.closest('button, [role="slider"]') to the guard at js/game.js:465, so the page-level Space shortcut only fires when focus is on the map or the body.

findings.title: During a game round the page has no headings and every control sits outside a landmark
findings.evidence: setView('round') (js/game.js:161-168) hides #pickCard, #boardsCard and #finalCard — which are the only children of <main> — and shows #roundPill (game.html:101), #dock (game.html:105) and later #sheet (game.html:127), all three of which are siblings of <main>, not descendants. Verified live during a round: [...document.querySelector('main').children].filter(c => !c.hidden) === [] and every visible h1/h2/h3 count === 0. The landmark list is HEADER, NAV, MAIN (empty), FOOTER.
findings.userImpact: A screen reader user orients on an unfamiliar page by pulling up the heading list or jumping to main. During the whole guessing phase — which is most of the game — the heading list is empty and main contains nothing. The only route to the controls is pressing Tab from the top and hoping, and there is nothing at all naming what round they are on or what they are supposed to do.
findings.suggestedFix: Move #roundPill, #dock and #sheet inside <main>, and give the round view a visually-hidden <h1> that nextRound() updates ("Round 2 of 5 — listen and pin the voice"), plus one on the reveal sheet.

findings.title: The recording prompt rotates every 5 seconds with no way to pause or stop it
findings.evidence: setInterval(() => { if (state !== 'idle') return; promptIdx = (promptIdx + 1) % PROMPTS.length; ... }, 5000) — it runs for as long as the idle card is up, with no pause control anywhere in the UI and no matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') check (js/theme.js honours that query for the wash at line 161 and the contour field at line 68, but this does not). The text swaps in #promptText (index.html:48).
findings.userImpact: WCAG 2.2.2 (Pause, Stop, Hide) requires auto-updating information that runs longer than five seconds to be pausable. Someone with dyslexia or a reading disability starts reading "Complain about traffic like you're on the phone with your cousin" and it is replaced mid-sentence, then again, forever — and the prompt is the instruction that decides what they say into the mic.
findings.suggestedFix: Stop the rotation on first user interaction with the card (hover, focus, or any keydown), or halt it after one full cycle. At minimum, skip it when prefers-reduced-motion: reduce matches, which is the same query theme.js already reads.

findings.title: Nine reveal captions are hard-truncated at 190 characters and stop mid-word — 89% of Spanish games show at least one
findings.evidence:
Nine `hint` strings are exactly 189–190 chars and end mid-word, verified served live (`curl http://localhost:8123/js/clips.js | grep -o "pinned at Mexico City with wide rad\""` matches). They are rendered verbatim at js/game.js:509 `$('#revealHint').textContent = clip.hint || ''`.

  clips.js:1571  "...speech remains dominant and intelligible. Used the transcoded MP3 (original FLAC was slightly over the 40M"
  clips.js:1610  "...Country-level tag only, no specific city, pinned at Mexico City with wide rad"
  clips.js:1630  "...Archival 1946 radio recording, PD un"
  clips.js:1711  "...(no specific city), pinned at Madrid with wide radiu"
  clips.js:2089  "...it's his own file-tagged 'South of France' accent that actually places "
  clips.js:2325  "...so treat the pin location as the broad Delhi–Meerut belt, not"
  clips.js:2367  "...so an Indian speaker using Urdu here is expected, not a signal"
  clips.js:2731  "...the first few seconds just name the article subject (an American scientist), not the speaker's locati"
  clips.js:2772  "...the essay's subject (Yueyang, Hunan) is a different province from the speaker's"

Monte-Carlo over the real dealDeck (100k games/deck): at least one truncated caption appears in 88.7% of Spanish games, 72.0% of Chinese, 69.9% of Hindi–Urdu, 42.1% of French. Arabic, English and Portuguese are clean.
findings.userImpact: A stranger from TikTok plays Spanish, locks a guess, and the reveal sheet — the one moment the app has their full attention — shows a sentence that stops mid-word: "pinned at Mexico City with wide rad". Four of the seven playable decks do this on most games. It reads as an unfinished product on the first screen anyone screenshots.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the nine hints as complete player-facing sentences. Then add a check to tools/check-decks.mjs: fail if any hint is >=185 chars or does not end in terminal punctuation — the current validator checks source/licence/loudness but never looks at `hint`.

findings.title: Fifteen reveal captions are internal curation notes shown to players, including ones that tell them their score was pinned arbitrarily
findings.evidence:
`hint` is the only prose a player reads after a round (js/game.js:509). Fifteen clips carry the curator's working notes instead:

  clips.js:1551  "Ideal case: topic is a Brazilian town, completely unconnected to Argentina. Country-level accent tag only, pinned at Buenos Aires with wide radius."
  clips.js:1671  "Only country-level origin is documented (no specific city), so the pin is placed at the capital, Lima, with a wide accept radius. Duration 2:38, verified via direct file-page fetch."
  clips.js:1610  "NOT the already-used Mexican medical-article reading · this is a different reader/topic. Short (1:36) but clean..."
  clips.js:1571  "Soft ambient background music plays low under the narration... Used the transcoded MP3 (original FLAC was slightly over the 40M"
  clips.js:2751  "Dense science-article reading, no intro chit-chat. Any segment works. Same voice as the Carver clip above."
  clips.js:1387  "...(14:46 total, pick any segment)"
  clips.js:2325 / 2367  both open with "9m42s, verified direct file." / "3m17s, verified direct file."
  plus clips.js:1691, 1731, 1342, 2812 and the truncated set above.

"Same voice as the Carver clip above" refers to a list the player never sees. "Any segment works" is an instruction to the pipeline.
findings.userImpact: A player who just lost 3,000 points on the Peru round is told, in the reveal, that the answer pin was placed at the capital because nobody documented a city and the radius is deliberately wide. That is an admission the round was unfair, delivered at the exact moment they are deciding whether the scoring is trustworthy enough to keep playing or to post to the leaderboard.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace all fifteen with the one-line 'what you were listening to' voice already used well elsewhere in the same file (e.g. clips.js:3049 "Brazil's southernmost gaúcho capital · closer to Uruguay than to Rio, and it shows in the vowels."). Move the provenance notes into `source.note` or a non-shipping field.

findings.title: Two rounds in one game land on the identical answer pin — 26% of Hindi–Urdu games, 22% of Spanish
findings.evidence:
dealDeck de-duplicates on the label string only: `const placeOf = (c) => String(c.label);` (js/game.js:208, used at :214–215). Two pairs have different label strings and byte-identical coordinates:

  clips.js:2107 yt-vogXu3dUXzE  "Delhi, India"                lat 28.6139 lng 77.209
  clips.js:2321 hindi-urdu-spoken-hindi-wikipedia-indo-european-language-  "Delhi–Meerut Region, India"  lat 28.6139 lng 77.209

  clips.js:1443 yt-1tdOI0X0phE  "Buenos Aires, Argentina"     lat -34.6037 lng -58.3816
  clips.js:1546 spanish-argentine-spanish-reading-about-a-brazilian-to  "Argentina"  lat -34.6037 lng -58.3816

200,000-game simulation running the real dealDeck: an exactly-identical pin appears twice in 26.1% of Hindi–Urdu games and 21.9% of Spanish games. Near-identical pairs also slip through: French "Brussels, Belgium" vs "Belgium" 32.2 km apart and "Marseille, France" vs "Southern France, France" 83.3 km (two pins under 50 km in 15.2% of French games); English "Kingston, Jamaica" vs "Jamaica" 55.8 km (16.1% of games). The comment at js/game.js:200–205 states this is exactly what the dedupe exists to prevent.
findings.userImpact: A player finishes round 2 with the amber truth pin on Delhi, then in round 4 the pin drops on the same pixel and the sheet says "Delhi–Meerut Region, India". One game in four. It reads as a bug, and it also hands them the answer: they already know where that pin goes.
findings.suggestedFix: Key the dedupe on rounded coordinates rather than the label, e.g. `placeOf = (c) => c.lat.toFixed(1)+','+c.lng.toFixed(1)`, which also catches the 32 km and 56 km pairs. The existing fallback loop at js/game.js:218 already covers decks too thin to fill five distinct places.

findings.title: World Languages awards a perfect 5,000 and a 🎯 for pins over 1,000 km outside the language area
findings.evidence:
Six languages clips carry `"r": 1500` (clips.js:3283, 3454, 3486, 3635, 3771, 3824) and lockIn scores against the nearest of up to seven `alt` centres (js/game.js:481–487), then stamps a bull's-eye when pts === 5000 (js/game.js:508). lang-french has 7 centres (Paris, Montréal, Brussels, Geneva, Dakar, Kinshasa, Abidjan) with r=1500, so the union of bull's-eye discs is 6.7% of the earth's surface (200k-point Monte Carlo). Verified distances, all inside r:

  London  -> Paris    343 km  = 5000 🎯 on the French clip
  New York-> Montréal 534 km  = 5000 🎯 on the French clip
  Berlin  -> Brussels 651 km  = 5000 🎯 on the French clip
  Rome    -> Geneva   697 km  = 5000 🎯 on the French clip
  Madrid  -> Paris   1053 km  = 5000 🎯 on the French clip
  Paris   -> Lisbon  1453 km  = 5000 🎯 on the Portuguese (Brazil) clip (r=1500, clips.js:3824)
  Paris   -> Zürich   488 km  = 5000 🎯 on the German clip (r=600, clips.js:3740)

So one pin on Paris is a declared bull's-eye on three different languages, and one pin on Berlin is a bull's-eye on Russian, German and French.
findings.userImpact: A player hears the French clip, isn't sure, and pins London. The app tells them "343 km away → +5,000 pts 🎯". They know London is not French-speaking, so the score stops meaning anything — and on the deck whose whole premise is 'where is this language spoken'. Note the blind-pin exploit is mild (always-Berlin averages 6,825/25,000), so this is a credibility problem rather than a leaderboard-breaking one.
findings.suggestedFix: Cut r on the seven multi-centre languages clips to roughly 500–700 km. With up to seven alt centres the union already covers the language's real spread; the 1500 km disc is doing the job twice.

findings.title: The Hindi clip's 20-second window is 11.5 seconds of silence, and the silence bills the player's listening budget
findings.evidence:
clips.js:2317 `hindi-urdu-spoken-hindi-wikipedia-indo-european-language-`, `start: 10`, so the played window is 10.0–30.0 s of the file. `ffmpeg -ss 10 -t 20 -i clips/hindi-urdu/hindi-urdu-spoken-hindi-wikipedia-indo-european-language-.mp3 -af silencedetect=n=-40dB:d=0.5` returns eight silent runs totalling 11.5 s, including single gaps of 3.80 s (1.88–5.69) and 3.45 s (13.54–16.99). Window mean_volume is -19.4 dB against a deck-wide range of -14.4 to -18.6.

This is the single worst window of all 111 local clips (next worst is lang-somali at 7.3 s, spread over short natural pauses).

The budget is charged against playhead delta, not speech: js/game.js:401–403 `const delta = media.time() - lastTickT; if (delta > 0 && delta < 1.5) budgetLeft -= delta`. Replaying the window three times spends ~35 s of the 60 s budget on dead air.

data/pinned-windows.json records `"speech_seconds": 15` for this exact window, which the audio contradicts. 100k-game simulation: dealt in 42.3% of Hindi–Urdu games.
findings.userImpact: Two out of five Hindi–Urdu games, a player taps play and gets ~8.5 seconds of Hindi broken by two four-second silences. It sounds like the audio cut out. They replay it, which is the correct instinct, and burn most of their 60-second budget on the same silence before the play button greys out.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-pin this clip's window. The file is 240 s and the 30–40 s region measures -16.3 to -17.5 dB mean with no long gaps — `start: 30` is a clean 20 s. Also worth adding a silence check to the window-pinning tool, since the recorded speech_seconds audit did not catch this.

findings.title: lang-swahili ships a truncated credit line and is the only clip in the app with no link to its original
findings.evidence:
clips.js:3542–3546:

  "who": "Voice of America Swahili Service (voaswahili.com",
  "host": "Voice of America",
  "license": "US government work (public domain)",
  "page": "",

The `who` string is cut with an unclosed parenthesis and renders verbatim into `#srcWho` (js/game.js:527). `page: ""` makes renderSource hide the link (js/game.js:537 `link.hidden = !src.page`), so the "open the original" affordance in game.html:137 disappears. I checked all 114 distinct non-YouTube `source.page` URLs with a live fetch — every one returns 200; this is the only clip with no URL at all. tools/check-decks.mjs requires host/licence/who but never requires `page`, which is why it passes. Dealt in 19.3% of World Languages games.
findings.userImpact: One World Languages game in five, the credit panel reads "Voice of America Swahili Service (voaswahili.com" with a dangling bracket and no way to reach the recording. On an app whose reveal panel is built to credit people properly, it is the one place the credit visibly failed.
findings.suggestedFix: Close the string and set `page` to the VOA Swahili source URL. Add `if (!s.page) note(...)` to the source check in tools/check-decks.mjs.

findings.title: Every YouTube clip's reveal caption is a word-for-word restatement of the licence line 30px below it
findings.evidence:
All 44 YouTube clips carry `hint: "Streamed from YouTube — the creator gets the view."` while their `source.license` is "Streamed from YouTube — the creator keeps the view". game.html:131 renders the hint and game.html:136 renders the licence in the same sheet, four rows apart. Two of the 44 (yt--djB-PWhdl0 at clips.js:1120 and yt-_3pnHcYuzOQ at clips.js:1153) use "·" where the other 42 use "—", so the identical sentence ships with two different punctuation marks.

Ratio matters: 13 of 22 English clips, 9 of 13 Hindi–Urdu and 6 of 13 French are YouTube, so most rounds in those decks get boilerplate where local clips get a real payoff line ("Broad West Riding · the vowels do the work.").
findings.userImpact: A player finishes an English round and the reveal says the same sentence twice in a row. Where a local clip would have told them something worth knowing about what they just heard, the YouTube rounds — the majority of the English deck — say nothing.
findings.suggestedFix: Set the YouTube hint from the gate record already stored on every one of these clips (`gate.title`, `gate.author`, `gate.evidence`) — e.g. "Street interview, Guardian News" — or leave `hint` empty so the sheet collapses to the licence line alone. The boilerplate is written at tools/source-clips.mjs:565 and tools/stage-vetted.mjs:43.

findings.title: A clip the owner's own leak audit flagged is still live and was never triaged
findings.evidence:
data/leak-audit.json contains exactly one entry: `{"id":"yt-0xDjLQpsmUM","deck":"french","label":"Marseille, France","start":149,"why":"SAYS PLACE: Paris"}`. The clip is unchanged in the deck at clips.js:1887 with `start: 149`. data/leak-triage.json (same timestamp, 08-13 09:02) resolves only the five entries from data/hosted-audit.json, all in the languages deck — this YouTube entry was never adjudicated either way.

The source video is "Ce que les Marseillais pensent des Parisiens", so the Paris mention is near-certainly a wrong-direction cue rather than a giveaway. Scoring consequence if a player follows it: Marseille to Paris is 660 km, r=60, french decay 350, giving 5000·exp(-600/350) ≈ 900 of 5000.

I could not listen to the window to confirm what is actually said at 149 s — flagging that the owner's tool raised it and nothing closed the loop.
findings.userImpact: A player hears "Paris" repeatedly in a clip whose answer is Marseille, pins Paris, and loses roughly 4,100 of 5,000 points for listening carefully to the one place name in the audio.
findings.suggestedFix: Either run the triage step over data/leak-audit.json the way it was run over hosted-audit.json and record a verdict, or move this clip's window off 149 s. Low urgency — but the unresolved audit file is the kind of thing that looks like a missed step rather than a decision.

findings.title: Double-tap on "next clip" skips a round — the advanceLock guard is a no-op
findings.evidence:
advance() sets `advanceLock = true`, then calls `nextRound()` **synchronously**, and nextRound() line 249 does `advanceLock = false` — all inside the same call stack, before advance() returns. The lock's lifetime is zero for every round except the last, so the guard added for exactly this bug (see the comment at 534-535: "a doubled 'next clip' tap used to skip a round outright") never fires.

Reproduced live at http://localhost:8123/game.html with two clicks 180 ms apart (a normal phone double-tap):
  round label before: "Round 1/5"
  after ONE double-tap on #nextBtn: "Round 3/5"   <-- round 2 never played

Once round and roundLog desync, the lockIn guard at line 478 (`if (roundLog.length > round) return;`) also stops working, because it assumes roundLog.length === round. A second run captured the actual POST body (fetch intercepted, nothing written to the live board):
  rounds: [ar-4531, ar-3190, ar-3190, ar-1907, ar-1907]  // 5 entries, 3 distinct clips
and a third run's final card listed: Hausa +187, German +941, German +941, Italian +1,379, Somali +233.

The server accepts it: rounds.length === 5 and sum === points both hold, so api/scores.js:122-124 passes and the score posts.
findings.userImpact: A player taps "next clip" twice — common on a phone, and the code comment shows it was already observed in the wild — and silently loses a clip. They pay for 5 rounds and hear 4 (or 3). The final card lists the same city twice, which reads as a bug. Worse for the leaderboard the launch is built around: after one skip, a double-tap on "lock it in" logs the same round twice and adds its points to `total` twice, so 25,000/25,000 can be reached by nailing 3 clips instead of 5. Two extra taps, no tooling required.
findings.suggestedFix: Don't let nextRound() own the lock. Either release it asynchronously (`advanceLock = true; round += 1; ...; setTimeout(() => { advanceLock = false; }, 400)`) or, better, make advance() idempotent per reveal: capture the round the reveal belongs to and bail if it has moved (`const r = round; if (r !== revealRound) return;`). Separately, harden lockIn against desync by keying on the round index rather than length: `if (roundLog.some(x => x.round === round)) return;` and store `round` in each log entry.

findings.title: A clip that fails to load leaves the round permanently stuck on "Clip is loading, one sec…"
findings.evidence:
playClip() returns early when `!media.ready()` (file mode: `audioEl.readyState >= 1`) and registers `media.whenReady(playClip)`, which is a one-shot `loadedmetadata` listener (js/media.js:157-160). If the fetch failed, `loadedmetadata` never fires — the element fires `error` instead, and there is no `error` listener anywhere on #clipAudio. media.load() is never re-called, so there is no retry.

Critically, the clip-swap rescue at js/game.js:299-312 lives inside the `media.play()` **rejection** handler, which is unreachable here — playClip returns before ever calling play(). So `clipSwaps` never increments and no replacement is dealt.

Reproduced live (pointed the arabic deck at a nonexistent mp3, started a game, tapped ▶ four times over 4.8 s):
  audio.readyState: 0, audio.error.code: 4, networkState: 3
  toasts fired: ["Clip is loading, one sec…" x4]
  playBtn.disabled: false, listens: "1:00 of listening left", pinHint unchanged
The state never resolves.

sw.js:42 deliberately excludes /clips/ from the cache, so there is no offline fallback for exactly this request.
findings.userImpact: On a patchy mobile connection — the launch's stated audience — one dropped clip request kills the round. The player taps play, is told "Clip is loading, one sec…", waits, taps again, gets the same message forever. The listening timer sits at 1:00 the whole time, so the UI insists nothing has gone wrong. They either guess blind or leave. It never recovers even after the network comes back.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an `error` listener on the audio element inside media.js and surface it as a rejection/event the game can act on, then route it into the same swap path as a play() rejection. At minimum: give whenReady a timeout, and on `error` or timeout run the clipSwaps swap (`deck[round] = replacementClip(); media.clear(); media.load(...)`) with a truthful toast, falling back to "the audio is stuck this round, lock a guess or skip ahead" plus `#playBtn.disabled = true` so the button stops lying.

findings.title: A removed, private, or embed-disabled YouTube video produces a silent dead round with no error handler
findings.evidence:
The player is constructed with only `onReady` and `onStateChange`. There is no `onError` handler, so YouTube error codes 100 (removed/private), 101/150 (embedding disabled by the owner), 2 and 5 are swallowed entirely.

The game cannot detect it either: `ready()` returns `ytReady` (true — the *player* is fine, the *video* is not), and `play()` returns `Promise.resolve()` unconditionally once `yt` exists. So playClip's `.then()` at js/game.js:295-297 sets `playing = true` even though nothing is playing. From then on every tap on ▶ hits `if (playing) media.pause()` → `yt.pauseVideo()`, which produces no state change on a video that never started, so `onStateChange` never emits 'pause' and `playing` is stuck true for the rest of the round.

Reproduced live: forced a deck of YouTube clips with videoId 'ZZZZdeadZZZ', started a game, tapped ▶ three times over 4.5 s:
  toasts fired: []          (zero — no message of any kind)
  listens: "1:00 of listening left"   (frozen)
  playerFill width: "0%", playIcon: still the ▶ triangle, playBtn.disabled: false
Control test in the same session with a real videoId (I4k8dR04TzA) played correctly: listens went 1:00 → 0:56, fill 23.7%, icon switched to ⏸ — so the environment was not the cause.

44 of the 155 clips are YouTube-sourced: accents 13/22, hindi-urdu 9/13, french 6/13, chinese 5/12, spanish 4/14, portuguese 4/12, german 3/3.
findings.userImpact: YouTube videos get deleted, set to private, or have embedding turned off by their uploader at any time, with no notice to you. When it happens, the player gets a round of total silence: no sound, no error, no swap, a play button that does nothing, and a timer frozen at 1:00 telling them they still have a minute of listening left. They have to pin blind. Because nothing is logged or reported, you will not learn about it either — the "didn't play right" flag chip is the only signal, and it depends on the player bothering.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `onError` to the YT.Player events in media.js and emit it as an event the game listens for (`emit('error')`). In game.js, treat it the same as a play() rejection: increment clipSwaps, swap in a replacement, toast honestly. Also make media.play() reject for YT when the state does not leave UNSTARTED within ~3 s, so `playing` cannot be stuck true, and reset `playing = false` on that path.

findings.title: The 60-second listening budget is completely bypassable on YouTube clips by using the scrubber or the ±5s buttons instead of ▶
findings.evidence:
YouTube's IFrame API starts playback when `seekTo()` is called on a *cued* (never-played) video. scrubTo() and seekBy() both call `seekTo()` → `media.seek()` → `yt.seekTo(t, true)` without ever going through playClip(), so the module-level `playing` flag stays false. The budget is only charged inside `media.on('timeupdate')`, which bails at js/game.js:397 with `if (!playing) return;` before it reaches the `budgetLeft -= delta` line.

Reproduced live on a fresh round with a real YouTube clip, never touching the play button — one pointerdown/move/up on #playerBar:
  before:  listens "1:00 of listening left", fill "0%"
  +6 s:    listens "1:00 of listening left", fill "47.9466%"
  +11 s:   listens "1:00 of listening left", fill "72.9173%"
The fill advancing in real time means the YT poll is running, which only happens in the PLAYING state. The budget never moved. YouTube's own `endSeconds` (media.js:97-101) stops it at the 20 s bound, and then another scrub replays it — for free, unlimited.
findings.userImpact: Two faces. For an honest player: touching the progress bar starts audio they did not ask for, and the ▶ button still reads as "not playing" — confusing. For anyone competing on a prize leaderboard: the 60-second budget, which is the game's only difficulty constraint, does not exist on any YouTube clip. On the German deck that is every clip; on hindi-urdu 9 of 13; on English Accents 13 of 22. Replay the 20-second window as many times as you like and the timer still says 1:00.
findings.suggestedFix: Charge the budget on wall-clock playback rather than on the `playing` flag: drop the `if (!playing) return;` early-out and instead derive "is sound coming out" from the media layer (`media.isPlaying()` — audioEl.paused for file, ytState === PLAYING for YT). Alternatively, have media.seek() for YT pause immediately after seeking when the game did not initiate playback (`yt.seekTo(t, true); if (!gameWantsPlay) yt.pauseVideo();`).

findings.title: The play button never shows a pause icon for the 111 local mp3 clips, and the scrubber steps at 4 fps instead of animating
findings.file: js/game.js:295-297 (playing set only in the play() promise) with js/game.js:414-418 and 346-353
findings.evidence:
`playing = true` is assigned only inside `media.play().then(...)`. For an <audio> element the `play` event fires as a queued task *before* the play() promise resolves, so `media.on('play')` at line 415 runs `updatePlayIcon()` while `playing` is still false — it paints ICON_PLAY — and `startRaf()`, whose tick at line 350 evaluates `rafId = (playing || dragFrac !== null) ? requestAnimationFrame(tick) : 0` and shuts the loop down. Nothing calls updatePlayIcon() or startRaf() again after the promise resolves.

Reproduced live on the arabic deck (/clips/ar/ar-3647.mp3):
  event order logged: loadedmetadata, canplay, play, playing   (play before playing/promise)
  after 1.5 s of playback: audio.paused = false, playIcon = '<path d="M8 5v14l11-7z">'  (the ▶ triangle)
  after tapping again:     audio.paused = true,  playIcon = '<path d="M8 5v14l11-7z">'  (identical)
  fill samples vs currentTime: 3.586% held over t=0.841→0.984, then 4.921% over t=1.021→1.268, then 6.339%
  — 1.34% jumps every ~268 ms, i.e. the 4 Hz `timeupdate` cadence, not per-frame rAF.
The same test on a YouTube clip produced ICON_PAUSE correctly, because YT's play() resolves in a microtask before the 'play' emit — proving the pause icon is intended and simply never reached for file clips.
findings.userImpact: 111 of 155 clips are local mp3s, including all 40 Arabic (the first tile and the leaderboard default) and all 26 World Languages. For those, the audio plays but the button still shows ▶, so the player's first instinct is to tap it again — which pauses the clip they just started. The progress bar visibly stutters four times a second, which on a launch-day product reads as a broken player. The whole comment at line 345 ("timeupdate only fires ~4x/second, which looks steppy. Paint on every frame instead") describes a feature that is dead for the majority of clips.
findings.suggestedFix: Set `playing = true` optimistically before awaiting, or drive it from the media layer instead of the promise. Simplest correct fix: in the `media.on('play')` handler set `playing = true` first, then `updatePlayIcon(); startRaf();` — and keep the promise's `.catch()` for the failure path (`playing = false`).

findings.title: Arabic scoring is far more forgiving than the code claims: a 300 km miss is a perfect 5,000, not 30%
findings.file: js/game.js:136-140 (scoreFor) and js/game.js:96-108 (MODE_DECAY comment) against js/clips.js
findings.evidence:
scoreFor returns 5000 outright when `km <= radius`. Every one of the 40 Arabic clips carries `r: 350`, while MODE_DECAY.arabic is 250. The comment at line 97-98 states "a 300 km miss in the Arabic deck used to keep 55% of the points and now keeps 30%" — arithmetically impossible, because 300 ≤ 350 short-circuits to 5000. Computed against the shipped data:
  scoreFor(300, 350) = 5000   (comment predicts 1500)
  scoreFor(400, 350) = 4094
  scoreFor(500, 350) = 2744
The bull's-eyes overlap heavily inside the deck. A single pin dropped on Beirut scores a perfect 5,000 on 8 of the 40 clips: Beirut 0 km, Irbid 151, Nablus 187, Amman 219, Jerusalem 236, Hebron 265, Gaza 283, Aleppo 297 — all under r=350. A single pin on Batna covers 7 more: Batna 0, Constantine 98, Setif 98, Annaba 207, Djelfa 283, Algiers 309, Blida 317. Two pins account for 15 of 40 clips at maximum score.
(Same pattern, by design per the comment, in World Languages: r values of 1500 with decay 750 mean Persian, Mandarin, Russian, Indonesian, French and Brazilian Portuguese are perfect anywhere within 1,500 km.)
findings.userImpact: Arabic is the first tile on the picker and the default leaderboard deck. As shipped it does not test pinning a city — it tests naming a region. Anyone who can hear "Levantine" and drop a pin somewhere between Beirut and Amman takes 5,000 without knowing whether it was Gaza, Irbid or Aleppo. 25,000/25,000 is cheap, so the board fills with tied perfect scores, and because api/scores.js:61 orders `points.desc,ts.asc`, the ranking among them is decided by who posted first. For a board attached to prizes that is the whole ladder collapsing.
findings.suggestedFix: Decide which the radius is: a genuine label-uncertainty allowance, or a scoring floor. If the ARCADE city labels really are only accurate to ±350 km, keep it but raise the ceiling differently (e.g. taper from full points at r/3 to 5000 at r). If the labels are city-accurate, drop r to something like 60-100 km for the Arabic deck, matching hindi-urdu (60-150). Either way, correct the worked example in the MODE_DECAY comment — as written it describes a curve that starts 350 km further out than the reader thinks.

findings.title: The rank in "Posted! You're #N" contradicts the leaderboard rendered directly below it
findings.evidence:
The rank counts raw rows: `points=gt.${points}` with `Prefer: count=exact`, i.e. every score row in the deck that beats yours, including multiple rows from the same nickname and including your own earlier better runs. The board served by the GET path deliberately does the opposite — it dedupes to one row per nickname ("Best run per nickname… a board where one grinder's ten runs fill all ten slots is a wall, not a ladder", lines 68-75) before slicing to 10.

submitScore (js/game.js:575-576) toasts the raw rank and then immediately calls `loadBoard()`, so both numbers are on screen at the same moment. With three repeat players holding five rows each above you, the toast says #16 while the board shows you 4th.
findings.userImpact: Right after posting, a player is told a rank and then looks at the top-ten list where they sit several places higher — or is told #16 while visibly appearing in a ten-row board. It reads as a broken leaderboard, which is the one feature the TikTok push is pointing people at. It gets worse the more the game is replayed, so it will be invisible at launch and obvious by day two.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the rank the same way the board does: count distinct nicknames whose best score beats yours. Cheapest version without a view — fetch `select=nickname,points&game_type=eq.X&points=gt.N&order=points.desc&limit=500`, count `new Set(rows.map(r => r.nickname.toLowerCase()))`, add 1. Or add a Postgres view keyed on `lower(nickname)` with `max(points)` and count against that.

findings.title: Tapping "leaderboards" in the header abandons the game in progress and leaves the last round's pins and arc drawn on the deck picker
findings.evidence:
`.brand` is `position: fixed; z-index: 12` (css/style.css:124-125), above `.hud` (z-index 5), so the header nav is tappable during 'round' and 'reveal'. showBoards() pauses audio and swaps the view but never calls `clearRoundLayers()` or `map.fitBounds(WORLD)`; #boardsBack does `history.replaceState(...)` then `setView('pick')` and likewise clears nothing. Compare #switchType at line 797, which does both.

Reproduced live from a reveal (pin dropped, locked in, "4,560 km away → +0 pts"):
  at reveal:      markers 2, overlay paths 1, tiles at zoom 3
  on boards:      markers 2, paths 1, zoom 3
  after "decks":  #pickCard shown, markers 2, paths 1, still zoom 3
The game state (round, total, roundLog) survives but nothing can return to it.
findings.userImpact: A player four rounds into a game taps "leaderboards" out of curiosity, then "decks" to get back, and lands on the deck picker with their run gone and no warning — plus a leftover guess pin, amber truth pin and dashed line sitting on a map still zoomed into wherever the last round was. The picker is the screen new arrivals from TikTok also see, so anyone who backs out of a game hands it to a friend looking like a half-drawn map.
findings.suggestedFix: Have #boardsBack restore the view it came from (remember the previous view in showBoards and return to it), and if it does drop to 'pick', call `clearRoundLayers(); map.fitBounds(WORLD);` the way #switchType does. If abandoning is intended, at least confirm it mid-game.

findings.title: Space bar cannot activate "lock it in" — the global shortcut swallows it and plays audio instead
findings.evidence:
The document-level keydown handler only exempts INPUT and TEXTAREA. With #lockBtn (or #backBtn / #fwdBtn) focused, `e.code === 'Space'` matches, `e.preventDefault()` runs — which cancels the button's native activation — and playClip() is called instead.

Reproduced live: pinned the map, focused #lockBtn, dispatched a Space keydown:
  defaultPrevented: true, reveal sheet shown: false, audio.paused: false
The guess was not locked; the clip started playing.
findings.userImpact: A keyboard or switch-control user tabs to "lock it in" and presses Space, the universal button-activation key. Nothing locks; the clip starts playing instead. Enter still works, so it is recoverable, but it will read as a dead button.
findings.suggestedFix: Skip the shortcut when the focused element is itself an interactive control: `if (document.activeElement?.closest('button, input, textarea, a, [role="slider"]')) return;` before the Space branch — or narrow the exemption to `document.activeElement === document.body`.

findings.title: When the game token never mints, the player is told to "play one through" after doing exactly that
findings.evidence:
mint() retries three times and then gives up silently, leaving `gameToken = null`. submitScore sends `token: null`; tokenAge() (api/feedback.js:39-48) returns null for a non-string, so api/scores.js:118-120 replies `invalid_token`, and the client maps both `too_fast` and `invalid_token` to: "Scores only post for a full game, start to finish. Play one through and try again."

The same message appears if FEEDBACK_SECRET and SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY are both unset in production, since mintToken() returns '' (api/feedback.js:32) and `d.token || null` turns that into null.
findings.userImpact: Someone whose connection blipped during the first three seconds of the game plays all five rounds honestly and is then accused of not finishing. They will play again, hit the same thing, and conclude the leaderboard is broken.
findings.suggestedFix: Track why the token is missing. If `gameToken === null` at submit time, say "couldn't reach the scoreboard when this game started, so it can't be posted" and offer a retry that re-mints and waits, rather than reusing the anti-cheat copy. Keeping the mint retry alive for the whole game (instead of stopping at attempt 3) would also help.

findings.title: An auto-swapped replacement clip can repeat a place already used earlier in the same game
findings.evidence: dealDeck de-dupes by `String(c.label)` specifically so "one game never asks the same place twice, since two identical answers in five rounds reads as a bug rather than a coincidence" (lines 202-206). replacementClip filters only on `c.id`: `const used = new Set(deck.map((c) => c.id));`. Decks have many clips per place — chinese has 12 clips across 8 distinct labels, hindi-urdu 13 across 10, accents 22 across 16 — so a swap can readily land on a second clip from a place already dealt.
findings.userImpact: After a clip fails to play and the game swaps one in, the player can get the same answer city twice in five rounds, and the final scorecard lists it twice. It is the exact outcome the deal logic was written to avoid.
findings.suggestedFix: Filter replacements by label as well: `const used = new Set(deck.map(c => String(c.label)));` and `pool.filter(c => !used.has(String(c.label)))`, falling back to the id-only filter if that leaves the pool empty.

findings.title: A one-character nickname is silently rewritten to "anon" while the toast still congratulates you by rank
findings.evidence: The input has `maxlength="20"` but no minimum. The server does `if (nickname.length < 2) nickname = 'anon';` and returns the corrected name in the response, but js/game.js:575 ignores `d.nickname` and toasts only the rank, then loadBoard() renders the board — which now shows "anon".
findings.userImpact: Someone types "M" or "J" as their handle, posts, is told "Posted! You're #3 on Arabic", and then scans the board for their name and cannot find it. On a launch where the leaderboard is the shareable artefact, that looks like the score was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Enforce it client-side (`minlength="2"`, disable the post button below 2 characters) or show what actually got saved: `toast(\`Posted as ${d.nickname} — you're #${d.rank} on ${deckName}.\`)`.

findings.title: A retrying token mint from an abandoned game can overwrite the current game's token and get a legitimate score rejected
findings.evidence:
`mint(attempt)` closes over nothing game-specific — it assigns to the module-level `gameToken` — and its retry chain is never cancelled. startGame() sets `gameToken = null` and starts a fresh chain, but a chain from an earlier abandoned game is still scheduled (attempt 2 at +15 s, attempt 3 at +27 s). If one of those late attempts succeeds during a *later* game, it overwrites that game's token with one minted at that moment. Should the new game then finish within 75 s of the overwrite, api/scores.js:118 rejects it as `too_fast`.

Precondition: the first game's initial mint must have failed at least once, so this only happens after a network blip. I have not reproduced it end to end — it is a code-reading finding.
findings.userImpact: A player on a flaky connection picks a deck, backs out, picks another, plays it properly, and is told their score "only posts for a full game, start to finish". Rare, and it needs a failed first mint, but it is unrecoverable within that game.
findings.suggestedFix: Tag each chain with the game it belongs to and drop late results: `const myGame = ++gameSeq;` inside startGame, then `.then(d => { if (myGame !== gameSeq) return; gameToken = d.token || null; ... })`.

findings.title: Header nav wraps into stacked single words on every phone width
findings.evidence: Measured live at 375x812, 375x667 and 390x844. The three links need 293.1px total (99.9 + 99.6 + 89.6 + gaps, at the ≤620px font size of 12px); the widest phone in the CSS pixel range (430px, iPhone 15/16 Pro Max) leaves only 259px after the 125px logo, 30px .brand padding and the 16px flex gap. Range check: wraps at 320/360/375/390/393/412/430, first fits at ~480px. Word-level rect measurement at 375px returns visualLines ['read','my','accent'] and ['guess','the','voice']. .brand grows from ~59px to 93.8px tall on both pages. No media query touches .modes below 620px except a font/padding shrink.
findings.userImpact: Every phone visitor — i.e. the entire TikTok audience — lands on a page whose top-left header reads as three ragged columns of stacked words ('read / my / accent', 'guess / the / voice', 'leaderboards'). It is the first thing on screen and it reads as a broken stylesheet.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a phone rule that stops the nav from being the flex item that shrinks: e.g. under @media (max-width: 620px) give .modes a { white-space: nowrap } and either shorten the labels ('read' / 'play' / 'boards'), drop the logo wordmark to the mark only, or make .modes a horizontally scrollable row.

findings.title: Game dock has no phone layout: the round's only instruction is ellipsised and the scrubber collapses
findings.evidence: Live measurement during a round. .dock is a flex row with three fixed buttons (34+50+34), a 12px gap x4, 28px padding and a flex-shrink:0 85px 'lock it in'. That leaves .dock-mid: 129px @430, 89px @390, 74px @375, 59px @360. #pinHint needs 199px and has white-space:nowrap + text-overflow:ellipsis, so it renders 'listen, then tap t…' @390 and 'listen, then t…' @375 (measured with the element's own computed font). #playerBar is the same 89px/74px wide for a 20-second window (4.4px per second). #listens ('1:00 of listening left', natural width 139px) wraps to 2 lines @390-430 and 3 lines @375 and below, so the dock is 110.1px tall @390 and 126.4px @375. When the budget runs out the string becomes 'listening time up. Trust your ear, drop the pin' (296px natural) and wraps further. The one archival clip (spanish, year<1990, ~36% of Spanish games deals it) shows #eraChip, which wraps to 79.6px and makes the dock 195.7px tall — 25% of the screen. No media query in the file touches .dock.
findings.userImpact: A first-time player on any phone is told 'listen, then tap t…' — the instruction is cut off before the word 'map', which is the entire thing they need to know. Once a pin exists the hint becomes 'drag the pin t…'. The scrubber is too narrow to scrub with a thumb, and the listening budget reads as a wrapped scrap of text.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a phone breakpoint that stacks the dock: put the play/skip cluster and 'lock it in' on one row and give .dock-mid the full dock width on a second row (e.g. @media (max-width: 620px) { .dock { flex-wrap: wrap } .dock-mid { flex-basis: 100%; order: -1 } }). Also give .dock-mid a real min-width so it can never be squeezed below the hint's needs.

findings.title: Below ~356px viewport the scrubber's hit area sits on top of 'lock it in'
findings.evidence: At 320x568: .dock-mid's own box collapses to 19px, but its grid children keep their 56.7px min-content width and overflow (computed overflow is 'visible'). Measured rects: #playerBar l=179 r=235.7, #lockBtn l=210 r=295 — a 25.7px overlap. document.elementFromPoint inside that overlap returns 'playerBar', and .player-hit has touch-action:none plus a pointerdown scrub handler. Threshold: the dock needs 279px of fixed content + 56.7px min-content for the middle = 335.7px, and .dock width is min(580px, 100% - 20px), so the overlap begins below ~356px viewport width.
findings.userImpact: On a 320px-wide screen (iPhone SE 1st gen, and any iPhone mini with iOS Display Zoom set to Larger Text) a thumb landing on the left third of 'lock it in' scrubs the clip instead of locking the guess — the primary action of every round silently does the wrong thing.
findings.suggestedFix: Same stacking fix as the dock finding; failing that, add overflow:hidden to .dock-mid so its children cannot escape their column, and let .dock wrap instead of overlapping.

findings.title: The reveal sheet covers the answer pin the map just flew to
findings.evidence: lockIn calls map.fitBounds(..., { paddingTopLeft: [60, 90], paddingBottomRight: [60, 300] }) — 300px reserved at the bottom for the sheet. Measured the real sheet across all 155 clips at 390x844: height 495px min, 534px median, 617px max (all 155 exceed 300px). Empirical check with real Leaflet geometry (guess = Paris, truth = Cairo, same padding call): truth pin lands at container y=388 while the sheet's top edge is y=377 — the answer pin is behind the sheet. The visible map strip between the round pill (bottom 107) and the sheet is only ~270px.
findings.userImpact: The payoff of every round — your pin, the real place, and the dashed line between them — is framed into a band whose lower 200-300px is under the reveal sheet, so on a phone the player usually sees only their own pin and a line running off under the sheet.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the bottom padding from the sheet's actual height at reveal time (e.g. measure #sheet after setView('reveal') and refit), or cap the sheet and pass Math.round(window.innerHeight * 0.6) the way js/app.js:166 already does for the result card.

findings.title: In landscape, 'next clip' is entirely below the reveal sheet's fold for 90 of 155 clips
findings.evidence: At 844x390 the sheet is 304.2px tall with a 300px client area. Looping every real clip's label/hint/source through the reveal DOM and measuring #nextBtn's offset inside the sheet: 90 of 155 clips put the button's top below the 300px fold (up to 82px below), and all 155 put its bottom below it. The sheet has no drag handle and no scroll affordance (the .sheet-handle rule only applies to #resultCard on index.html).
findings.userImpact: A player who turns their phone sideways — natural for a map game — finishes a round and sees a reveal panel with no visible way to continue. They have to guess that the panel scrolls. On the 65 remaining clips they see a clipped sliver of the button.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a short-viewport rule for .sheet (e.g. @media (max-height: 500px) { .sheet { max-height: 92dvh } }) and/or pin #nextBtn to the sheet as a sticky footer so it is always on screen.

findings.title: The privacy/data footer is capped at 50% of the screen width and partly hidden behind the card
findings.evidence: 'position: fixed; bottom: 10px; left: 50%; transform: translateX(-50%)' with no width — a shrink-to-fit fixed box positioned from left:50% can only use the remaining 50% of the containing block, so max-width: calc(100% - 24px) never applies. Computed width is exactly 187.5px at 375, 195px at 390, 422px at 844 — always 50% of the viewport. The index.html line ('it listens to your accent, not your words · audio never stored unless you donate it · privacy') therefore renders as 4 lines of 10px mono (measured 70px tall, line tops 592/608/623/639 at 375x667), and the idle card's bottom edge (605.8) paints over the first line. With a longer rotating prompt the card grows to 544px, falls back to top alignment, and covers two lines. Same 50% cap on game.html's footer (195px wide, 3 lines).
findings.userImpact: The only place the app states that audio is not stored is squeezed into half the screen as four lines of 10px type, with its opening clause hidden behind the card. On a launch where 'is this recording me?' is the first question a stranger asks, the answer is unreadable.
findings.suggestedFix: Give .foot an explicit width instead of relying on max-width: e.g. left: 12px; right: 12px; transform: none; margin: 0 auto, or width: calc(100% - 24px); left: 0; transform: none. Also raise .hud's bottom padding (or lower .foot) so the card can never sit on it.

findings.title: Result card no longer docks as a bottom sheet on phones — it centres over the map answer
findings.file: css/style.css:154 (.hud { align-content: safe center }) vs :709 (.card.peek { margin-top: auto; margin-bottom: 0 })
findings.evidence: This is a regression from the uncommitted edit that landed during this pass (git diff shows .card changed from margin:auto to margin:0 auto and .hud gained align-content: safe center; align-items: start). With align-content doing the centring, the grid row is sized to the item (gridTemplateRows computes 371.359px, not the 710px content box), so .card.peek's margin-top:auto has no free space to absorb and computes to 0px. Measured at 390x844 after calling renderResult with a normal verdict: card top 251.3, bottom 622.7 — dead centre, 169px of empty space below it. It was bottom-docked at 792 before the change (verified with a synthetic control div using the old margin:auto in the same document: bottom 792). Meanwhile js/app.js:166 still frames the answer with paddingBottomRight bottom = Math.round(innerHeight * 0.46) = 388px, i.e. into the band y 84..456 — exactly where the card now sits.
findings.userImpact: On a phone the verdict card floats in the middle of the screen instead of riding as a bottom sheet, with dead space under it, and it covers the glowing zone on the map that the flight just centred — the thing the peek layout exists to keep visible.
findings.suggestedFix: Since vertical auto margins no longer work inside .hud, express the peek dock with alignment instead: .card.peek { align-self: end } (with .hud's align-content already handling the fits/overflows case), or move .card.peek out of the grid flow to position: fixed; bottom: 52px.

findings.title: Final-score recap truncates every place name to about 14 characters
findings.evidence: Measured at 390x844 with real deck labels: .runner-name renders at 100px while the labels need 226px ('Georgetown, South Carolina, USA (US South)'), 193px ('Thomastown, County Kilkenny, Ireland'), 148px ('Northeast Scotland, Scotland'), 143px ('Boston, Massachusetts, USA'). All five rows ellipsise.
findings.userImpact: After five rounds the summary card lists 'Georgetown, So…', 'Thomastown, Co…', 'Northeast Scot…' — the recap of where the voices were from does not fit, so the last screen of the game looks unfinished.
findings.suggestedFix: Let the name column flex (grid-template-columns: 1fr auto auto with the track bar fixed-width, or drop the track bar on phones) so the label gets the width the points column does not need.

findings.title: ±5s dock buttons and the leaderboard 'decks' back link are far below the 44px touch minimum
findings.evidence: Measured at 390x844: #backBtn and #fwdBtn are 34x34; #boardsBack ('decks') is 55x13; #srcLink ('open the original') is 18px tall. The concurrent edit raised .fb-btn to 44px and .flag-chip to 40px but did not touch these three.
findings.userImpact: The ±5s buttons are used repeatedly every round and sit 12px from a 50px play button, so a miss hits play/pause instead. #boardsBack is the only way off the leaderboards view and is a 13px-tall target.
findings.suggestedFix: Give .dock-skip width/height 44px (shrink the icon, not the button) and .back-link a padding of at least 12px 4px with a matching negative margin so the layout does not move.

findings.title: Round pill starts 85px off-centre and overlaps the wrapped nav
findings.evidence: Two separate issues in one element. (1) .round-pill sets transform: translateX(-50%) and animation: settle 0.22s, but @keyframes settle declares transform: translateY(8px) → transform: none, so the centring transform is overridden for the whole animation and only reapplies when it ends — the pill renders at left:50% (measured left 195 for a 169.7px pill at 390px viewport, where centred is 110.1) and jumps 85px left after 220ms, at the start of every round. (2) The pill (z-index 15) sits at top 74..107 while the wrapped .brand (z-index 12) runs to 93.8; measured 6.8px overlap on 'guess the voice', and document.elementFromPoint over that link's third line returns 'roundPill'.
findings.userImpact: Every round opens with the score pill sliding in from the wrong place, and it covers/steals taps from the bottom line of the header nav link right underneath it.
findings.suggestedFix: Give the pill its own keyframes that preserve the centring (from { opacity: 0; transform: translateX(-50%) translateY(8px) }), the way @keyframes dockUp already does for .dock. The overlap resolves itself once the nav stops wrapping.

findings.title: Tapping 'leaderboards' mid-round silently discards the game
findings.evidence: The header nav is visible during a round (.brand has no hidden state and sits at z-index 12). #boardsBtn/the #boards hash both call showBoards(), which calls setView('boards') and hides #dock. The only way out is #boardsBack, which calls setView('pick') — there is no path back to 'round'. round/total/roundLog stay in memory but are unreachable.
findings.userImpact: A player four rounds into a game who taps 'leaderboards' to check the standings loses the run with no warning and no way back; the only option offered is the deck picker.
findings.suggestedFix: Hide or disable the leaderboards nav item while #dock is visible, or have #boardsBack return to the round it came from when a game is in progress.

findings.title: Toast messages paint over the dock controls during a round
findings.file: css/style.css:654 (.toast, bottom: 72px, z-index 30) vs :531 (.dock, bottom: 18px, z-index 15)
findings.evidence: Measured at 390x844 with the dock shown: dock occupies y 734..844 (110.1px tall from bottom:18px), toast occupies 737.9..780 — a 42.1px overlap, and the toast's z-index 30 puts it above the dock's 15.
