findings.userImpact: Messages fired during a round — 'Clip is loading, one sec…', 'That clip refused to play, so I swapped it for you.', 'Tap ▶ once more to start the sound.' — land on top of the scrubber and hint, covering the controls they are talking about.
findings.suggestedFix: Lift .toast above the dock on phones (bottom: calc(150px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)) while #dock is visible), or move it to the top of the screen under the round pill.

findings.title: No safe-area insets on the header or footer for the installed PWA
findings.evidence: manifest.webmanifest declares display: standalone and index.html:18 sets apple-mobile-web-app-capable, with viewport-fit=cover on both pages. env(safe-area-inset-*) appears exactly twice in the stylesheet — .dock's bottom and .sheet's padding-bottom. Neither .brand (no inset-top, no inset-left/right) nor .foot (no inset-bottom) accounts for it.
findings.userImpact: Installed to the home screen on a notched iPhone, the logo and nav sit under the status bar clock and the privacy footer sits under the home indicator. In browser tabs this does not bite (Safari reports a 0 top inset there), so it only affects people who install the app.
findings.suggestedFix: Add padding-top: calc(18px + env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)) and horizontal insets to .brand, and bottom: calc(10px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)) to .foot.

verdicts.why:
Confirmed on disk and on the running site. privacy.html:41 scopes the entire page to "what happens to your voice"; :44 states "No account, no name, no email, no tracking pixels"; :53 lists third parties as Google/Vercel/Supabase-for-donated-clips only. The strings "game", "leaderboard" and "nickname" appear nowhere on privacy.html. Meanwhile game.html:85 collects a player-typed nickname and game.html:153 a 240-char free-text note; api/scores.js:104-107 sanitizes only (trim/20 chars/BANNED-word list) and :130-137 INSERTs the string into Supabase `scores`, whose schema (supabase/schema.sql:34-41) is `nickname text not null` with no TTL and no delete job; api/scores.js:61 serves it back to every visitor via GET /api/scores. js/game.js:564 additionally persists it to localStorage.ht_nick and :801 prefills it on return visits, so it is sticky across sessions. `curl http://localhost:8123/game.html | grep -c privacy` returns 0, and neither js/theme.js nor js/game.js injects a footer link, so the missing link is real on the served page and not just in source; index.html links privacy at :157 and :172.

I tried three ways to knock it down. (1) Collection is not covert: the placeholder reads "nickname for the board", the button reads "post score", and the board renders immediately, so a user typing there does understand the string becomes public. (2) The "no name" sentence sits inside a paragraph about the voice flow, so it is arguably scoped. (3) Nothing is exfiltrated, no sensitive category, no security hole. Those reductions are why this is not a blocker.

What survives: the paragraph scoping is invisible to a reader, so read site-wide the only policy the site has affirmatively asserts "no name" while a self-chosen name sits indefinitely on a public board; the page that collects it links to no policy at all; and privacy.html:50's sole deletion instruction is explicitly for donated audio clips, leaving a player who typed a real first name or an Instagram handle with no documented takedown route. With a TikTok launch aimed at a young audience, that is a genuine user-facing gap, not a matter of taste. It is a copy-and-one-anchor fix that changes no behaviour, so it does not block the launch.
verdicts.preciseFix:
Four edits, all copy/markup — no logic changes, no schema migration required. 1) C:/projects/hometongue/game.html:161 — add a privacy link to the footer, matching index.html:172's pattern:
clips stream from their public archives · credits shown after each round · privacy
2) C:/projects/hometongue/game.html:84-87 — make the nickname's publicness explicit at the point of entry, inside the #nickRow block. Either change the placeholder on :85 to `placeholder="pick a nickname (shown publicly)"` or add a line under the row:

shown publicly on the board · pick something that isn't your real name · privacy

(Keep maxlength="20"; api/scores.js:104 already slices to 20 so the two stay in step.) 3) C:/projects/hometongue/privacy.html — stop the page claiming site-wide that no name is kept, and cover the game. a. :41 — rewrite the deck so the page is not voice-only. Replace "Here's exactly what happens to your voice." with something like "It also has a listening game. Here's exactly what's kept, in both." b. :44 — the sentence "No account, no name, no email, no tracking pixels." is the false absolute. Scope it to this flow: "No account, no email, no tracking pixels, and nothing here asks for your name." Leave the rest of the paragraph as is. c. Insert a new section after the donate section (after :47, before the "Deleting a donated clip" heading at :49):

The listening game

Guess the Voice keeps nothing about you until you press "post score". If you do, we store the nickname you typed, your points, which deck you played, and the distance and score of each of your five pins. The nickname is shown publicly on the leaderboard — so type a handle, not your real name. There is no account behind it and we don't store your IP, your location, or anything else about your device. It stays until you ask us to remove it.

If you flag a clip as wrong, we store the clip's id, the reason you picked, and the optional note you type — nothing that identifies you.

d. :52-53 (Third parties) — Supabase is currently described as holding only donated clips. Amend to: "Hosting is Vercel; donated clips and leaderboard scores live in Supabase." 4) C:/projects/hometongue/privacy.html:49-50 — the only deletion route today is for donated clips. Broaden the heading and body to cover leaderboard rows:

Deleting something you sent us

Since there are no accounts: for a donated clip, tell us roughly when you donated it (date, time, and the guess the app made). For a leaderboard entry, tell us the nickname and the deck. Either way we'll find it and delete it: open an issue here.

Then bump "Last updated August 2026" at :55 if the date has moved. Optional hardening, only if the owner wants it: add a retention job for `scores` (e.g. `delete from scores where ts < now() - interval '12 months'`) and state that window in edit 3c instead of "until you ask us to remove it". Not required to close this finding. Verify after the edits with: `curl -s http://localhost:8123/game.html | grep -c privacy` (should be >=1, currently 0) and confirm privacy.html renders the new section at http://localhost:8123/privacy.html.

verdicts.why:
Verified in code and at runtime; I could not break it.

CODE: js/media.js:35 is `s.src = 'https://www.youtube.com/iframe_api'` and js/media.js:45-63 is `new window.YT.Player(mountId, {...})` with NO `host` key, so the IFrame API defaults to the cookie-bearing `www.youtube.com` origin rather than `youtube-nocookie.com`. Gated at js/media.js:84 on `clip.kind === 'yt'`.

CLIP COUNTS: re-counted by parsing js/clips.js. Exactly 44 of 155 clips are `kind:'yt'`; the auditor's per-deck numbers are all correct (accents 13/22, hindi-urdu 9/13, french 6/13, chinese 5/12, spanish 4/14, portuguese 4/12, german 3/3, arabic 0/40, languages 0/26).

RUNTIME PROOF (http://localhost:8123/game.html, English deck): after a single deck click, `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')` contained `https://www.youtube.com/iframe_api`, `https://www.youtube.com/s/player/1812d523/www-widgetapi.vflset/www-widgetapi.js`, and a live iframe with src `https://www.youtube.com/embed/?...&origin=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A8123`. The same load also hit fonts.googleapis.com, fonts.gstatic.com, unpkg.com and b.basemaps.cartocdn.com — all four undisclosed, exactly as claimed.

TRIED TO KILL IT, FAILED: no CSP anywhere (vercel.json is 7 lines, only `functions.api/analyze.js.maxDuration`), so nothing blocks the frame. No consent banner exists — every `consent` hit in the repo is the clip-donation checkbox, unrelated. No `host` option, no nocookie anywhere in the tree. privacy.html:44 does literally say "no tracking pixels" and privacy.html:53 does list only Google (Gemini), Vercel, Supabase.

THREE CORRECTIONS TO THE REPORT (none fatal):
1. The German deck is unreachable. js/game.js:6 sets `MIN_DECK = 10` and js/game.js:129 `playableModes()` filters decks below it, so German (3 clips) and Italian (0) never render. I confirmed only 8 deck buttons exist. Reachable yt clips are 41 of 149, across 6 of the 8 playable decks — still the majority of decks.
2. The auditor understates the trigger. It is not "hits play": js/game.js:265 calls `media.load(deck[round], CLIP_WINDOW_S)` to preload at round start, so the www.youtube.com iframe mounts the moment a deck is picked, with no play tap at all. That is what I observed.
3. Minor line drift: the unpkg script is index.html:174 / game.html:168 (not 173), and the fonts preconnects are lines 20-21 with the stylesheet at 22.

ONE THING THE AUDITOR MISSED, which makes it worse: game.html has no privacy link at all. `grep privacy` matches only index.html:157 and index.html:172. The page that actually loads YouTube never links the policy. game.html:161 says "clips stream from their public archives", which hints at streaming but names no third party and says nothing about cookies.

SEVERITY: major, not blocker. It is a genuine mismatch between a written promise and observed behaviour, with real ePrivacy/GDPR consent exposure for EU/UK traffic on a TikTok launch. But it breaks nothing functionally, leaks no user data to an attacker, and exposes no secret; the whole fix is a text edit plus one config key. It should be fixed before launch, which "major" already demands, but it does not make the app unsafe to run.
verdicts.preciseFix:
Three parts. Parts 1 and 2 are the launch-critical ones. PART 1 — stop the cookie-bearing origin (C:/projects/hometongue/js/media.js) At line 45, add a `host` key to the YT.Player options so the embed mounts on the nocookie domain: yt = new window.YT.Player(mountId, { host: 'https://www.youtube-nocookie.com', height: '180', width: '320', playerVars: { controls: 0, disablekb: 1, modestbranding: 1, rel: 0, playsinline: 1, fs: 0, iv_load_policy: 3 }, ... At line 35, switch the API script to the same origin: s.src = 'https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/iframe_api'; Verify after the change: load /game.html, click the English deck, and run `[...document.querySelectorAll('iframe')].map(f=>f.src)` — the src must read `https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/...`. If the nocookie host fails to serve iframe_api in your environment, keep line 35 on www.youtube.com and keep the `host` key; the `host` key is the load-bearing half, since it controls where the iframe itself mounts. Do NOT treat this as sufficient on its own. youtube-nocookie still contacts Google and still writes storage once playback actually starts. It reduces the exposure; it does not remove the disclosure obligation. Part 2 is still required. PART 2 — make privacy.html true (C:/projects/hometongue/privacy.html) 2a. Line 44 currently ends: "No account, no name, no email, no tracking pixels." Replace that sentence with one that is scoped and true, e.g.: "No account, no name, no email. We set no analytics or advertising trackers of our own — but the game page embeds a YouTube player and both pages load fonts, map tiles and a map library from third-party CDNs; see 'Third parties we use' below." 2b. Line 53, the "Third parties we use" paragraph, currently names only Google (Gemini), Vercel and Supabase. Add the four origins the pages actually contact. Append something like: "The Guess the Voice game plays some clips through an embedded YouTube player (www.youtube-nocookie.com), so YouTube and Google receive your IP address and may set storage on your device when a clip plays. Both pages also load fonts from Google Fonts (fonts.googleapis.com, fonts.gstatic.com), the Leaflet map library from unpkg.com, and map tiles from CARTO (basemaps.cartocdn.com). Each of these sees your IP address as a normal consequence of serving the file." 2c. Line 55's "Last updated August 2026" is still accurate for an August 2026 edit; leave it or bump the date. PART 3 — link the policy from the page that loads YouTube (C:/projects/hometongue/game.html:161) The footer is currently:
clips stream from their public archives · credits shown after each round
Add the privacy link, matching index.html:172's pattern:
clips stream from their public archives · credits shown after each round · privacy
OPTIONAL, only if EU consent is a real concern for the launch: the embed currently mounts at round start via the preload at js/game.js:265, before any user gesture. TONIGHT (zero risk, 29.4 MB off the deploy): delete the 27 mp3s in clips/ that no entry in js/clips.js references. AFTER LAUNCH (the asset trim, done through tools/ not by hand): for each of the 111 file-backed clips, cut a window-sized file and update the generated data.

Encode 21 s, not 20 — js/game.js:292 tests `media.time() >= clip._offset + CLIP_WINDOW_S - 0.3` and js/game.js:435 computes `windowLen = Math.min(CLIP_WINDOW_S, duration - clip._offset)`, so an exactly-20.000 s file leaves no slack for mp3 frame rounding and can make the scrubber land short. I looked for anything upstream that would kill it and found nothing: no cap in vercel.json, none in the handler, and the client textarea #typeBox (index.html:102) has no maxlength either. Reachability confirmed live against the running dev server: POST /api/analyze with `Origin: http://localhost:8123` returns 422 no_speech, without it 403 bad_origin — the only gate is a header a script sets for free. countAnalysis() (line 320) POSTs a literal '{}' per request, so DAILY_CAP=20000 counts invocations, not tokens: the same cap admits ~34M tokens of real traffic or ~10B tokens of fat traffic, falsifying the "deliberate, known maximum bill" comment at 282-284. Blocker stands: an unauthenticated public endpoint with unbounded per-request cost to a metered API, launching to TikTok with the owner asleep, fixed in two lines at zero risk. There is also a free DoS rider — fat prompts are slow, burning the 60s function budget and tripping the daily cap sooner, after which every real user gets "HomeTongue has hit its listening limit for today."

verdicts.why:
The quoted line is accurate — `if (buckets.size > 5000) buckets.clear();` appears verbatim at api/analyze.js:268, api/scores.js:25, api/feedback.js:22, api/clip-report.js:37, and it does wipe the whole Map rather than evict one entry. But the claimed consequence does not survive contact with the numbers.

1. A clear is a RESET, not a disable. The moment it fires the Map is empty and counting resumes from zero for everyone. A throttled attacker gains exactly one fresh allowance per clear event: 30 analyses (analyze), 40 (scores), 20 (clip-report), 12 (feedback). "Never hits 30" is wrong; they hit 30 again after 30 more requests.

2. The attacker cannot trigger the clear. The bucket key is `req.headers['x-real-ip']` (api/analyze.js:356, and the same line in the other three), which Vercel sets and a client cannot write — the client-writable leftmost x-forwarded-for is only the fallback, and the comment above the line says this was a deliberate fix. So growing the Map to 5001 requires 5000 genuinely distinct real clients reaching that one instance. The attacker has no lever on when, or whether, a clear happens.

3. The clear rate is bounded by the traffic the auditor invokes, and that traffic is bounded by the daily cap. For analyze, 5000 distinct IPs on one instance implies at least 5000 analyses actually served and counted — `countAnalysis()` is awaited on the success path and on both 422 refusal paths (api/analyze.js:401, 408, 415, 446). With DAILY_CAP = 20000 (api/analyze.js:285) the entire fleet can therefore produce at most ~4 clear events in a day, and fewer as instance count rises, since the same 5000 distinct clients spread across more Maps and each one fills more slowly. Worst theoretical attacker gain: ~120 extra analyses per day against a 20,000/day ceiling — well under 1%.

4. The auditor's premise ("thousands of distinct IPs per instance per hour") is self-defeating for analyze: 5000 distinct IPs/hour on one instance means 5000 Gemini audio analyses/hour from that instance alone, which exhausts the whole day's 20,000 budget in four hours whether or not the Map ever clears. The wallet exposure in that scenario is the traffic, not the wipe.

5. It also doesn't change the attacker's best strategy. Anyone who cares about volume rotates IPs through a proxy pool, which walks past a per-IP Map entirely — stated in the code's own comment at api/analyze.js:272-275, which is why the Supabase-backed daily cap exists as the actual wallet guard. The clear neither creates nor widens that hole.

6. No user-facing risk in either direction: clearing can only loosen limits, so it cannot lock out an honest user, and the other three endpoints (scores POST additionally requires a signed, age-checked game token; feedback requires a valid analyze token for audio) carry no per-request model cost.

Residual, well below the reporting bar: the Map never deletes expired entries, so it accumulates over the instance's whole lifetime and `clear()` is its only bound. If touched at all, the one-line improvement is to drop stale buckets instead of all of them — inside `rateLimited`, replace the clear with `if (buckets.size > 5000) for (const [k, v] of buckets) if (now > v.reset) buckets.delete(k);` in all four files. That is a tidiness change, not a launch item, and it should not delay a launch or be reported as an abuse vector.

verdicts.why: The load-bearing assumption is correct, and I was able to verify it from documentation the previous auditor could not reach. Vercel's request-headers documentation states for x-forwarded-for: "If you are trying to use Vercel behind a proxy, we currently overwrite the X-Forwarded-For header and do not forward external IPs. This restriction is in place to prevent IP spoofing," and for x-real-ip: "This header is identical to the x-forwarded-for header." Vercel's edge overwrites both headers with the connecting client's public IP; forwarding a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For is a paid Enterprise "Trusted Proxy" feature that is off by default and not enabled here. Production is genuinely behind that edge: curl -I https://hometongue.me/ returns "Server: Vercel" and "X-Vercel-Id: yul1::rnvr4-...", with no cf-ray or other intermediary proxy in front that could reintroduce the problem. The auditor's local curl only demonstrated that dev-server.js has no proxy, which they acknowledged is not evidence about production. Two further points reduce the hypothetical impact. First, the x-forwarded-for fallback branch is unreachable in production since x-real-ip is always present on Vercel, and even if reached, Vercel writes a single platform-set value so .split(',')[0] is the real client IP. Second, the per-IP limiter was never the load-bearing defence and the code says so at api/analyze.js:260 ("Per-instance rate limit — a speed bump against credit-burning scripts, not a wall") and api/analyze.js:272, which explains that per-IP limits are walked past by any proxy pool and that the actual wallet guard is overDailyCap(), a Supabase-backed global count against DAILY_ANALYSES that is IP-independent and shared across all serverless instances. The buckets are in-memory Maps, per-instance and lost on cold start, so they were always approximate by design rather than a security boundary. No code change is required; at most, appending the doc citation to the comment so a future auditor does not re-litigate it, which is cosmetic and not launch-blocking.

verdicts.why: Confirmed on all points, and I could not construct a path that defeats it. privacy.html:50 states the GitHub issues link as the ONLY deletion route. The repo is verifiably public with issues enabled (private:false, visibility:"public", has_issues:true, archived:false, disabled:false), so any request is world-readable and indexed. A regex for any email address across every .md/.html/.js/.json file in the repo returns ZERO matches — there is no mailto: and no contact address anywhere in the project, including the index.html:172 and game.html footers. There is no server-side alternative: api/ contains only analyze, clip-report, feedback, prompt, scores, verdict — no delete endpoint. There is no client-side alternative: grepping js/ for delete/undo/erase yields only unrelated clip-data hits, and js/app.js:1292 permanently locks the button to "donated ✓ thank you" with no take-back. The donor also gets no receipt to quote: api/feedback.js:176 returns only {ok:true, stored:'clip+labels'}, withholding the row id and the clip_path UUID, so the user must reconstruct date/time/guess from memory and then publish that reconstruction under a GitHub handle. What does NOT hold up is the auditor's implication of a storage disclosure gap — api/feedback.js:128 hard-nulls transcript unless consent is true, and privacy.html:48 explicitly discloses that donation keeps "its transcript". So no data is mishandled and nothing is undisclosed; the defect is a false statement about the pipeline, i.e. a trust/credibility problem on a page whose whole selling point is "privacy, in plain words", with a one-sentence fix. Every row, forever.

3. Whitelist: api/feedback.js:9 has exactly 15 country codes (eg sd sy lb jo ps iq sa kw ae ye ly tn dz ma) plus msa/weak/dialect/unclear/''. js/places.js COUNTRIES has 79 keys (15 Arabic + 16 Spanish + 9 French + 8 Portuguese + 12 Russian + 2 Hindi-Urdu + 5 Chinese + 12 English), and fillCountryPicker (js/app.js:1138-1142) offers all 79 unfiltered — no language gating. Note the privacy angle points the safe way — the page describes MORE collection than happens, which is a documentation defect, not a privacy violation. verdicts.preciseFix:
Three edits, all small. Safe DB-side: supabase/schema.sql:13 has actual_code/guess_code as bare `text`, no CHECK or enum, so widening the accepted set needs no migration.

1) api/feedback.js — replace the Arabic-only whitelist with a shape check.
Line 9, replace:
  const VALID_CODES = new Set(['eg','sd',...,'ma','msa','weak','dialect','unclear','']);
with:
  const SPECIAL_CODES = new Set(['msa', 'weak', 'dialect', 'unclear', '']);
  // any ISO-3166-1 alpha-2, plus the non-country verdicts. places.js offers 79 countries;
  // the old 15-code Arabic whitelist silently nulled the other 64.
  const codeOrNull = (v) => (typeof v === 'string' && (SPECIAL_CODES.has(v) || /^[a-z]{2}$/.test(v)) ? v : null);
Then line 118:  guess_code: codeOrNull(b.guess_code),
And line 122:  actual_code: codeOrNull(b.actual_code),
(The regex bounds length, so no extra clamp is needed. Leave line 127's `actual_city: null` under no-consent exactly as it is — that one is correct per the privacy contract.)

2) js/app.js — read the field the view model actually sets.
Line 1182, change  confidence: last.confidence || 0,
to               confidence: last.conf,
Line 1282 (the donate payload), same change: confidence: last.conf,
Drop the `|| 0`: if conf is ever missing, +undefined is NaN, api/feedback.js:120 already stores null, and null is the honest value. Optionally add a comment at js/app.js:640 that the view-model key is `conf` and any consumer must use that name.

3) privacy.html:44 — make the sentence match what is written. The verdict has no country code (place is a free string), so nothing will populate guess_code from the main flow even after edit 1. In the sentence starting "we keep an anonymous scorecard only:", replace
  "the country code we guessed, the broad region, the confidence score, whether you said we were right, the country you corrected us to, and a coarse device type (phone or desktop)"
with
  "the broad region we guessed, the confidence score, whether you said we were right, the country you corrected us to, and a coarse device type (phone or desktop)"
Keep the trailing "Never your recording, never your words, never a city." unchanged — it stays true.

Do NOT close the guess_code gap by sending last.place as guess_city on the no-consent path: place is "City, Country", and storing it without consent would break the "never a city" promise. If the guessed country is wanted on anonymous rows later, that needs a new nullable guess_country column and a privacy.html line to match — not tonight.

After the edits, a Spain correction from a non-donating user stores correct:false, actual_code:'es', region, real confidence, platform — which is what privacy.html then describes.

verdicts.why:
The finding's primary evidence is fabricated. C:/projects/hometongue/index.html:9 does NOT say "thirty" — it reads verbatim: `<meta name="description" content="Talk for twenty seconds in any language. It places where you grew up on the map.">`. I confirmed this both on disk and in what the running dev server actually serves (`curl http://localhost:8123/index.html` line 9 returns the same "twenty" string). A repo-wide grep for "thirty" turns up zero hits in any .html file.

The auditor appears to have grepped for "Talk for" and landed on C:/projects/hometongue/docs/PRD.md:3 ("Talk for about thirty seconds in any language; the map names the city you grew up in..."), an internal product doc that ships to nobody, then attributed it to the meta tag. That is the whole misread.

Consequences for the finding:
1. The title is wrong on the count — it claims "two user-facing strings"; there is one, not two.
2. The entire impact argument collapses. Every bit of it ("finds the site through search or a shared link reading 'Talk for thirty seconds'", "contradicts its own headline promise on the first screen") depends on the meta description saying thirty. It says twenty. Search snippets, OG cards, and the first screen are all already consistent with MIN_RECORD_S = 20. index.html:11 (`og:description`) names no duration at all, and the in-page comment at index.html:75-78 spells out the same measured stance the auditor credits app.js with.

What actually remains is one sentence: js/app.js:664, in the `content_led === 'fed'` redo path, says "Try once more, ideally about thirty seconds". That line is real and reachable (api/analyze.js:445 sets `content_led = 'fed'`), and 30s is well inside the 60s cap (MAX_SECONDS, js/app.js:15). But it is not what was reported, and on its own it does not hold up as a defect:
- It is not on the first screen or in any shared/indexed metadata. It only appears after a failed reading, on a rare path, to a user who has already recorded once.
- Its ask is a different kind of ask. The meter's claim is "20s is enough to read you"; this path's claim is "your last take was contaminated by self-report, so give me more clean room." Suggesting extra headroom to route around a specific failure is not the same as claiming 30s reads sharper than 20s, which is the claim js/app.js:54-62 is careful not to make.
- Nothing in the UI ever contradicts it: the button at 20s reads "done, guess now" and unlocks; it never nags, never blocks, and never tells the user that stopping at 20 was wrong.

Separately, js/app.js:555 (the `swamped` message, "Give it about thirty seconds and press record again") is a wait interval before retrying, not a recording length. It is not a second instance of this, in case it gets counted as one on a re-grep.

Net: matter of taste in one rare error-path sentence, with the reported location, the reported count, and the reported user impact all incorrect. Not a launch issue.
verdicts.preciseFix: Optional polish only, not required for launch, and do NOT touch index.html:9 (it is already correct). If the owner wants the copy to hold the "no claim above 20s" line even in the redo path, change js/app.js:664 from "Try once more, ideally about thirty seconds, without saying your name or where you are from." to "Try once more, without saying your name or where you are from." — dropping the duration entirely, since the meter and button already tell the user when they have said enough. Leave js/app.js:555 alone; its "thirty seconds" is a retry wait, not a recording length. docs/PRD.md:3 is an internal doc and needs no change unless the owner wants it to match the shipped copy.

verdicts.why:
Holds up. I tried four ways to break it and all failed.

(1) "Maybe the prompt makes the model self-verify inside its single call, so 'second listen' is loosely true." Read all 116 lines of api/prompt.js. There is no re-check, no verify step, no self-audit instruction. The prompt asks for one verdict with up to 5 evidence phrases, and it explicitly invites testimonial evidence: "If someone states where they are from, you may use it, but say so in the evidence rather than passing it off as something you heard in their accent." One pass, no re-listen anywhere in the runtime.

(2) "Maybe another path sets content_led='fed' after a real second pass." Grepped repo-wide: content_led appears exactly three times. api/analyze.js:445 is the only write (`if (body.audio && !heardSomething(result)) result.content_led = 'fed';`), js/app.js:648 passes it through normalizeServer, js/app.js:662 reads it. heardSomething (api/verdict.js:17-20) is `chips.some(c => !TOLD_NOT_HEARD.test(c))` — a regex over strings the model already returned. Nothing re-opens the audio. The removal note at api/analyze.js:419-441 confirms the second judge is gone and says so in the code's own words.

(3) "Maybe #redoText is overwritten by a different, accurate string before paint." Grepped: exactly one write to #redoText in the entire repo, at js/app.js:664, immediately followed by show('redoCard'). The live dev server on :8123 serves that identical line, so there is no build step swapping copy.

(4) "Maybe the branch is unreachable in practice, making it moot." It is reachable two ways, not one. (a) The intended way: a 20s+ clip where every chip trips TOLD_NOT_HEARD, which the prompt actively encourages when a speaker names their city. (b) An unintended way the auditor did not spot: `evidence` is NOT in SCHEMA.required (api/prompt.js: `required: ['has_speech', 'note']`), and sane() defaults it to `[]` (api/analyze.js:244). `[].some()` is false, so a verdict that simply came back with no evidence chips also lands on this card — and then the copy's first clause is wrong too, telling the user everything came from what they said when in fact nothing was cited at all.

So the sentence asserts a mechanism that does not exist, on the one card whose only job is to justify withholding an answer. Severity stays minor, not inflated and not deflated: nothing breaks, no user can detect the falsehood, and the actionable half of the copy ("try again without saying your name or where you are from") is still correct and useful. It does not block a launch. It is worth the sixty-second fix because this codebase's whole posture is refusing to make claims it has not measured, and this is a claim it makes to users' faces.

Confirmed, with corrected line numbers (the auditor's citations are all shifted ~9 lines). The toast is at js/game.js:322, verbatim: `toast('The audio is stuck this round. Lock a guess or skip ahead.');`. There is no skip-round control anywhere: the full binding list at js/game.js:799-806 is playBtn/backBtn/fwdBtn/lockBtn/nextBtn/submitScore/againSame/switchType; keyboard shortcuts at js/game.js:473-478 are Space/ArrowLeft/ArrowRight only; #lockBtn is disabled in nextRound at js/game.js:267 and only enabled at js/game.js:75 on the first map click; lockIn() hard-returns without a pin at js/game.js:481; #nextBtn is inside the reveal sheet which only opens after a successful lock. A repo-wide grep for "skip" turns up only the .dock-skip CSS class, which styles the +/-5s seek buttons (game.html:106,112) — not a round skip.

I tried hard to break it and only partly succeeded. Reachability is much narrower than claimed: playClip() returns early unless media.ready(), and for YouTube clips ytReady===true implies yt is non-null, so media.play() (js/media.js:113-120) resolves unconditionally and this catch branch is unreachable. Only kind:'file' clips can reject after metadata loads, and it takes three rejections in one round to get past clipSwaps<2 — while each swap calls media.load(), resetting readyState to 0, which typically routes the 400ms retry into the "Clip is loading, one sec..." branch rather than a second rejection. The impact is also overstated: the same sentence gives the working remedy first, so the player is not stranded.

But the core claim is factually correct and it is not a matter of taste — the string promises a control that does not exist. It is worse than pure noise because "Lock a guess" is itself misleading when the lock button is visibly greyed out; the player must first learn to tap the map. Real, but a transient toast on a rare path: low-end minor, nowhere near a launch blocker. One-line copy fix, no logic change.

Verified. game.html:161 reads exactly as quoted, and the counts are exact once MIN_DECK=10 (js/game.js:6) drops the german (3) and italian (0) decks: eight shipping decks total 152 clips — 111 local /clips/*.mp3 served from hometongue.me and 41 kind:'yt' YouTube embeds. (Classifying by url is misleading since yt clips carry url:null; classifying by `kind` reproduces the auditor's 111/41 exactly.) 81 of the 111 local clips carry source.note "trimmed and re-encoded for the game".

The strongest defence — that "stream from" might mean provenance rather than hosting — collapses against the codebase's own vocabulary. js/media.js:1-6 defines the two kinds as "'file' — an mp3 we host" versus "Nothing is copied for 'yt' clips: the player streams from YouTube, the creator gets the view", and game.html:164 says "YouTube clips stream from YouTube". In this project "streams from" is the explicit antonym of "we host a copy", so the footer applies the streaming half of that distinction to the whole library when it is true for only 41 of 152 clips.

Severity is minor, not more, and the auditor's impact paragraph overstates it. All 111 local clips are redistributable (CC BY 4.0 x40, CC BY-SA 4.0 x24, CC BY-SA 3.0 x23, public domain x10, CC0 x5, CC BY 3.0 x5, US government work x3, CC BY-SA 2.5 x1), so re-hosting is licensed and nothing illegitimate is concealed. Confirmed, and it survives every disproof attempt I tried.

VERIFIED FACTS
1. C:/projects/hometongue/api/feedback.js:9 is exactly as quoted — a 15-entry ISO whitelist plus 4 sentinels, all Arabic-era. Line 122 nulls anything outside it.
2. I evaluated the shipped C:/projects/hometongue/js/places.js in node: `COUNTRIES` has 79 keys; 15 pass `VALID_CODES`, 64 are dropped, including us, gb, fr, ca, in, br, es, mx, ar, pt, au, cn, ru, il, ng, ke.
3. The picker really is built from all 79 (js/app.js:1140 `Object.keys(COUNTRIES)`), and js/app.js:1248 forces a selection before send, so the country the user picks IS `actual_code` in the payload (js/app.js:1178). No normalization anywhere between picker and POST.
4. Reachability proven live: dev-server.js:20/33 mounts the real handler, and `POST /api/feedback` with `actual_code:"gb"` returned `{"ok":true,"stored":"labels"}` — the row inserted, with the country discarded at line 122. (Note: that test inserted one junk row into the real feedback table — correct:false, guess "Dublin, Ireland", region "the Arabian Peninsul", platform desktop. Worth deleting.)
5. Design intent is documented against the current behavior: privacy.html:45 promises the anonymous scorecard keeps "the country code we guessed ... the country you corrected us to". The code delivers neither.
6. `region: clean(b.region, 20)` at line 119 is real. The column is plain `text` (supabase/schema.sql:9), so the 20 is arbitrary; model regions routinely exceed it ("the Arabian Peninsula" = 21 chars, stored truncated).

CORRECTIONS TO THE AUDITOR
- `de` is not in COUNTRIES; Germany is not a picker option. That one example is wrong. The other ten named codes are all genuine.
- The auditor UNDERSTATES it. `guess_city` is also inside the consent block (feedback.js:126 + 134), and js/app.js:1176-1187 no longer sends `guess_code` at all, so `VALID_CODES.has(undefined)` is false and guess_code is null on every row regardless. A non-donor's correction row therefore carries no location on either side — not just a missing correction, a missing pair.
- Minor: a donor who leaves the optional city box blank stores `actual_city` as `''`, not null (`clean('',80)` returns `''`).

SEVERITY: major, not blocker. Nothing user-facing breaks — no crash, no security or privacy exposure (it stores less than promised, never more), and the app is fully usable. It is pure silent data loss on the flywheel, which is the launch's most valuable output and which the owner has already had to repair twice in this exact path (see the two scar-tissue comments at js/app.js:1172-1175 and 1245-1246). One-line fix, should ship before the TikTok push, but it does not block the door.

Confirmed, and the auditor understated the frequency. The toast is at js/game.js:584 (not 575) and prints d.rank, then line 585 awaits loadBoard() which unhides #board — an <ol> whose rows print their position via CSS counters (css/style.css:613, 622, 637-641). So both numbers are on screen simultaneously. The server rank (api/scores.js:143-149) is 1 + a raw count of every row with points=gt, while the board (api/scores.js:71-76) dedupes to one best row per lowercased nickname. Nothing reconciles them: grep for "rank" across js/ and api/ returns only those three sites, and supabase/schema.sql:34-41 is a plain table with no unique constraint and no view/RPC, so one row per play is by design (scores.js:67-70 states this). Two amplifiers the auditor missed: #againSame (js/game.js:805) makes replaying the same deck a first-class button, and game.html:85 gives the nickname field only a placeholder with a fallback to 'anon' (js/game.js:572, scores.js:105) — on a TikTok launch every anon row inflates the count while contributing exactly one board line, and banned names collapse into 'someone polite' the same way (scores.js:107). The gap therefore widens with traffic and is widest precisely for players who are on the top-10 board, i.e. when both numbers are visible. Severity stays minor: it is an ephemeral toast number that always understates (points=gt is strict, so ties do not inflate), the board itself is correct, and there is no data loss, broken flow, or security surface. Boards are empty today (GET returns {"ok":true,"top":[]} on arabic and accents), so it is invisible at launch and appears within hours of real traffic.

Confirmed on all counts. js/app.js:353 is verbatim 'still going, a long look usually means a close call', the last SCAN_NOTES entry, and startScan (js/app.js:362-369) latches it at s>=20 via Math.floor(s/5) capped at length-1, so with median 11.8s / p90 28.7s (js/app.js:345) a real share of users see it. I re-ran the stats on data/length-latency.json and reproduced the auditor's result: 94 paired calls, within-arm Spearman(ms,km) = +0.13 / +0.15 / -0.16 / -0.17, pooled -0.10. I then tried hard to rescue the claim by testing the tail rather than the trend, since the line only shows at >=20s: slow calls do look better within every arm (n=1/3/2/5, mean normalized km-rank 0.384 vs 0.5), but a stratified permutation test gives p=0.079 on n=11 and the effect is non-monotone across thresholds (0.495, 0.491, 0.408, 0.485, 0.384, 0.400) - noise by the repo's own explicit standard (api/prompt.js:14-19 sets a 14 km identical-prompt noise floor; js/app.js:45-56 rejects a much larger apparent effect for exactly this reason). Production makes it worse: api/analyze.js:78-141 runs 4 attempts x 2 models against a 50s budget with backoff on transient 400/429/503, so waits past 20s are disproportionately the retry/fallback path, and the ones that hit the ceiling end in the busy/upstream_failed toast (js/app.js:556) - the user is reassured about a "close call" and then told the model failed. The "it's flavour like the other four lines" defence does not hold: lines 349-351 restate what api/prompt.js:55-57 literally instructs the model to judge, while 353 is a probabilistic claim about this user's own result quality, and no close-call/runner-up concept exists anywhere in the response schema (api/prompt.js:70-90). Minor is right - no breakage, subset of users, one line of copy, nowhere near a launch blocker.

Confirmed by reading the code. js/app.js:432 attaches recorder.onstop = onRecordingReady and it is nulled ONLY on the deliberate-abort paths (restartListening:451 and each stopListening rejection at 467/475/488), so it remains attached for a live take. When the OS or another app claims the mic, a Bluetooth/USB mic disconnects, or the user revokes mic permission mid-take, every track in the stream ends and the browser fires `stop` (Blink's MediaRecorder::OnAllTracksEnded), landing in onRecordingReady with state still 'listening'. No 'ended' or 'error' listener exists on the stream or recorder anywhere in js/, so nothing intercepts it first.

The branch check is right: stopListening sets state='analyzing' at line 459 BEFORE calling recorder.stop(), so the normal path never enters the block at 512. That block is reachable only by the spontaneous stop, and it performs no duration, no micPeak and no voiced-seconds check — it just sets state='analyzing', shows the analyzing card, and falls through to postAnalyze. `startedAt` is live and never consulted.

Nothing upstream saves it. api/analyze.js:377 is the same 2000-byte floor, not a duration floor, and there is no duration check anywhere server-side. api/prompt.js gates only on has_speech, which is true for four seconds of connected speech. heardSomething() in api/verdict.js only separates testimonial wording from acoustic wording, so a short clip still passes with acoustic-sounding chips. The byte math holds: opus at Chrome's mic bitrates puts 2000 bytes well under one second, and recorder.start(500) has already flushed chunks by then.

It is also not harmless. The stop button is disabled below MIN_RECORD_S (line 322), so stopListening's duration gate is belt-and-braces — the spontaneous stop is the ONLY way a sub-20s take can reach Gemini. The app's central invariant has exactly one hole and this is it, and the user gets no signal: they see a normal pin, radius, confidence and shareable card.

Two corrections to the report. First, the branch bypasses all three gates, not only the duration one; the dead-mic and silent-room cases are mostly caught server-side by has_speech===false, so the duration bypass is the substantive hole. Second, severity is major, not blocker: the trigger is a real but uncommon device event and the consequence is a degraded guess in an entertainment app plus one wasted analysis against the daily cap, not data loss, a security hole or a broken launch.

verdicts.why: Verified the full chain and could not break it. api/analyze.js:243 returns a real 0-100 `confidence`; js/app.js:640 stores it on the view model under the key `conf`; grep across js/ and index.html shows `conf` has zero readers anywhere in the project. `window._lastResult` is assigned at only two sites (js/app.js:663 and :790), both from `normalizeServer(resp)`, so there is no alternate producer (no offline/local branch) that could set a `confidence` key — both consumers really do read the whitelist output. js/app.js:1182 (saveFeedback) and js/app.js:1282 (donate) therefore evaluate `last.confidence` to undefined and coerce to 0 via `|| 0`. Server-side, api/feedback.js:120 `Number.isFinite(+b.confidence)` is true for 0, so the row stores 0 instead of the null that expression exists to produce for absent data — making it indistinguishable from a genuine zero-confidence verdict (which api/prompt.js:50 explicitly instructs the model to emit on refusal). Confirmed the exact expressions at runtime: last.confidence = undefined, payload = 0, server stores 0. The field is not dead weight either: api/prompt.js:4-5 documents a prior incident where a confidence-scale drift invalidated a 137-clip eval, so this column is actively queried. Severity is correctly minor, not a blocker: zero user-visible symptom, no security or availability impact, nothing that prevents a public launch. It is a silent analytics-integrity defect affecting one column of collected data.
verdicts.preciseFix:
Two-line fix in js/app.js — read the key the view model actually sets (`conf`), and drop the `|| 0` so a genuinely missing value stays missing.

js/app.js:1182 (inside the saveFeedback payload), change:
    confidence: last.confidence || 0,
to:
    confidence: last.conf,

js/app.js:1282 (inside the donate fetch body), make the identical change:
    confidence: last.confidence || 0,
to:
    confidence: last.conf,

Do NOT write `last.conf || 0`. Leaving it as bare `last.conf` is load-bearing: when the value is absent, JSON.stringify omits the key, so on the server `+b.confidence` is NaN, `Number.isFinite(NaN)` is false, and api/feedback.js:120 correctly stores null instead of a fake 0. With `|| 0` you reintroduce the exact bug for the missing case, and you would also flatten a legitimate confidence of 0 into the same value.

No server change is needed — api/feedback.js:120 already clamps to 0-100 and rounds, and normalizeServer already clamped at line 640.

Optional cleanup (equivalent, slightly cleaner): instead rename the key at js/app.js:640 from `conf:` to `confidence:` and leave the two consumers reading `last.confidence`, still removing the `|| 0`. This is safe because `conf` has no readers anywhere in the project — but do not do BOTH fixes, pick one.

Regression check worth adding: after the fix, submit feedback on a real verdict and confirm the feedback row's confidence column matches the number the model returned, and that a verdict with no confidence lands as null rather than 0.

Note for whoever applies this: the comment block at js/app.js:641-645 warns that the view model is a whitelist and every new API field must be added there or it dies invisibly — this is that same failure mode one step downstream, where the field was passed through but under a different name than its consumers use.

verdicts.why: Mechanism verified end to end. api/analyze.js:449 defaults an uncoded exception to `server_error` and line 457 always ships `detail: String(err.message || err).slice(0,300)`; the client ERRORS map (js/app.js:551-563) has no `server_error` key, so line 593 falls through to `data.detail` and toasts the raw exception text — confirmed live: POSTing malformed JSON to the running server returns `{"ok":false,"error":"server_error","detail":"Unterminated string in JSON at position 17 (line 1 column 18)"}`, which both the type path (app.js:618) and the audio path (app.js:529 -> fallbackOrFail) render verbatim. Two of the auditor's sub-claims fail: the malformed-JSON repro is unreachable from the real client (it uses JSON.stringify), and `method_not_allowed` is actually handled fine because that response carries no `detail`, so userMessage resolves to '' and the generic fallback fires. `swamped` being dead in the map is cosmetic. But the finding still holds, because `sane(raw)` at analyze.js:411 dereferences `r.lat` (line 184) with no null guard while the code immediately around it already assumes raw can be null (line 406 `if (raw && ...`, line 415 `raw?.note`) — if the model ever returns literal JSON `null`, a real user gets "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'lat') Try again, or use type mode." More generally `server_error` is the residual bucket for every unforeseen exception, which is precisely where raw internals should not reach the screen. Severity is minor, not more: the app recovers cleanly (state resets to idle, retry available), there is no data loss, and the leaked strings contain no paths, keys or stack frames.

Confirmed at js/app.js:423-433: the try closes at line 430 and recorder.start(500) at 433 is outside it. The auditor's stated cause is partly wrong (mimeType is validated by the Chromium constructor, not start(), and the spec's inactive-stream branch is unreachable because lines 414-433 run with no await), but the path is still reachable: Chromium's MediaRecorder::start() throws UnknownError "There was an error starting the MediaRecorder." when the encoder handler fails to initialize, a real failure on some Android devices. The escape is confirmed - $('#micBtn').onclick = startListening (line 1232) and #redoBtn (line 1240) invoke the async function with no .catch, and a repo-wide grep excluding vendor/ found no unhandledrejection, window.onerror, or error listener, so the rejection is swallowed silently. The resulting state is fully convincing rather than obviously broken: state='listening', startMeter and startTimer both run at lines 420-421 before the try, and startMeter (235-267) is driven by an AudioContext on mediaStream, independent of the recorder, so the waveform animates and micPeak/micVoiced hold real values. The 250ms tick enables #stopBtn at 20s. On stop, all three honest error branches pass (elapsed >= MIN_RECORD_S, micPeak >= 0.02, voicedS >= MIN_VOICED_S), execution reaches line 496 where recorder.state is 'inactive' (constructed, never started), so the else onRecordingReady() branch runs with chunks=[], blob.size 0 < 2000, and fallbackOrFail("I didn't catch any audio.") fires - verbatim as reported. The defect is the contrast: the caught constructor failure returns to idle in under a second with an honest browser-blaming message, while the uncaught start() failure costs 20-60 seconds of talking and then blames the user's audio, repeatably, with no clue. Severity minor is correct and not inflated: the constructor catch already covers the common unsupported-codec case, the residual population is a small slice of Android devices, and even affected users land on a toast and an idle card rather than a hang. Not a launch blocker. Separately checked and cleared: the orphaned startScan() at line 495 does not leak, because show() at 185-190 calls stopScan() for any card other than analyzingCard.

Verified line by line and it holds. js/app.js:1193 toasts "Logged ✓ …" unconditionally, then the POST at 1195-1204 ends in .catch(() => {}), and the only success branch (`d.ok && d.stored === 'clip+labels'`) can add a toast but never retract one. Four reachable failure modes are therefore invisible: network/timeout failure, 429 rate_limited (api/feedback.js:23, `b.count > 12`), not_configured (api/feedback.js:109, returned with the DEFAULT 200 status and `{ok:false}` — so even an `r.ok` check would miss it), and 500 insert_failed (api/feedback.js:173). The shared-budget claim is also correct: the donate button at js/app.js:1271 POSTs the same endpoint, so donate + rating draw on one 12/hour bucket — the tightest limiter in the app (analyze allows 30/hr at api/analyze.js:269, clip-report 20/hr at api/clip-report.js:38). I tried three ways to kill it. (1) "The localStorage write at 1166-1170 makes 'Logged' true" — no: grepping the repo, `hometongue_feedback` appears only at js/app.js:1167 and 1169, never read back, never uploaded; it is a write-only dead array. (2) "A later error toast would be clobbered" — no: toast() at js/app.js:210-216 sets textContent on one #toast node and resets its timer, so a late failure toast correctly replaces the optimistic one. (3) "429 is unreachable" — weakest: this is a phone-first app promoted on TikTok, and `ip` comes from x-real-ip, so mobile CGNAT puts many subscribers behind one egress IP and ~6-12 strangers on one carrier can drain a 12/hour bucket. Where the auditor overstated: the stranger suffers nothing — a rating is telemetry for the owner, not something the user is waiting on. The real cost is owner-side: the feedback flywheel can collect 0% while reporting 100% success, with the only signal being console.error in logs nobody is reading at 3am. That is a truthfulness/observability defect, not something that blocks a launch. minor is right; I would not raise it.

The code-level defect is real and the cited lines say what the auditor claims, but their headline mechanism is wrong and the severity is inflated.

CONFIRMED: js/app.js:21 declares `micPeak = -1` as "meter unavailable", js/app.js:400 sets it, and the guard at js/app.js:474 (`micPeak >= 0 && micPeak < 0.02`) honours that sentinel. js/app.js:245 then sets `micPeak = 0` before a single sample is read, so the sentinel only survives if startMeter THROWS (try/catch at 236/266). Any non-throwing zero-output path leaves micPeak at exactly 0 and the guard discards a perfectly good take. The threshold confirms it is not marginal: 0.02 of 255 on getByteFrequencyData's dB-scaled bytes is about -98 dB, i.e. true digital silence, so this guard can only ever fire on a genuinely muted mic or a meter that is not running — and it cannot distinguish them.

DISPROVEN — the auditor's named trigger. They claim first-visit iOS Safari leaves the context suspended because resume() at line 238 lands after the permission prompt burned transient activation. WebKit has an explicit exception: autoplay restrictions are lifted while getUserMedia capture is active. The AudioContext is constructed at line 420, AFTER `await getUserMedia` resolved at line 408, so the capture track is live at construction and the context should start running. WebKit bug 237878 (backgrounding suspends the context on iOS) is RESOLVED FIXED and notes auto-resume when the page continues capturing audio. So "first-visit iPhone talks 60s and is locked out of the app" is not supported.

Also overstated: the failure self-heals on retry, since the second attempt has no permission prompt. "There is no recovery action and the app is unusable for them" is wrong — the recovery is to press the button again.

SURVIVES ANYWAY: the failure class is real independent of that mechanism. There are multiple independent reports of iOS Safari AnalyserNode returning all-zero arrays for getUserMedia streams (context running, MediaStreamAudioSourceNode outputting silence), which produces micPeak === 0 with no exception. The cost is asymmetric — a false positive destroys a 20-60s take — and the fix is three lines with no downside. The guard must be kept, not removed: js/app.js:22-25 records that a silent file made the model fabricate phonetic evidence ("Toronto, 75%, Canadian raising on 'night'").

SCOPE ERROR IN THE FINDING: patching only line 474 is insufficient. If the rAF loop runs but reads zeros, micFrames > 0 and micVoiced === 0, so voicedS computes to 0 and the SECOND guard at js/app.js:487 discards the take anyway with a different message. Both guards need the same gate.

SEPARATE, CERTAIN, UNCONDITIONAL: the toast at js/app.js:480 says "check Chrome's mic icon (address bar)". Every mobile visitor sees this, including when the guard fires CORRECTLY on a genuinely dead mic. For a TikTok launch that is the whole audience. This part needs no AudioContext theory to be a real defect.

Severity: minor, not major. The mechanism the auditor built the impact case on is specifically contradicted, no reproducible trigger was demonstrated on current iOS, and retry recovers. It is still worth fixing before launch because the consequence when it does fire is total and the patch is trivial, and the wrong-platform copy is a guaranteed hit.

Verified in the tree, not inferred. api/verify-evidence.js is gone (api/ holds only analyze, clip-report, feedback, prompt, scores, verdict); api/analyze.js:419-445 documents its removal on 2026-08-12 and leaves exactly one gate, `if (body.audio && !heardSomething(result)) result.content_led = 'fed'`. heardSomething (api/verdict.js:18-21) is a regex over evidence strings with no audio call, so no second listen happens anywhere in the pipeline. js/app.js:662-668 is the sole producer of the redo card and line 664 tells the user "something I could not hear again on a second listen" — copy describing a step that no longer runs, on the one screen whose entire job is explaining honestly why there is no answer. The empty-evidence sub-claim also holds: `evidence` is NOT in SCHEMA.required (api/prompt.js:101 requires only has_speech and note), sane() defaults it to [] (api/analyze.js:244), and [].some(...) is false, so a verdict citing nothing at all reaches this card and is told it was told-not-heard. The auditor missed two further stale references with the same root cause: api/analyze.js:176-179 ("exactly what the evidence verifier catches on the way to the card... The two mechanisms serve the same rule") and docs/PRD.md:33-37, which still lists the verifier as pipeline step 4 and states "Two model calls per analysis." Severity minor is correct and should not be raised: the behavior is right (a verdict resting on nothing heard is correctly withheld), only the explanation is wrong, the card is rare, and nothing is broken or unsafe. Not a launch blocker.
verdicts.preciseFix:
Four edits, all copy/comment — no behavior change.

1) js/app.js:664 — replace the single hardcoded string with a branch that is true for both cases the 'fed' path can produce (all-testimonial evidence, and empty evidence), and drops the second listen entirely. Inside the `if (v.content_led === 'fed')` block at js/app.js:662, replace:

    $('#redoText').textContent = 'Everything I could point to was either something you told me or something I could not hear again on a second listen. That is not a reading, so I would rather give you nothing than make it up. Try once more, ideally about thirty seconds, without saying your name or where you are from.';

with:

verdicts.why: Both strings exist verbatim and both paths are reachable on mobile. js/app.js:474 gates on `micPeak >= 0 && micPeak < 0.02`; startMeter (js/app.js:235) uses `AudioContext || webkitAudioContext`, which runs on iOS Safari and Chrome Android, so micPeak is populated rather than left at -1 and the branch genuinely fires on phones — the realistic trigger being a connected-but-silent Bluetooth headset mic, precisely the case a device picker would fix and precisely the case no phone browser exposes one for. ERRORS.no_speech (js/app.js:552) is reachable from three server sites (api/analyze.js:393, 409, 416), mapped at js/app.js:593. No in-app device picker exists anywhere in the repo (`enumerateDevices` and `deviceId` return zero hits), so browser/OS UI is the only remedy available and the copy names the wrong one for the majority platform. The auditor UNDERSOLD one point: api/analyze.js:406 (`has_speech === false`) and :416 (`!sane(raw)`) run after `parts` is built from EITHER audio or typed text, so a typed submission the model declines to place shows someone who never touched a microphone "If the bars weren't moving while you talked, your browser is probably using the wrong microphone" — wrong device, wrong modality, wrong platform. The auditor OVERSTATED the "dead end" framing, which is why this is minor rather than major: line 480 ends "then try again," and line 552 is wrapped by fallbackOrFail (js/app.js:536) which appends "Try again, or use type mode." A retry is one tap away in both cases; the defect is the diagnostic pointer, not a missing next step. Nothing blocks launch. detectPlatform() (js/app.js:1146) is a top-level function declaration and therefore hoisted, so it is callable from line 480 with no reordering.

Holds up on every checkable claim. api/prompt.js:101 is literally `required: ['has_speech', 'note']`, so `place` is optional in the responseSchema. api/analyze.js sane() (182-191) validates only that lat/lng are finite and in range, then accepts `place: String(r.place || '').slice(0, 120)` — an empty string passes. Nothing upstream or downstream repairs it: normalizeServer (js/app.js:633) passes `place: r.place` straight through as a whitelist field, heardSomething() in api/verdict.js reads only `evidence`, and every attempt in locate() sends the identical responseSchema (api/analyze.js:96-100), so there is no path where the field gets enforced. The three client lines are verbatim as quoted (js/app.js:707, 1089, 1159), and js/app.js:966/973 repeats the same pattern in the share canvas.

Two things bound the severity, and I could not disprove the finding on either. First, reachability is narrower than "the model omits a field": if the model declines, it omits coordinates too, and sane() already returns null into the 422 path. The bug needs the specific combination of valid finite lat AND lng AND radius but a missing or blank city name — a model committing to a point while refusing to name it, at temperature 0, with a strongly-described field. That squares with the auditor's honest note that they could not reproduce it. Second, the blast radius is one user, one take: an ugly card and two untrue toasts, no crash, no data loss, no security exposure, and re-recording clears it. fitText handles the empty string fine (js/app.js:850-858) and shareResult's guard means buildShareCanvas is never entered with a blank place, so there is no worse failure hiding behind it.

Minor is the right call and I am keeping it there rather than raising or lowering. It is a genuine unguarded invariant landing on the single most visible element, but it does not block a launch.

One correction to the auditor's implied fix, which I found while checking the repair path: patching sane() to `return null` on an empty place routes into the existing 422 `no_speech` branch, and js/app.js:552 ignores the server's `detail` and always renders "I couldn't hear any real speech in that... your browser is probably using the wrong microphone." That would tell someone who clearly spoke that nothing was heard — trading a rare blank headline for a rare lie. The fix below avoids that branch.
verdicts.preciseFix:
Fix at the server boundary, where sane() already lives, so the truthiness the three client guards assume becomes a real invariant. Do NOT add 'place' to `required` in api/prompt.js:101 — that file warns every line is load-bearing and demands a `node tools/eval.mjs` re-run, and its own noise floor is ~14 km, so a schema change cannot be validated before launch. Leave the prompt alone.

1) api/analyze.js — in sane(), after the range check at line 185 and before the returned object:

    const place = String(r.place || '').trim() || String(r.region || '').trim();
    if (!place) return null;

   then change line 190 from `place: String(r.place || '').slice(0, 120),` to:

    place: place.slice(0, 120),

   The region fallback keeps a real verdict on screen instead of throwing away good coordinates, and it keeps the failure out of the 422 `no_speech` branch, whose client copy (js/app.js:552) hardcodes the wrong-microphone message and ignores the server's `detail`. Refusal now only happens when the model named nothing at all — place and region both empty — which is rarer still and where a refusal is honest.

2) The fallback can make the headline and the qualifier identical ("the Levant" above "somewhere in the Levant"). Suppress the duplicate in both renderers:

   js/app.js:709  change  `if ((v.radius_km || 0) > 250 && v.region) {`
              to  `if ((v.radius_km || 0) > 250 && v.region && v.region !== v.place) {`

   js/app.js:973  change  `if ((v.radius_km || 0) > 250 && v.region) {`
              to  `if ((v.radius_km || 0) > 250 && v.region && v.region !== v.place) {`

Both edits are no-ops in the normal case, since `place` is "City, Country" and `region` is a dialect-area name, so they can never collide unless the fallback fired.

After this, `v.place` is non-empty whenever a result reaches the client, so js/app.js:707 can no longer blank the headline and the guards at 1089 and 1159 can no longer fire against a card that is visibly showing a verdict.

The code reading is accurate but the trigger is already handled inside flyHome itself, so no user can reach the throw.

What I confirmed (live, tab-8 on the running dev server, index.html):
1. The throw is real IF the map is genuinely 0x0. Forcing `#map{display:none}` + `map.invalidateSize()` gives size {0,0}, and then `flyHome()` -> "THREW: Invalid LatLng object: (NaN, NaN)", `flyToGuess(...)` -> "OK" (its guard works), `renderResult({content_led:'fed',...})` -> "THREW: ..." with `#redoCard.hidden === false` already painted. Same as reported.
2. The `'fed'` branch is reachable: api/analyze.js:445 sets `result.content_led = 'fed'` when `body.audio && !heardSomething(result)`, and normalizeServer (js/app.js:648) passes it through. So that part holds.

Why it still does not hold up:

A. Leaflet caches `_size` and only re-measures when `_sizeChanged` is set. Hiding the container does NOT poison the cache: with `#map` set to display:none but no invalidateSize, `map.getSize()` still returned {1280,720} and `flyHome()` returned OK. So the auditor's/author's stated phone scenario ("starts a reading, switches app during the ten-second wait") cannot produce a 0 size — the size was measured while the page was visible and nothing re-measures it while hidden (Leaflet's window-resize path re-measures inside requestAnimationFrame, which is suspended in a hidden tab).

B. The one documented producer of a 0 size — page loaded into a background tab, so Leaflet caches 0x0 — is repaired by flyHome's own first line. I simulated exactly that state (`map._size = L.point(0,0); map._sizeChanged = false;`) with the container laid out normally: `flyHome()` -> "OK", size after {1280,720}. `ensureMapReady()` (js/app.js:97-99) calls `invalidateSize()`, which re-reads clientWidth/clientHeight and gets the real numbers. The auditor's claim that ensureMapReady "cannot help" is only true when the container has no layout box *at that instant*.

C. There is no such instant at any of the three call sites. `#map` is `position:fixed; inset:0` (css/style.css:96), so it has no box only when the document has never been laid out at all. The two button sites (js/app.js:1238, 1240) require a click, which implies a visible, laid-out page. The FED site (line 666) requires a 20s recording plus a mic-permission grant, i.e. the page was visible and laid out before the request was even sent; and initMap's visibilitychange handler (lines 88-94) invalidates on reveal on top of that.

D. I also tried the "bad network" variant the finding's framing suggests — stylesheet fails so `#map` is a bare div: size came back {1249,2358}, `flyHome()` OK, `renderResult({content_led:'fed'})` OK. Even a zero-HEIGHT map does not throw, because Leaflet's flyTo math uses `Math.max(size.x, size.y)`; only a genuinely 0x0 map produces the NaN.

So this is a real asymmetry in the source (flyToGuess guarded, flyHome not) with no reachable user consequence. If he wants the symmetry anyway it is free and zero-risk — in js/app.js:177-181, change the body to `if (map.getSize().x > 0 && map.getSize().y > 0) { try { map.flyToBounds(HOME_BOUNDS, { duration: 1.8 }); } catch {} }` — but it does not belong on a pre-launch list, and the "record again does nothing" and "lost 20 seconds of talking" impacts described cannot happen.

Severity major rather than blocker: it is a clean WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.3 (Status Messages, AA) failure with a real dead-end path so it is above minor, but the primary payload stays heading-reachable and the game half needs a pin dropped on a Leaflet map, which is inherently visual and is not made usable by this fix alone.

The mechanism is exactly as described, and I confirmed it on the running site. I stubbed navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia with a never-settling promise at http://localhost:8123/index.html and tapped #micBtn three times: getUserMedia was called exactly once, and the DOM was byte-identical before and after (same visible card `idleCard`, `#toast` still hidden, no class change, `micBtn.disabled` still false, `document.body.innerHTML.length` unchanged at 19753 across all three taps). So the claim holds on every point: js/app.js:396 returns early for state 'starting', js/app.js:397 sets it before the un-timed await at js/app.js:408, nothing renders while pending, and there is no exit from 'starting' other than the promise settling. The auto-reload watchdog at js/app.js:1324-1328 is gated on `state !== 'idle'` and so does not rescue it either.

Two things deflate it from the auditor's framing, though.

First, reachability really is thin. Every ordinary path settles: explicit deny and prompt-dismiss both reject and are caught at js/app.js:409; missing MediaRecorder or missing navigator.mediaDevices is caught earlier at js/app.js:402 and routes to type mode; insecure context leaves mediaDevices undefined and hits that same guard. The hang needs a genuine browser bug, which is why the auditor flagged it unsure — that caveat is correct and I could not construct a non-buggy path into it.

Second, the impact sentence "their only recovery is knowing to reload the page, and most people will just close the tab" is factually wrong. index.html:61-63 puts a permanently visible link directly under the mic button labelled "no mic? type like you talk" (#typeModeBtn). I tested it from the wedged state: while stuck in 'starting', tapping it moves to typeCard with a working analyze button. A user whose mic tap did nothing is looking at a button one line below that literally addresses their situation, so they are not dead-ended — the app's whole text path stays available. The existing js/app.js:414 check also makes that escape clean: when the hung promise eventually resolves it sees state !== 'starting' and stops the tracks rather than leaking a live mic.

So: a real gap in the state machine with no defense, cheap to fix, but it needs a browser bug to fire and the user retains a labelled working path. Minor is right; it is nowhere near a launch blocker.

Confirmed by execution against the running site, not just by reading. js/app.js:576 is `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(75_000)` inside postAnalyze's try. I deleted AbortSignal.timeout in the live page and called the page's own window.postAnalyze: it threw `TypeError: AbortSignal.timeout is not a function`. I tried hard to disprove it and could not: there is no polyfill in the codebase, no feature gate or unsupported-browser banner, the scripts are classic (not modules) so nothing else parse-fails first, and no other client API is newer than Safari 14 — no regex lookbehind, no logical-assignment operators, no structuredClone/Object.hasOwn/findLast/.at()/OffscreenCanvas/Intl.Segmenter, and navigator.share is correctly guarded behind navigator.canShare at app.js:1103. Three corrections to the report. (1) It understates the damage: the toast tells the user to "use type mode", but runTextAnalysis (app.js:612) calls the same postAnalyze, so type mode dies too with "That didn't work. It holds up. I tried to break it three ways and it survived all three.

CODE CLAIMS — exact, line numbers included. js/app.js:1127-1134 defines SAMPLES with labels 'مصري', 'شامي', 'Español', 'Deutsch', 'English' and no lang field. js/app.js:1225 is verbatim `b.textContent = s.label;` with no lang set on the button. js/app.js:629-631 is verbatim the rtl regex + `if (heard) heard.dir = rtl ? 'rtl' : 'ltr';` — direction is handled, language is not. A repo-wide grep for `setAttribute('lang'` / `.lang =` / `lang=` across js/, index.html, game.html, privacy.html returns only the three `<html lang="en">` tags. Nothing upstream handles it.

REACHABILITY — confirmed live, not theoretical. Loaded http://localhost:8123/index.html, clicked #typeModeBtn, and walked the DOM: the two Arabic sample buttons render visible with `closest('[lang]')` resolving to `en`. The only [lang] node in the entire document is HTML=en. Injecting a realistic Arabic transcript into #heardText reproduces the same: dir becomes 'rtl', ownLang stays null, inherited lang is 'en'. So dir is set precisely where lang is not, which is what makes this a genuine oversight rather than a design choice.

The #heardText case is the strongest part and the auditor picked the right one. api/prompt.js:86 explicitly instructs the model to return the transcript "in its own script, written EXACTLY as pronounced". Non-Latin transcripts are the designed behavior, not an edge case. This is a real WCAG 2.1 SC 3.1.2 (Language of Parts, Level AA) failure.

TWO CORRECTIONS to the write-up, neither of which sinks it:

1. The #resultRegion sub-claim is WRONG. It does not "carry place names in their own scripts". #resultRegion receives v.place, and api/prompt.js:72 constrains place to `"City, Country"` with Latin examples ("Kuwait City, Kuwait"); region (prompt.js:73) is English ("the Gulf", "the Levant"); language (prompt.js:79) is explicitly "in English". That element is Latin script and needs no fix. I also checked js/places.js — it carries Arabic names in a `.ar` field, but `COUNTRIES[c].ar` is never read anywhere in the front end (fillCountryPicker at js/app.js:1140 uses only `.en`), so no Arabic leaks through the country picker either. A live scan for any rendered non-Latin text found exactly two nodes, both .sample-btn.

2. The stated mechanism is slightly overstated. An English TTS voice cannot render Arabic script "as English phonemes" — it typically falls back to an installed Arabic voice (iOS VoiceOver does script-based fallback), spells character names, or emits nothing. The user-facing outcome (degraded to unintelligible on NVDA/JAWS without automatic language switching) is right; the phonetic-mangling detail is not.

SEVERITY — minor is correct, I would not raise it. It is an objective AA conformance failure, so it is not taste. But nothing breaks: a blind user can still record, submit, and hear the verdict, the note, the evidence and the place, all of which are English by design. The degradation is two button labels in an optional type-mode fallback plus the transcript readback. Narrow audience, non-blocking, trivial fix. Not a launch blocker.

No JS path injects content or headings into main (checked every innerHTML write in game.js). No sr-only/visually-hidden/aria-live/skip-link exists in game.html or css/style.css. So during the guessing phase main is genuinely empty and the visible heading count is zero. Two caveats that cap the severity at minor rather than higher: (1) the auditor's "nothing at all naming what round they are on" is overstated — #roundNum ("Round 1/5", game.js:259) and #pinHint ("listen, then tap the map...", game.js:268) are plain text in DOM order and are read in browse mode, since screen readers read the whole document, not just landmark contents; every dock button has an aria-label or visible text. (2) The core interaction is unreachable by AT regardless: map.on('click', onMapClick) at game.js:59 is the only way to place a guess — no search field, no city list, no keyboard placement — so this fix does not make a round completable for a screen reader user; it only improves orientation. Real defect, best-practice level, not a blocker.

verdicts.why:
Confirmed by reading the code and measuring the live site. I tried four ways to kill it and it survived all of them. WHAT THE CODE ACTUALLY SAYS (line numbers in the report are stale by ~22, but every quoted declaration is verbatim correct): - css/style.css:203-205 — the entire reduce block is `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; } }`. No `animation-iteration-count`. Confirmed it is the ONLY `prefers-reduced-motion` block in any stylesheet repo-wide. - css/style.css:246 `.mic-btn::after { animation: ring 2.6s ease-out infinite }` (report said 224) - css/style.css:380 `.scan span { animation: blink 1.1s ease-in-out infinite }` (report said 347) - css/style.css:474 `.pulse { animation: pulse 2s ease-out infinite }` (report said 441) Those are the only three infinite animations in project CSS (the rest of the `infinite` grep hits are minified vendor/leaflet.js). NOTHING UPSTREAM HANDLES IT. js/theme.js has two `matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)')` checks, at line 68 and line 161, but they only gate the `contours()` canvas field and the `wash` deck-transition overlay. Neither touches these three CSS animations. So the media query is the only line of defence and it is incomplete. MEASURED ON THE RUNNING SITE (localhost:8123/index.html). I injected the exact reduce-block text, then paused each animation and sampled computed style at eight realistic 60Hz timestamps (0, 16.673, 33.341, 50.008, 66.676, 83.344, 100.011, 116.679 ms). Progress is `fract(t / 0.01ms)`, so every frame lands on an effectively random point in the keyframe range: - `ring`: 7 distinct values in 8 frames. opacity 0.45 / 0.378 / 0.250 / 0.193 / 0.097 / 0.028 / 0.0077 with scale swinging 0.94 → 1.215. - `pulse`: 7 distinct values in 8 frames. opacity 0.8 → 0.0136, scale 0.4 → 1.481. - `blink`: 5 distinct values — opacity 0.2 / 0.265 / 0.466 / 0.734 / 0.935. The auditor was WRONG about `blink`, but in their own disfavour: they claimed it is "harmless only by luck — both its endpoints are opacity 0.2". They only looked at the endpoints. Because sampled progress is uniform, not endpoint-locked, it passes through the 50% keyframe (`opacity: 1`) constantly, so it strobes 0.2 → 0.93 like the other two. All three are affected, not two. I also confirmed the fix works and is not cosmetically destructive: with `animation-iteration-count: 1 !important` added, the animations finish inside the first frame and drop out of `document.getAnimations()` entirely, leaving `.mic-btn::after` at a clean static opacity 0.3 with no transform (measured). REACHABILITY IS NOT IN DOUBT. `.mic-btn` is the primary CTA in the idle state of index.html, visible on first paint. `.pulse` is real too — js/app.js:133 builds the answer marker as `L.divIcon({ className: 'pulse-wrap', html: '
' })`, so it renders on every result map. `.scan` is in index.html:111 during analysis. SEVERITY: major, agreeing with the auditor but at the lower end of it. Not a blocker — the app remains fully functional, and the affected marks are thin 1.5–2px ring outlines rather than large flashing areas, so this is an irritation-and-symptom-trigger problem rather than a photosensitive-seizure one. But it is a genuine accessibility inversion: the setting a vestibular/migraine user turned on specifically to protect themselves produces a full-amplitude refresh-rate flicker on the first interactive element they see, which is strictly worse than the 2.6s ease they were trying to avoid. Given a TikTok-driven, mobile-heavy launch audience where iOS Reduce Motion adoption is non-trivial, and a fix that is one declaration with zero risk to anyone else, it should not ship as-is.

Confirmed, and reproduced with real keyboard input rather than just programmatic focus. All three static claims check out: game.html:166 is the aria-hidden wrapper, media.js:45 replaces #ytMount with an iframe, and the deck counts match exactly (44 yt clips; accents 13/22, hindi-urdu 9/13, german 3/3).
