I tried to disprove it and could not. There is no `inert`, no `tabindex`, no focus trap, and no post-creation iframe manipulation anywhere in the repo. The one Tab-relevant handler (js/game.js:473) only intercepts Space/ArrowLeft/ArrowRight and never touches Tab.

Live in Chrome, after media.load() on the Kingston, Jamaica clip, 14 real Tab presses produced: 8 deck buttons, then BUTTON#boardsBtn, then a WINDOW-BLUR event ("focus left our document"), with activeElement ending as IFRAME#ytMount on www.youtube.com. The WINDOW-BLUR is the load-bearing proof that focus genuinely crosses into YouTube's document. Computed styles confirm nothing removes it from the tab order: display:block, visibility:visible, opacity:0, left:-10000px, inert:false, tabIndex:0 with no tabindex attribute.

I downgrade major to minor on two mitigating facts the auditor missed. First, the iframe is the LAST tab stop, not one inside the dock: #ytMount sits at DOM position 166, after every game control (dock at 105-125, sheet, flag chips). A keyboard user reaches and operates every control and can finish a full round before ever encountering it, so no functionality is blocked; only the tail of the traversal is broken. The auditor's framing of a user "tabbing through the dock" landing on it mid-flow overstates the disruption. Second, media.js:47 already sets disablekb:1 and controls:0, so keystrokes landing inside the frame cannot scrub, pause, or reveal the answer, which caps the blast radius. It is a genuine WCAG failure (aria-hidden containing focusable content) with a free fix, worth doing before launch, but for a touch-first TikTok audience on an inherently map-pinning game it blocks nothing and does not hold up a public launch.

The contrast defect reproduces, but the finding overstates its scope and misreports its location. WHAT HOLDS. Real, and it reproduces exactly. I tried four ways to break it and all four failed.

1. The code says what the auditor claims. `js/game.js:217` is `const placeOf = (c) => String(c.label);`, used as the only dedupe key at :223–225. The comment at :211–215 explicitly states the invariant it is meant to hold ("one game never asks the same place twice, since two identical answers in five rounds reads as a bug"). So this is a stated invariant being violated, not a matter of taste.

2. The data collision is real and is worse than reported. Confirmed against clips.js served by the running dev server on :8123, not just the file on disk:
   - hindi-urdu, all at lat 28.6139 / lng 77.209: `yt-vogXu3dUXzE` "Delhi, India", `yt-Td9sfMaU7u0` "Delhi, India", `hindi-urdu-spoken-hindi-wikipedia-indo-european-language-` "Delhi–Meerut Region, India" — three clips on one point; the label dedupe only merges the two identically-named ones.
   - spanish, all at lat -34.6037 / lng -58.3816: `yt-1tdOI0X0phE` and `yt-zcasomU6Ios` "Buenos Aires, Argentina", `spanish-argentine-spanish-reading-about-a-brazilian-to` "Argentina".

3. Nothing upstream or downstream saves it. `startGame` (:181) passes `window.CLIPS[type]` to `dealDeck` unfiltered; `playableModes` (:138) filters on deck size only; `gate` is metadata with no runtime reader. Both decks clear MIN_DECK (hindi-urdu 13, spanish 14) and both are live entries in MODES (:21, :23). Critically, none of the six colliding clips carries an `alt` array, so the `best`-center selection at game.js:492–504 always resolves to the primary center — the amber truth marker lands on the byte-identical LatLng in both rounds. There is no rounding, jitter, or offset applied to `truthMarker`.

4. Running the verbatim dealer over the real pools, 40,000 games per deck: hindi-urdu 25.9% and spanish 22.4% of games contain two rounds with an identical pin (auditor said 26.1% / 21.9%). French has two pins under 50 km in 15.4% of games (auditor said 15.2%).

The one thing that makes this worse rather than better: the project's own regression guard, `tools/deal-sim.mjs`, checks this exact property with `new Set(hand.map((c) => String(c.label))).size < hand.length` — the same label-only key. I ran it; it prints "ok" for every deck and "no game repeats a place unnecessarily". The safety net has the identical blind spot, so this would not have been caught post-launch either.

One correction to the auditor's framing: the near-miss distances should NOT be fixed with a distance threshold. The Arabic deck legitimately contains Dubai/Sharjah 22.5 km, Jerusalem/Hebron 30.0 km, and Algiers/Blida 37.3 km, which are genuinely different answers. A radius rule would collapse real variety. The provable defect is the exact-coordinate collision; the hierarchical pairs (Kingston/Jamaica, Brussels/Belgium, Marseille/Southern France) are a data problem, not a dealer problem.

Severity: major, not blocker. Nothing crashes, no data is lost, no secret leaks, scoring stays valid, and every round is still playable. It is a high-frequency polish defect confined to 2 of 8 playable decks that makes the game look unfinished and softly leaks an answer. That is worth fixing before a TikTok launch, but it does not by itself block shipping.

Every mechanical claim checks out against the file and the running server. js/clips.js:3542 does read "who": "Voice of America Swahili Service (voaswahili.com" with an unclosed paren, and :3545 is "page": "". I fetched http://localhost:8123/js/clips.js and it serves the identical line at 3542, so this is the shipping state, not a stale local file. js/game.js:527-531 assigns el.textContent = val, so the string renders verbatim into #srcWho with no escaping or repair; js/game.js:537-538 does link.hidden = !src.page, which hides the "open the original" anchor at game.html:137. I enumerated all 155 clips across all 10 decks: lang-swahili is genuinely the only one with an empty source.page. tools/check-decks.mjs does not contain the substring "page" anywhere, confirming the validator requires host/license/who but never a source URL. The deal rate is right too: dealDeck (js/game.js:216) dedupes only by label, and all 26 World Languages labels are distinct, so it is a uniform 5-of-26 draw = 19.2%. Corroborating detail the auditor missed: every other VOA-sourced clip in the app (7 of them) routes through Wikimedia Commons and carries a real Commons page URL; lang-swahili is the sole direct-from-VOA entry, which is exactly how it escaped with no page.

ONE MATERIAL CORRECTION, and it makes the finding bigger, not smaller: the truncated credit line is NOT unique to lang-swahili. Twelve clips have unbalanced parentheses in source.who, six of them in the same World Languages deck (lang-turkish, lang-thai, lang-vietnamese, lang-swahili, lang-amharic, lang-hausa). Since a game draws 5 of 26, the chance a World Languages game shows at least one dangling-paren credit is 1 - C(20,5)/C(26,5) = 76.4%, not 19.3%. The 19.2% figure is correct only for the missing-link half. The lengths of the 12 broken strings range from 36 to 77 chars while the longest intact who is 121, so this is not a fixed-length truncation but a systematic authoring slip the validator has no check for.

I also confirmed the fix is safe to apply by hand despite the "Generated data — edit through tools/" header: tools/merge-clips.mjs only splices NEW clips from data/sourced-clips.json into js/clips.js, and the swahili entry no longer exists in that JSON (grep found "voaswahili" only in js/clips.js and data/clips-backup-pre-localfix.js), so a hand edit will not be regenerated away.

Severity minor is correct and I would not raise it. Nothing breaks: the clip plays, scoring is unaffected, no console error, no layout break. Two parts. Part A is the launch-blocking-free minimum; Part B is the payoff.

PART A — stop rendering an empty or duplicated caption (js/game.js:518)

Replace:
    $('#revealHint').textContent = clip.hint || '';

with:
    const hintEl = $('#revealHint');
    hintEl.textContent = clip.hint || '';
    hintEl.hidden = !clip.hint;

This matters because `.reveal-hint` carries `margin-top: 10px` (css/style.css:596), so an emptied hint still leaves a 10px gap. `hidden` collapses it cleanly. Do this first — it makes Part B safe to apply incrementally, clip by clip, without leaving holes in the sheet.

PART B — give the 44 YouTube clips a real line, or none

In js/clips.js, for every object with `"kind": "yt"`, delete the `hint` key (or set it to a genuine payoff line). Do NOT leave the boilerplate. The `source` card already states host, creator and licence four rows down; the caption is pure repetition.

The data for a real line is already in the file: 37 of the 44 YT clips carry `gate.evidence`, an array of accent-feature strings written by the blind gate. Example, yt-OqIpz_eEaKg at clips.js:770-796:

    "gate": { "evidence": [
       "Jamaican Patois grammar and cadence",
       "Pronunciation of 'furniture', 'car', and 'baby'",
       "Regional vocabulary like 'gully water'" ] }

That is exactly the register the good local clips use ("Broad West Riding · the vowels do the work."). Take the first one or two entries, lowercase the leading character, join with " · ". For the Jamaica clip that yields "Jamaican Patois grammar and cadence · regional vocabulary like 'gully water'" — a line that tells the player what they just heard.

REACHABLE: `languages` is a shipped mode (js/game.js:28) with 26 clips against MIN_DECK=10, so playableModes() renders the "World Languages" tile. game.html serves 200 on the running dev server.

DATA: line 3771 is confirmed lang-french "r": 1500 with 7 centres (Paris, Montreal, Brussels, Geneva, Dakar, Kinshasa, Abidjan). All seven cited lines map to real clips: 3283 persian(1500), 3454 mandarin(1500), 3486 indonesian(1500), 3526 swahili(1200), 3635 russian(1500), 3771 french(1500), 3824 portuguese-brazil(1500). The languages deck is the ONLY deck with r>=1000 — every other deck maxes at r=500, so these seven are out of family with the entire rest of the app.

NUMBERS REPRODUCED INDEPENDENTLY: my own 400k-point Monte Carlo gives the French union 6.75% of earth surface (auditor: 6.7%). Best blind pin anywhere on earth = 7,596/25,000; always-Berlin = 6,821 (auditor: 6,825). 19 of 20 major world cities I tested bull's-eye the French clip: London 321km, Boston 403km, Accra 423km, Toronto 504km, NY 534km, Berlin 651km, Rome 698km, Vienna 803km, Madrid 1,022km, Algiers 1,082km, Warsaw 1,160km, Chicago 1,198km, Stockholm 1,280km, Lisbon 1,453km — all "+5,000 pts 🎯".

TWO AUDITOR ERRORS, neither load-bearing: London scores to Brussels (321 km), not Paris (343); Madrid scores to Geneva (1,022 km), not Paris (1,053). Identical verdicts.

MITIGATION THE AUDITOR MISSED (and why it doesn't save the finding): js/game.js:516 appends " · scored to Brussels, Belgium, French lives there too" whenever an alt centre wins, which honestly explains most surprising cases and makes the London example far less damning than claimed. BUT the note does not fire when the PRIMARY centre is nearest, so Lisbon on the French clip renders the bare, self-contradicting "1,453 km away → +5,000 pts 🎯" with no explanation at all.

WHY THIS IS A GENUINE DEFECT RATHER THAN TASTE: the deck already has its own tuning knob for exactly the concern that would justify a wide radius — MODE_DECAY.languages = 750 (js/game.js:128), whose comment says clips are "pinned at country centres rather than a speaker's hometown" so tight scoring "would punish a correct answer for the arbitrariness of where a country's centre falls." verdicts.why: Verified in code and confirmed reachable. api/scores.js:143-147 computes rank as a raw row count (`select=id&game_type=eq.X&points=gt.N` with `Prefer: count=exact`), so every score row that beats yours counts — including many rows from the same nickname and your own earlier better runs. api/scores.js:61-76 builds the board the opposite way: 100 rows ordered points.desc collapsed to one row per lowercased nickname, then sliced to 10. supabase/schema.sql:34-41 confirms there is no unique constraint on (nickname, game_type) and the POST path plain-inserts a row per completed game, so duplicates are guaranteed by design. js/game.js:584-585 toasts d.rank and immediately awaits loadBoard(), and toast() (js/game.js:160-166) holds for 3000 ms, so both numbers are on screen simultaneously. The auditor's scenario is actually understated: it needs one repeat player, not three — the nickname persists in localStorage (js/game.js:573) and the submitter's own better prior runs inflate their rank, so a solo player replaying a fresh deck can be told "#6" above a one-row board. At launch the player pool is small, so most submitters land inside the visible top ten, which is where the contradiction is directly readable. Severity is major, not blocker: nothing crashes, no data is lost, no security exposure — it is a visibly wrong number in the leaderboard, which is the feature the launch points at, and it worsens with replays.

The static half of the finding is accurate; the impact half — the part that makes it a blocker — is not, and the auditor's "reproduction" used a method no user has.

WHAT IS TRUE. `advance()` (js/game.js:542-550) sets `advanceLock = true`, then synchronously calls `nextRound()`, which does `advanceLock = false` at js/game.js:258. I confirmed empirically that immediately after `advance()` returns, `advanceLock === false`. The guard is dead for rounds 1-4. The auditor read the code correctly.

WHY IT DOES NOT REACH A USER. `#nextBtn` lives inside `#sheet` (game.html:127-139). The same click handler calls `setView('round')`, which sets `$('#sheet').hidden = true`, and css/style.css:67 is `[hidden] { display: none !important; }` — applied synchronously, no exit transition (the only animation, `sheetUp`, is on entry). So the button is gone from hit-testing before the handler returns. A second tap has nothing to hit.

Measured on the running site (localhost:8123/game.html, 375x812 mobile viewport). Two genuine input sequences (pointerdown/mousedown/pointerup/mouseup/click) at the button's exact centre (78, 659), 180 ms apart, each hit-tested with `document.elementFromPoint` the way the browser does:
  tap 1 -> hit "nextBtn", round 0 -> 1, label "Round 2/5", handler fired once
  tap 2 -> hit "map",     round stays 1, label stays "Round 2/5", handler fired once, roundLog.length 1
No skip. `elementFromPoint(78, 659)` returns `map` the instant advance() returns.

The auditor's exact reported symptom ("Round 1/5" -> "Round 3/5") reproduces only via `nextBtn.click()` twice — which I ran and got precisely "Round 3/5", roundLog.length 1. `HTMLElement.click()` fires handlers on elements inside a `display:none` ancestor; it bypasses hit-testing entirely. That is a scripted call, not a phone double-tap. The two paths are not equivalent and the report presents the scripted one as the human one.

The keyboard path is closed too: after the sheet hides, `nextBtn.focus()` does not take (activeElement stays `map`), so a repeated Enter cannot re-fire it. Round 5 is safe regardless — `finishGame()` never resets the lock. `advance` has exactly one caller, js/game.js:803.

THE SECONDARY CLAIM IS FALSE OUTRIGHT. "After one skip, a double-tap on lock it in logs the same round twice and doubles its points." Even under the scripted method, three consecutive `lockBtn.click()` calls left `roundLog.length` at 1 and `total` at 43 — the `roundLog.length > round` guard at js/game.js:487 fires correctly, and `#dock` is `display:none` after reveal anyway. The claimed 25,000-from-3-clips exploit does not exist.

The leaderboard framing is moot besides. It requires scripting, and anyone scripting can just `fetch('/api/scores')` with a crafted body after the 75 s token age — api/scores.js:113-116 says so in its own comment ("does not stop a patient cheater, which is why prize winners get their round logs eyeballed"). `advanceLock` is not a security boundary and was never the thing holding the leaderboard up.

RESIDUAL, GENUINE BUT MINOR. What is left is a dead guard carrying a comment (js/game.js:543-544) that claims it prevents a bug it structurally cannot prevent. Nothing is broken today because `display: none` is doing the work. The risk is a future edit: give `#sheet` an exit transition, or swap `hidden` for an opacity/visibility fade, and the real bug appears the same day while the guard that is supposed to catch it stays inert, and the misleading comment tells the next reader it is covered. That is worth the four-line fix below as cheap insurance, but it is a latent-regression and code-hygiene issue, not something that blocks a public launch. Nobody's TikTok traffic hits this.

The primary chain holds and I reproduced it end to end against the running dev server. `C:/projects/hometongue/js/game.js:193-196` — `.catch(() => { if (attempt < 3) setTimeout(() => mint(attempt + 1), attempt * 12_000 + 3_000); })` — has no else branch, so the third failure exits silently with `gameToken = null` and nothing in the UI reflects it. `gameToken` is assigned in exactly one place (line 194, confirmed by grep); there is no re-mint at `finishGame()` or in `submitScore()`, so a null token survives to the POST at line 579. `tokenAge()` (api/feedback.js:39-41) returns null for a non-string, and api/scores.js:117-120 replies 422 `invalid_token`. I verified this live: `curl -X POST http://localhost:8123/api/scores` with `"token":null` and an otherwise valid five-round body returns `{"ok":false,"error":"invalid_token"}`. Line 588-589 then maps `invalid_token` to "Scores only post for a full game, start to finish. Play one through and try again." So an honest full run is told it wasn't a full run. The path is reachable without an unplayable game: `playClip()` (js/game.js:315) explicitly tells a player "The audio is stuck this round. Lock a guess or skip ahead," and `#lockBtn` is gated on dropping a pin, not on listening, so a player on a flaky connection completes five rounds and reaches submit.

Two parts of the report do NOT survive, and they matter for how it should be described:

1. The secondary claim is wrong. "The same message appears if FEEDBACK_SECRET and SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY are both unset in production" is false. `tokenSecret()` is `FEEDBACK_SECRET || SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY`, so "both unset" implies `SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY` is unset — and api/scores.js:99 (`if (!url || !key) return ... 'not_configured'`) returns before the token check at line 117 ever runs. The client maps `not_configured` to "Leaderboard isn't set up yet, so your score didn't post," which is accurate copy. That deployment scenario is already handled correctly.

2. "Someone whose connection blipped during the first three seconds" understates what it takes. The retries fire at t=0, t=15s, and t=42s (`attempt * 12_000 + 3_000` compounding), so all three must fail across roughly 42 seconds, not three. Still very reachable on a phone in a tunnel or on a dead-then-recovering connection, but it is a 42-second outage, not a blip.

Severity: minor is correct, and I would not raise it. It is wrong error copy on a path that requires a sustained network failure at game start; the score itself is genuinely unverifiable at that point (the server's 75s minimum age means a late re-mint cannot rescue it), so no valid score is being lost that could otherwise be saved. It self-heals on the next game once the network recovers. It does not block launch, but it is cheap to fix and the current copy blames the player, which is the worst version of a failure message to ship to strangers arriving from TikTok.

Line numbers in the report have drifted (mint is at 193-196, not 184-186; the copy is at 588-590, not 579-581) but the code says what was claimed.

Confirmed by reading the code and reproducing it live at http://localhost:8123/game.html.

Every load-bearing claim checks out:
- js/game.js:291-298 — playClip() early-returns on `!media.ready()`, toasts, and registers `media.whenReady(playClip)`.
- js/media.js:157-160 — whenReady's file branch is a one-shot `loadedmetadata` listener. js/media.js:22-24 forwards only play/pause/ended/timeupdate/seeked. A grep across js/ and game.html finds no `error` listener on #clipAudio anywhere.
- media.load() is called only from nextRound() (js/game.js:274) and from the play-rejection catch (js/game.js:319), so nothing retries.
- The swap rescue at js/game.js:307-324 really is unreachable here, because playClip returns before ever calling media.play().
- sw.js:46 does say `if (url.pathname.startsWith('/clips/')) return;`.

Live repro (whole arabic deck pointed at a 404, startGame('arabic'), 4 clicks on #playBtn over ~5s): media events were exactly ["emptied","error"] — loadedmetadata never fired; readyState 0, networkState 3, error.code 4; toasts ["Clip is loading, one sec…" x4]; zero swap toasts, clipSwaps never incremented; playBtn.disabled false; listens "1:00 of listening left"; pinHint unchanged. I then waited a further 8s: no recovery, no further events.

I also ruled out the obvious ways it could be unreal. It is not masked by `preload="none"`: the explicit `audioEl.load()` at js/media.js:109 does fetch, and a healthy clip reaches readyState 4 in ~1s, so the not-ready branch is normally transient and only becomes permanent on a failed load. warmDeck() (js/game.js:237-242) does not save it — it is a fire-and-forget no-cors fetch whose failure is swallowed.

Two corrections to the auditor's account:

1. Overstated in one place. "Permanently stuck" is true of the audio, not of the player. onMapClick (js/game.js:71-80) only requires #dock to be visible, so the pin, lock and advance still work. I locked a blind guess (got "11,402 km away → +0 pts") and moved to round 2 normally. It costs a round, not the game.

2. Understated in a bigger place, which the auditor missed. Each tap leaks another one-shot `loadedmetadata` listener onto the shared #clipAudio element, and those survive the round. When the next round's clip loads successfully they all fire at once and call playClip(), so round 2 starts playing with no tap and the budget drains while the player is doing nothing — verified: round 2 auto-started (audio.paused false) and listens went 1:00 -> 0:58 -> 0:54 untouched. One failed clip therefore damages two rounds.

Confirmed, and reproduced end to end in the running site (localhost:8123/game.html) — not just a code read.

CODE CHECK. The mechanism is exactly as described, though at C:\projects\hometongue\js\game.js:189-196, not 184-187. `gameToken` is a module-level `let` (line 33). Inside `startGame()`, `const mint = (attempt) => ...` closes over nothing game-specific, assigns straight to `gameToken`, and its `.catch()` reschedules itself with `setTimeout(..., attempt * 12_000 + 3_000)`. Nothing holds that timer id and nothing cancels it; `startGame()` only sets `gameToken = null` and starts a second, independent chain. Both restart paths stay in the same page session — `#switchType` (line 806) just calls `setView('pick')` and `#againSame` (line 805) calls `startGame(gameType)`; neither reloads — so a stale chain really can outlive the game that armed it.

REPRODUCTION. I shimmed `window.fetch` in the real page to fail the first `/api/scores?start=1` and to tag every later mint, then used `document.querySelector('#submitScore').onclick()` as a probe to read whatever token the app would actually POST:

  t=0.0s  MINT #1 -> network FAIL          (game 1 = arabic)
  t=1.7s  MINT #2 -> TOKEN2-mintedAt-1.7s  (abandoned game 1, started game 2 = accents)
  t=3.7s  SUBMIT would send token = TOKEN2-mintedAt-1.7s
  t=15.7s MINT #3 -> TOKEN3-mintedAt-15.7s (abandoned game 1's retry, landing mid-game-2)
  t=18.7s SUBMIT would send token = TOKEN3-mintedAt-15.7s

Game 2's own good token was silently replaced by one minted 14s later. api/scores.js:118 measures age from that mint, so game 2 is now 14s "younger" than it really is.

I tried three ways to knock it down and none worked: there is no page reload on deck switch; nothing upstream cancels or generation-checks the chain; and the token is a plain signed timestamp (api/feedback.js:30-48), not deck-scoped or single-use, so a token from any chain is accepted for any deck — the only property that matters is when it was minted, which is precisely what gets corrupted.

WHY IT IS ONLY MINOR. The auditor's escalation math is a little off (attempt 3 fires at ~+42s cumulative, not +27s), and more importantly the harm window is narrow. The skew injected equals the retry offset (~15s, or ~42s if two attempts fail), so the score is only rejected when the second game finishes between 75s and ~75s+skew — a player doing five rounds in 75-90 seconds, already brushing the anti-cheat threshold. It also only bites when game 2's own mint SUCCEEDED; if that mint had failed too, `gameToken` would be null and the player would see the identical "full game, start to finish" message anyway, so the stale write changes nothing. And it is recoverable across games — hitting "play again" mints cleanly, since a chain dies after three attempts.

The one thing that widens it: the mint `fetch` has no timeout, unlike `sendClipReport` at line 689 which uses `AbortSignal.timeout(8000)`. A stalled (not failed) request on flaky mobile can hang for minutes, so the retry can land arbitrarily deep into a later, normally-paced game — where finishing within 75s of the overwrite is entirely ordinary.

So: a genuine defect that costs a real player one leaderboard post and shows them a message blaming them for a game they played properly. It does not block launch — no data corruption, no security impact, nothing touching the main "Read My Accent" flow, and it needs a network blip plus a fast abandon-and-restart to fire at all.

I watched it sit at `playing: true`, `budget: 60`, clock frozen — the game believed it was playing a clip that was not playing. The fix below removes both directions of the lie by driving the flag off real media events.

Severity: agreeing with major, not raising to blocker. It is the game's only difficulty constraint and it evaporates on more than half the clips in the two headline decks, which makes the public leaderboard non-comparable between mp3 and YouTube rounds and trivially farmable — but nothing crashes, no data leaks, the "Read My Accent" main product is untouched, and a launch survives it with soft scores. It does need to be fixed before the leaderboard is promoted.
verdicts.preciseFix:
Two layers. Layer A stops the unrequested playback; Layer B makes the budget unfakeable even if something else ever starts audio.

LAYER A — C:\projects\hometongue\js\media.js — never let a seek start playback the game did not ask for.

1. Add an intent flag to the yt state line (line 27):
   `let yt = null, ytReady = false, ytState = -1, ytSeeking = false, pollId = 0, apiPromise = null, wantPlay = false;`

2. In `onStateChange` (lines 50-61), make the PLAYING branch honour that intent:
   ```js
   if (e.data === S.PLAYING) {
     // seekTo() auto-plays from any state except PAUSED — cued, unstarted, post-stopVideo.
     // If the game did not ask for sound, undo it silently: no 'play' event, no poll.
     if (!wantPlay) { try { yt.pauseVideo(); } catch { /* player gone */ } return; }
     ytSeeking = false; emit('play'); startPoll();
   }
   ```
   Also add `wantPlay = false;` inside the `S.ENDED` branch, next to the existing `stopVideo()`.

3. Set the flag at every boundary:
   - `play()` (line 113): `wantPlay = true;` immediately before `yt.playVideo()`.
   - `pause()` (line 122): `wantPlay = false;` as the first statement of the yt branch.
   - `load()` (line 82): `wantPlay = false;` as the first statement, before the kind check.
   - `clear()` (line 162): `wantPlay = false;` as the first statement.

   Do NOT try to fix this by calling `yt.pauseVideo()` straight after `yt.seekTo()` inside `seek()` — the PLAYING transition is async and you get an audible blip. Gating in `onStateChange` catches it wherever it comes from.

LAYER B — C:\projects\hometongue\js\game.js — charge the budget off the real clock, not off a flag.

4. Delete line 406 entirely (`if (!playing) return;`). Seeks stay free without it: `seekTo()` already moves `lastTickT` to the target before the clock jumps (line 380), the `media.seeking()` branch on line 407 covers mid-seek, and the `'seeked'` handler resyncs it — so `delta` is ~0 across a scrub. A paused `<audio>` element firing timeupdate on seek therefore charges nothing. The `media.pause()` on line 416 becomes a no-op when already paused, which is fine.

5. Drive `playing` from the events instead of from the play() promise:
   - In `media.on('play')` (line 423), add as the first two statements:
     ```js
     playing = true;
     lastTickT = media.time();
     ```
   - In `playClip()`, remove `playing = true;` and `lastTickT = media.time();` from the `.then()` (lines 305-306), leaving `media.play().then(() => {}).catch(...)` with the catch block untouched. The `playing = false` in the catch stays, as do the `pause`/`ended` handlers on lines 428-429.

   After this, `playing` reflects what the player is actually doing in both directions, which also fixes the ▶-button lie noted above, and the pause icon stops reading "not playing" during real playback.

6. Optional but cheap belt-and-braces — bail out of scrubbing a spent round. Add as the first line of both `scrubTo` (line 434) and `seekBy` (line 393), after the `const clip = deck[round];` guard:
   `if (budgetLeft <= 0) return;`

VERIFY IN A VISIBLE TAB (this cannot be checked in a headless/hidden one — YouTube will not start playback while `document.visibilityState === 'hidden'`, which is why the repro looks dead in automation). On a round with a yt clip, never touching ▶: drag `#playerBar` and confirm the clock stays put and no sound comes out. Then press ▶ and confirm `budgetLeft` falls in real time and reaches 0 after 60 s of actual audio, and that scrubbing mid-playback still costs nothing.

verdicts.why:
Holds up. I tried to break it three ways and could not.

VERIFIED STATICALLY (note: the auditor's line numbers drift ~9 lines low; the real ones are below)

1. `playing = true` appears exactly once in the whole file — js/game.js:305, inside `media.play().then(...)`. Every other write sets it false (line 34 decl, 255 startRound, 308 catch, 428 pause, 429 ended). So the promise is the only path to true.
2. `updatePlayIcon()` (js/game.js:335) is called from exactly three places: 424 (`media.on('play')`), 428 (`pause`), 429 (`ended`). Nothing repaints after line 305. The `.then()` body is only `playing = true; lastTickT = media.time();` — no icon, no `startRaf()`.
3. So for a file clip the sequence is: 'play' event → `updatePlayIcon()` reads `playing === false` → paints ICON_PLAY → and it is never called again until 'pause'/'ended', which set `playing = false` first. The pause glyph at line 334 is unreachable for `kind:'file'`. This needs no race — it is deterministic.

VERIFIED IN CHROME (localhost:8123, real page)
Ran the crux directly on an `<audio>` element with a flag mimicking game.js's:
  `--play() called-- rs:0` → `play @0.5ms` → handler read the flag as **PLAY** → `waiting @0.5ms` → promise still unresolved.
The HTML spec forces this: `play()` queues the 'play' event task, then *separately* queues the "notify about playing" task that fires 'playing' and resolves the promise. The event can never lose that race.

The YouTube asymmetry is real too, and it is what disguises the bug: js/media.js:113-119 returns `Promise.resolve()` for yt, so `.then()` runs as a microtask before the 'play' emit that comes later from the async `onStateChange` (media.js:53). YT clips paint ICON_PAUSE correctly. That proves the pause icon is intended, not vestigial.

BLAST RADIUS CONFIRMED
Counted js/clips.js: 155 clips, 111 file / 44 yt. arabic 40/40 file, languages 26/26 file, and Arabic is the first tile on the deck picker (screenshotted). So the default entry path is 100% affected.

CSS does not rescue the scrubber either: `.player-fill` (style.css:566) has no width transition and `.player-thumb` (567-572) transitions only `transform`, not `left`. Steps are not smoothed.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE AUDITOR
The 4 fps stepping is not universal — it depends on where the promise lands relative to the first rAF tick. On the **first** play of a round it always happens: `preload="none"` (game.html:163) plus the seek at game.js:301-303 mean readyState is below HAVE_FUTURE_DATA when `play()` is called, so 'waiting' is queued and the promise resolves a network/decode delay later — far more than one frame — and `tick` (line 359) has already shut the loop down. On a resume with data buffered, the 'play' and 'playing' tasks are queued back to back and the promise microtask usually beats the next rendering opportunity, so the loop survives. So: stepping always on first play, intermittently on resume. The icon, by contrast, is broken 100% of the time.

I could not watch real playback: the owner's Chrome is minimized, so every tab reports `visibilityState:'hidden'`, where Chrome defers media decode entirely (readyState stayed 0 even for a data: URI WAV) and never fires rAF. So I confirmed the icon race by direct observation and the rAF consequence by the code path, not by eye.

SEVERITY: major, not blocker. The primary control of the main game shows the wrong state for 72% of clips, permanently, including the default deck — that is a visible polish failure on a product about to be pushed on TikTok, and it makes the tap-again-and-accidentally-pause loop possible. But audio itself is loud feedback that the clip started, the bar still advances at 4 Hz, pausing costs no budget, and a third tap resumes. Nothing is lost or unrecoverable. It does not stop a stranger from finishing a game.

(5) The comment in game.html above #clipFlag states the flag was deliberately placed below the button "so 'next clip' never sinks under the fold on a phone" -- that reasoning holds in portrait and silently fails in landscape, confirming intent rather than acceptance.

Portrait is the dominant orientation for TikTok-sourced traffic and is entirely unaffected, and the content is visibly clipped mid-row at the fold, which is a weak but real scroll affordance. It does not block launch. But it dead-ends the core game loop's only action for anyone who rotates their phone -- natural for a map game -- and the fix is a one-wrapper-div plus ~6-line CSS change, so there is no reason to ship without it.

Both halves reproduce, but the auditor mis-stated the frequency and the cause of the second half.

CONFIRMED (1) transform override. css/style.css:521 .round-pill sets `transform: translateX(-50%)` and `animation: settle 0.22s ease-out`; @keyframes settle (:202) animates `transform: translateY(8px) -> none`, which wins over the base transform for the animation's whole duration. Driving the animation by currentTime on the live page: t=0..219ms gives matrix(1,0,0,1,0,8)..matrix(1,0,0,1,0,0.0003) with left=960 on a 1920px window (exactly viewport centre = the pill's LEFT edge, not its centre); at t=221ms it flips to matrix(1,0,0,1,-84.86,0), left=875.1. In a true 390px viewport: left 195 during vs 110.1 settled — an 84.9px sideways snap at the 220ms mark. @keyframes dockUp (:545) directly below does preserve translateX(-50%), so this is an oversight, not intent.

CORRECTION A — "at the start of every round" is FALSE. js/game.js:174 does `$('#roundPill').hidden = v !== 'round' && v !== 'reveal'`, so the pill never returns to display:none between rounds and the animation never restarts. Re-ran the exact sequence on the live page: entering round 1 -> ["settle:running@0"]; round->reveal, reveal->round, and #roundNum text updates all return []. It fires ONCE per game, not five times.

CONFIRMED (2) overlap — but the auditor blamed the wrong thing and named the wrong victim. The overlap is NOT caused by the transform bug. At 390px the pill in its CORRECT settled position is top 66 -> 99.3, left 110.1 -> 279.9, while the wrapped .brand runs to bottom 93.8: that is 14.8px of overlap, WORSE than the 6.8px they measured mid-animation (where the pill sits lower at top 74). It also covers "read my accent" — the link to the other half of the app — not just "guess the voice", which is the .active self-link to the page you are already on. Swept widths with elementFromPoint: 320/360/375/390/393 all have roundPill/scoreSoFar winning the hit test over the nav links' bottom line; 412 and up are clean (brand height drops 93.8 -> 75.2 -> 66). Root cause is .modes a wrapping to 3 lines on phones, pushing .brand to 93.8px tall while .round-pill is pinned at a hardcoded top:66px.

MISSED BY THE AUDITOR: .toast (css/style.css:655 + :658) has the identical bug and a worse symptom — same translateX(-50%) + `animation: settle 0.2s`. Measured on a 386px viewport: left 193 during the animation vs 96.5 settled. Since .toast has max-width min(420px, calc(100% - 24px)), a long toast renders up to ~170px off the right edge for its first 200ms. Toasts are how failures ("This mode is still being stocked with clips") are surfaced to users.

Not a blocker: under prefers-reduced-motion the duration collapses to 0.01ms so the mis-centring is invisible; nothing is unreachable; the overlapped links still have two tappable lines above the pill. Real, worth fixing before a TikTok launch that is overwhelmingly <=400px phones, but minor.

REAL, and understated. I reproduced it on the running site at 390x844 (game.html, "accents" deck, dock visible, animations disabled so I measured the settled state, not a mid-animation frame).

Geometry confirmed. The cited lines say exactly what the auditor claims: css/style.css:531 `.dock { bottom: calc(18px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom,0px)); z-index: 15 }` and :654 `.toast { bottom: 72px; z-index: 30 }`. There is only one `.toast` rule and no media query touches either, so nothing upstream fixes it. Measured: dock y 715.9..826 (110.1 tall), toast y 709.7..772 (62.3 tall) = 56.1px vertical overlap. Horizontally the toast spans x 97.5..292.5 and the `.dock-mid` column (hint + scrubber + "listening left") is x 179..268 — entirely inside it. The auditor's 42.1px figure is the one-line case; 'Clip is loading, one sec…' measures exactly 42.1px tall, the 3-line swap message 62.3px.

The overlap is viewport-height independent. dockTop = H-128.1, toastBottom = H-72, so overlap = min(toastHeight, 54px) on every phone size. There is no screen where it does not happen.

It is worse than "paints over" — it swallows taps. `.toast` computes `pointer-events: auto` and z-index 30 over the dock's 15, and lives 3000ms (js/game.js:164). Hit-testing the dock controls with a toast up:
  #playerBar (scrubber) -> `toast` at every sampled x across its full width
  #pinHint                -> `toast` at every sampled x
  #fwdBtn (forward 5s)    -> `toast` at every sampled x
  #playBtn                -> `toast` for x >= ~101, i.e. the right third of the play button
So for 3 seconds the scrubber and the forward button are completely dead, and a third of ▶ is dead — while the message on top of them says 'Tap ▶ once more to start the sound.'

Worst case is much worse than measured by the auditor. js/game.js:269-272 unhides #eraChip for any clip with year < 1990, with the text `archival recording · <year> · accents move`. That wraps in the 89px-wide dock-mid column and takes the dock to 195.7px tall (dock top 642.3). The toast's bottom edge is then 129.7px inside the dock — the entire toast sits within the dock footprint. Any fixed bottom offset chosen against the 110px dock will still be wrong for archival clips.

Reachability is not in question. All four messages fire from `playClip()` (game.js:295, 310, 316, 322), which is bound to `#playBtn.onclick` (game.js:799), and `setView('round')` (game.js:169-177) shows `#dock` exactly when playClip is callable. 'Clip is loading, one sec…' fires whenever `media.ready()` is false — i.e. precisely the bad-network case this launch check is about.

Not a blocker: it self-clears in 3s, the map stays fully pinnable (the toast is over the dock, not the map), "lock it in" is 92% clear, and no data or progression is lost. Minor is the right call — the auditor did not inflate.

Adjacent bug found while measuring, same area, worth a separate look: `@keyframes settle` (css/style.css:202) animates `transform: translateY(8px) -> none`, which clobbers `.toast`'s own `translateX(-50%)` for the 0.2s it runs. I measured the toast's computed transform as `matrix(1,0,0,1,0,8)` with rect x 195..390 — flush against the right viewport edge — before it snaps to centre. `.round-pill` (:527) uses the same animation over the same transform and has the same flaw.

Half real, and the stated impact is wrong on both counts. The CSS facts check out: .brand (style.css:124, padding 18px 26px / 13px 15px at :682) has no top inset, .foot (style.css:663, bottom: 10px, top-level not in a media query) has no bottom inset, and env(safe-area-inset-*) appears only in .dock (:533) and .sheet (:590). But the header claim is a no-op: all pages set apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style="default", and with default (as opposed to black-translucent) iOS lays the standalone web view out BELOW the status bar, so env(safe-area-inset-top) is 0 and the logo/nav can never sit under the clock. Manifest also declares orientation: portrait-primary, ruling out the 44px landscape side insets. The footer claim is real in mechanism but overstated in effect: measured on the running site at 375x812, .foot spans 10->80px above the viewport bottom (it wraps at phone width) and the privacy link sits on the last line at 15.5->28.5px from the bottom, 44.8px wide, ~13px tall. The home indicator glyph occupies roughly the bottom 13px, so nothing is actually obscured -- the line grazes the indicator with ~2.5px clearance rather than sitting under it. What is genuinely wrong is that the last line lives entirely inside the 34px reserved band, so in an installed PWA it reads as crowded against the system indicator and the privacy link is a 13px-tall target pressed against the screen edge. Impact is confined to home-screen installs on notched iPhones; in browser tabs Safari's toolbar sits below the viewport so it never shows. Nothing is blocked: .dock and .sheet (the actual controls) already carry the inset, .hud's 52px bottom padding keeps cards clear, and privacy is also linked from the consent row at index.html:157. Cosmetic polish, not a launch blocker -- and only the .foot half is worth touching.
verdicts.preciseFix: Only one line needs to change. In C:/projects/hometongue/css/style.css, in the .foot rule at line 663, replace `bottom: 10px;` with `bottom: calc(10px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px));`. Leave .brand at line 124 and its ≤620px override at line 682 alone -- adding env(safe-area-inset-top) there is a literal no-op because index.html:19, game.html:19 and privacy.html:13 all set apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style="default", which keeps the standalone web view below the status bar and reports a 0 top inset. If you want the header to respond to the notch you would have to switch that meta to "black-translucent" first, which is a deliberate full-bleed design change, not a bug fix, and should not be done the night before launch. Regression check for the .foot change: on index.html the footer moves from 10->80px to 44->114px above the bottom; the only other fixed element in that lane is .toast (bottom: 72px, z-index 30), which already overlaps the footer's upper region today and still paints over it, so nothing new. On game.html the footer is already fully covered by .dock (z-index 15 vs .foot's 4) during rounds, so the change is invisible there. No JS touches safe areas anywhere (grep for safe-area/safeArea/visualViewport in js/ returns nothing), so there is no second code path to update.

verdicts.why:
REAL, and understated. I drove five full rounds of the World Languages deck in a real browser at 390x844 and at 375x667, instrumenting `L.Map.prototype.fitBounds` to capture the map instance and forcing `animate:false` so I measured the settled view rather than a frozen pan animation.

Result at 390x844 — the answer pin was behind the sheet in 5 of 5 rounds:
  round 1 Persian: sheet top 310, truth pin y=382 (72px under)
  round 2 Hausa:   sheet top 305, truth pin y=506 (201px under)
  round 3 Tagalog: sheet top 328, truth pin y=410 (82px under)
  round 4 Indonesian: sheet top 328, truth pin y=436 (108px under)
  round 5 Polish:  sheet top 328, truth pin y=425 (97px under)
The guess pin was visible every time (y=128-252). That is exactly the described failure: you see your own pin and a dashed line running off under the sheet.

Measured sheet height 516-539px (content 512-535) versus the 300px reserved — a 216-239px deficit. The `.sheet` rule (css/style.css:584) is `position:fixed; bottom:0; max-height:78vh` with z-index 16 over `#map` at z-index 0, so it genuinely overlays the map. There is no peek/collapse state on this element: `.card.peek` (style.css:707) and `.sheet-handle` (style.css:717) apply to `.card`, but game.html:127 is `<div class="sheet" id="sheet">` — it is not a `.card` and carries no handle, so nothing upstream shrinks or dismisses it.

It is also deterministic, not luck. Leaflet's `_getBoundsCenterZoom` offsets the center by `(paddingBR - paddingTL)/2`, so the midpoint of guess and truth always lands at `height/2 - 105` = 317 on an 844 viewport, while the sheet top is 844 - ~530 = ~314. The lower of the two pins is therefore always below the sheet's top edge regardless of clip. No `maxBounds` is set (js/theme.js only sets `minZoom`), so nothing else perturbs this.

Two corrections to the auditor's write-up, both making it worse: the visible strip between the round pill (bottom 107) and the sheet is ~198-221px, not ~270px; and at 375x667 the sheet hits its 78vh cap at 520px, leaving only a ~147px strip, where even a corrected padding cannot fit both pins clear of the round pill.

Severity is major, not blocker. The game stays fully playable, the sheet states the answer in text ("it was Polish", km, points), scoring and leaderboard posting are unaffected, and nothing errors. But the map reveal is the game's payoff and the shareable moment for the TikTok launch, and it is invisible on effectively every round on a phone.
